V
Much recent progress has been made in the study of the Buddhist history of 
both the Tangut Xia kingdom and the Mongol Yuan dynasty, especially with 
regard to the spread of Tibetan Buddhism in Central Eurasia and China proper. 
Previous scholarship on the practices of Tibetan Tantric Buddhism within and 
without the Mongol Yuan court, such as “the Secret Meditation of Supreme 
Bliss” 秘密大喜樂禪定 and “the Dance of Sixteen Heavenly Devils” 十六天魔
舞 was very limited. Thus little attention was paid to the interaction between 
Chinese and Tibetan Buddhism. Research has now demonstrated that Tibetan 
Tantric Buddhism had been spreading into Central Eurasia and China proper 
since the 11th century, and became increasingly popular and influential in the 
latter through the Uyghurs, Tanguts and Mongols, who converted to Tibetan 
Buddhism (Shen Weirong 2010b).
Countering longstanding perceptions, we now know that the practices of 
Tibetan Tantric Buddhism both within and without the Yuan court was in no 
way related solely to tantric sex, but in fact encompassed a range of practices 
and rituals connected with various traditions of Tibetan Buddhism. Both “the 
Secret Meditation of Supreme Bliss” and “the Practice of Yantïr” 演揲兒法 (the 
yogic practice of the magical wheels), which have been construed as simple 
sexual pyrotechnics, were actually part of the yogic practices of the Path with 
its Result Teachings (lam ’bras) of the Sa skya pa tradition (Shen Weirong 2013, 
Toh Hoog Teik 2007).
Indeed, Tibetan Tantric Buddhism permeated both the Mongol and Chinese 
societies of the Yuan. Its influence was not easily eradicated, despite vigorous 
attempts by Chinese literati in the late Yuan and early Ming to blame Tibetan 
Buddhism and Tibetan monks for the collapse of the Mongol Yuan dynasty. Yet 
Ming Chinese Buddhists surpassed their Yuan counterparts in the practice of 
Tibetan Tantric Buddhism. Thus it is clear that Chinese Buddhist history is best 
studied in light of the intersection of Chinese and Tibetan Buddhism.
I propose several steps in this direction:
1.	
The identification of new sources. The current inquiry on the dissemi-
nation of Tibetan Tantric Buddhism in Central Eurasia and China 
proper in the Tangut Xia kingdom and Mongol Yuan dynasty began with 
the rediscovery of Tibetan Buddhist texts in the collection of Khara 
Khoto manuscripts preserved in Russia. Failure to uncover more such 
precious materials and distinguish them from other texts of Chinese 
Buddhism would consign the broad expansion of Tibetan Tantric 
Buddhism in Central Eurasia and China proper between the 11th and

<!-- Page 309 -->

296
Shen
15th century to permanent obscurity (Shen Weirong 2010a). Texts of the 
same nature as the Khara Khoto collection are being discovered all over 
the world. Archaeologists have unearthed them in northwestern China 
and philologists have identified them in the collections of libraries and 
museums. Further research on these texts is sure to reveal new aspects 
of the Chinese and Tibetan Buddhist history of the Tangut Xia, Mongol 
Yuan and Chinese Ming dynasties.
2.	
The use of textual criticism. These newly discovered Chinese texts of 
Tibetan Tantric Buddhism require careful philological inspection. This is 
firstly because non-Buddhist Chinese sources cannot provide ready-
made and pure materials of Buddhist history. Second, it is challenging 
for Chinese historians to properly understand Chinese texts of a pure 
Tibetan Tantric Buddhist nature: the many terms of “barbarian origin” 
that appear in these texts make for difficult going. Thus, it is crucial to 
be able to deal with these kinds of Buddhist texts in multiple languages. 
Only through comparative textual criticism will we eventually be able to 
identify the author (together with the compiler and the translator) of 
the text, make clear the religious context of the composition as well as 
the process and date of the transmission, often from India to Tibet and 
China, ascertain the doctrinal classification and association of the text 
in terms of its contents, and to evaluate its reception by Chinese 
Buddhists.
3.	
The use of interdisciplinary studies. To fully exploit these Chinese 
translations of Tibetan Tantric Buddhism for the study of Chinese and 
Tibetan Buddhist history, an interdisciplinary approach is called for. 
That is, the translations ought to be studied from the perspectives of 
Sinology, Tibetology, Buddhology, and Tangut, Mongol and Uygur 
Studies.
The discovery of a large number of Chinese translations of Tibetan Tantric 
Buddhist texts as well as the knowledge of a Buddhist community of the 
Western regions in the Ming capital permit a preliminary reconstruction of the 
spread of Tibetan Buddhism in Ming China. A fuller picture of this history 
awaits an interdisciplinary and multilingual inquiry into additional Chinese 
translations of Tibetan Tantric Buddhist texts.

Chapter 11
Sino-Tibetan Buddhism: Continuities and 
Discontinuities: The Case of Nenghai’s Legacy in 
the Contemporary Era
Ester Bianchi
The interest of Han Chinese in Tibetan tantric teachings and practices is on 
the rise in contemporary China.1 To some extent, this can be seen as a continu-
ation of a phenomenon that marked the first half of the 20th century, when 
Chinese Buddhist monks sought in Tibet the Tibetan Dharma, while in China 
monks and nuns, lay people and simple Buddhist believers engaged in Tibetan 
tantric practices. Among these masters and practitioners, the “Chinese Lama” 
Nenghai 能海 (1886–1967)—to whom I have already devoted a number of 
studies—stands out as one of the most significant personalities of the Gelukpa 
tradition.2 In the present study, I shall attempt to assess Nenghai’s legacy at the 
beginning of the 21st century, focusing on the life and works of the youngest of 
his immediate disciples, Zhimin 智敏 (1927–). The contemporary “fever for 
Tibetan Buddhism” provides the general context for this inquiry.
	
“Exoteric and Esoteric Buddhism” in Nenghai’s Tradition
Nenghai’s tradition is stamped by a fusion of Chinese and Tibetan elements, 
which reveal themselves in the iconographic and architectural features of his 
1	 In the last thirty years, many Han Chinese people have shown a growing interest in Tibetan 
Buddhism, both as a form of revival of the Sino-Tibetan Buddhist traditions which were active 
before the Cultural Revolution, and as a new phenomenon involving Tibetan lamas and tulkus, 
who can count hundreds or even thousands of Han Chinese devotees, and instruct them both 
in Tibetan areas or in China proper. On the contemporary “fever for Tibetan Buddhism” among 
the Han Chinese people, see Bianchi 2014, Jones 2011, Terrone 2010, 2012, Smyer Yü 2012 and 
Yu Lingbo 2001.
2	 On Nenghai, see Bianchi 2009, Dingzhi 1995, Qingding, Longlian and Zhaotong 1997, Zhimin 
and Fu Jiaoshi 1984. On the spread of Tibetan Buddhism in China during the first half of the 
20th century, see the many contributions included in the collective volumes edited by Esposito 
2008, and Kapstein 2009; also see Bianchi 2004, Chen Bing 2008, Huang Yingjie 1995, Jagou 
2004, Tuttle 2005, and Wang-Toutain 2000.

Sino-Tibetan Buddhism
monasteries as well as in the organization of everyday life and in the religious 
calendar followed by his monastic communities. At a more profound level, his 
teachings too betray such synthesis, even if to a lesser extent. Nenghai inte-
grated the Tibetan lineage and doctrinal tradition transmitted to him by his 
Tibetan master Khangsar Rinpoche,3 with elements taken from Chinese 
Buddhism, “purely joining in one doctrine Tibetan and Chinese teachings” 
(Longlian 1946, 11–12). Thus I shall follow Monica Esposito (2008, 472),4 in 
referring to his tradition as a form of Sino-Tibetan Buddhism.
The above notwithstanding, the most common Chinese definitions of 
Nenghai’s tradition, instead of referring to Sino-Tibetan blends, all hint at a 
combination of open/exoteric (xian 顯) and tantric/esoteric (mi 密) Buddhism. 
More precisely, the tradition is discussed in terms of xianmi yuantong 顯密圓
通 (accommodating exoteric and esoteric teachings), xianmi shuangxiu 顯密
雙修 (combining exoteric and esoteric practices), xianmi yuanrong 顯密圓融 
(perfectly combining exoteric and esoteric teachings), xianmi shuanghong 顯
密雙弘 (spreading both exoteric and esoteric dharma) and so on.5 At a 
moment of intense interest in Tantras among Chinese Buddhists6 alongside a

Sørensen, these scriptures “were produced as part of a strategy of appropriation” (Sørensen

and worship of Cundī, also advocates a combination of exoteric and esoteric practice and

302
Bianchi
renewal of the conflict between xian and mi,7 Nenghai adopted Tsongkhapa’s 
lamrim perspective8 and could thus argue that
… exoteric teachings are the manifest aspect of tantric teachings, and the 
latter are the secret aspect of exoteric teachings. They are both essential. 
If one does not have knowledge of the exoteric teachings, one cannot 
comprehend the nature of tantric teachings; if one does not know the 
content of tantric teachings, one cannot understand the scope of the exo-
teric teachings. Exoteric teachings are the fundaments of tantric 
teachings, and tantric teachings are their skillful means (Dingzhi 1995, 
44).9
Since mi (esoteric/tantric) in Nenghai’s tradition almost exclusively refers to 
Tibetan Vajrayāna, Tibetan elements predominate in his highest teachings and 
practices. As for exoteric doctrines and, to some extent, also lower Tantras, 
however, Chinese and Tibetan features are fully entwined, as they are seen as 
aspects of the same broad tradition—in line with the “Pan-Asian Buddhism” 
theory which was so influential during the first half of the 20th century.10
It is precisely this twofold combination (Chinese and Tibetan, xian and mi) 
that was received in contemporary China. Immediately after the Cultural 
Revolution, Nenghai began to be regarded as one of the most important 
Chinese monks of modern times.11 This status favoured the re-emergence of 
his tradition, which began to flourish again already in the 1980s thanks to a 
number of his disciples and other masters reconnecting themselves with his

and 1997; for English translations from the Tibetan, see Cutler and Newland 2002, and 
Thurman 1992, 59–66.

His contribution to the revival of Tantrism was widely recognized, as well as his role as a

Yu Guanghui 2013, Zhao Gaiping 2009, and Zheng Jihuai 1996. Nenghai’s life was also nar-
rated in a documentary film entitled: Dangdai Xuanzang Nenghai shangshi 當代玄奘能
海上師.

303
Sino-Tibetan Buddhism
lineage. Rather than being perceived as mere representatives of the Gelukpa 
school, these masters, who are all ethnic Chinese, are commonly considered as 
belonging to the “tradition of Lama Nenghai” (Nenghai shangshi chuancheng 
能海上師傳承), thus implying its unique features not only in regard to Chinese 
Buddhism but also, implicitly, to Tibetan Buddhism.
Nenghai’s work on exoteric themes are still widely read and are easily avail-
able in Buddhist bookshops both in China and in Taiwan. On the other hand, 
his tantric works (translations and commentaries), by contrast, are reserved 
for disciples who have been bestowed the proper initiations and reside in his 
communities, a clear sign of the importance Nenghai attached to the “gradual 
path” leading to Tantras and to the secrecy of tantric practices.12 Nenghai’s 
monasteries, which began to reappear soon after freedom of religious belief 
was restored, strove to emulate the organization of the misheng jingang dao-
chang 密乘金剛道場 (tantric vajra bodhimaṇḍas) Nenghai had founded 
between 1938 and 1953 as places for doctrinal studies and tantric practice.13
Among Nenghai’s direct disciples, Renqing 仁清 (1900–1992), better known 
by his lay name Meng Wendeng 蒙文登, was formally designated as his princi-
ple dharma heir (famai chuanren 法脈傳人).14 Notwithstanding this, several 
other disciples are generally recognised as his chief successors in regard to 
tantric teachings. 
12	
In many cases, however, new and modern editions are preferred to Nenghai’s translations 
of exoteric or doctrinal works. Probably, this is a sign of the improvement in the language 
skills of authors and translators; as already noticed by Françoise Wang-Toutain, Nenghai’s 
skills in Tibetan are somewhat dubious (Wang-Toutain 2008). As for tantric works, I have 
never found any of Nenghai’s translations outside his own monasteries; reportedly, 
­Fangguang, the Taiwanese publishing house that publishes Nenghai’s exoteric works, 
some years ago tried in vain to contact Nenghai’s disciples in Mainland China in order to 
publish his tantric works (Huang Yingjie, personal communication, May 2014). To my 
knowledge, the only exception is Nenghai 1991, which was published in the collective 
work Zangmi xiufa midian 藏密修法秘典 (Secret Scriptures of Tibetan tantric practices). 
On this collective work, see Tuttle 2009. 
13	
Nenghai’s seven original misheng jingang daochang were located in the following monas-
teries: Jincisi 金慈寺 (founded in 1938, Chengdu), Yunwusi 雲霧寺 (1943, Mianzhu), 
Zhenwushan 真武山 (1944, Chongqing), Cisheng’an 慈聖庵 (1947, Emeishan), Tiexiangsi 
鐵像寺 (1948, Chengdu), Shanghai jingang daochang 上海金剛道場 (1949, Shanghai), 
and Qingliangqiao Jixianglüyuan 清涼橋吉祥律院, or Jixiangsi 吉祥寺 (1953, Wutai­
shan).
14	
Meng Wendeng was the younger brother of the renowned scholar Meng Wentong 蒙文
通 (1894–1968), professor of history at Sichuan University. He did not serve, however, as 
professor in the same department, as claimed in many sources (see for instance: <http://
www.haikong.com>) (Department of History and Culture, Sichuan University, personal 
communication, September 2014).

<!-- Page 317 -->

304
Bianchi
Qingding 清定 (1902–1999) began following Nenghai in 1942, and was later 
entrusted by him to spread tantric teachings in the South-East. Arrested in 1955 
because he had been in the Nationalist army, after his rehabilitation Qingding 
took up the role of abbot of Chengdu Zhaojuesi 昭覺寺, which he reorganized 
as a place of “tantric and pure land practices” (mijing shuangxiu 密淨雙修), 
thus introducing Nenghai’s tradition into one of the major Chinese monaster-
ies of Chengdu. 
Qinghai 清海 (1922–1991) and Jidu 寂度 (1910–2004) were responsible for 
reviving Nenghai’s tradition on Wutaishan. Qinghai remained with Nenghai 
for twenty-seven years, first at the Jincisi 金慈寺, that is, the first jingang dao-
chang located south of Chengdu, and then on Mount Wutai, where he stayed 
until Nenghai’s death. In 1978 Qinghai moved back to Wutaishan, where he set 
up a new jingang daochang in Guangzongsi 廣宗寺, and later became abbot of 
the Yuanzhaosi 圓照寺, one of the mountain’s main monasteries. Jidu 寂度 
(1910–2004) too moved to Wutaishan with Nenghai in the 1950s and returned 
there after the Cultural Revolution, taking up abbotship at Tayuansi 塔院寺 in 
1981, which was consequently partially converted from Chinese to Sino-Tibetan 
Buddhism.15 
Yongguang 永光 (1901–1988), for his part, stands out for his role in carrying 
on Nenghai’s legacy in Sichuan. He joined the master on his pilgrimage to 
Lhasa in 1928, stayed in Tibet for nineteen years and, after the Cultural 
Revolution, was appointed abbot of the Shijingsi 石經寺, the monastery on 
Longquan hills (Sichuan) which in the new era replaced the Jincisi. Finally, I 
shall mention Longlian 隆蓮 (1909–2006), the only nun among Nenghai’s prin-
cipal disciples and abbot of the nunnery in Tiexiangsi 鐵像寺, as well as the 
already mentioned Zhimin (1927–), to whom the second part of the present 
study is devoted.16
15	
For the Sino-Tibetan monasteries presently active on Wutaishan (Dabaosi 大寶寺, 
Guangzongsi, Jifusi 集福寺, Jixiangsi, Santasi 三塔寺, Shangshitasi 上師塔寺, Tayuansi, 
Wenshudong 文殊洞, Yanjiaosi 演教寺, and Yuanzhaosi,) see Bianchi 2017. The first and 
second generations of Nenghai’s disciples on Wutaishan were not only devoted to the 
establishment of new Sino-Tibetan communities, but also favoured the restoration of the 
Jixiangsi, Nenghai’s original monastery on the mountain. On Nenghai’s years spent on 
Wutaishan, see Tuttle 2006, 12–14; Wen Jinyu 2003; Zhao Gaiping 2009 and Zheng Jihuai 
1996. For a general outline of Wutaishan, see Hou Wenzheng 2003. 
16	
Among Nenghai’s direct disciples I shall also mention Chengfo 成佛, Dinghui 定慧, Jing-
tian 靜天, Liu Mingyuan 劉明淵 (Tongyi 通一), Ren Jie 任傑, Renxiang 仁祥, Wanfa 萬
法, Yongci 永慈, Xingfa 興法, Zhaotong 照通, and Zhenyi 貞意. On Qingding, see Qing-
ding n.d., Qingding 1999 and Yu Lingbo 2001, 5–10. On Qinghai, see Tuttle 2006, 14–18 and 
Zhao Gaiping 2009, 68–69. On Jidu and other of Nenghai’s principle disciples, see Liu

modern China,” see Bianchi 2016, and Qiu Shanshan 1997.

Between Past and Present: Zhimin and His Revitalization of 
Nenghai’s Tradition
Of the original misheng jingang daochang founded by Nenghai, only a few are 
currently active. These include Tiexiangsi in Chengdu,17 Jixiangsi 吉祥寺 on 
Wutaishan,18 and to some extent the Shanghai jingang daochang 上海金剛道
場19, although they cannot be described as being in a phase of significant 
growth or development. In order to appreciate the contemporary revival of 
Nenghai’s tradition, greater attention should be focused on new locations. A 
prominent example is the Duobaojiangsi 多寶講寺, which is directed by Lama 
Zhimin (Zhimin shangshi 智敏上師), presently one of the leading Buddhist 
masters of the Zhejiang area.20 This monastery is clearly modelled on the 
Jincisi, but at the same time it reveals some signs of discontinuity, particularly 
in the introduction of new elements which are alien to the original doctrinal 
lineage. This seems to me an effort to revitalize and ‘rejuvenate’ the tradition, 
thus safeguarding its survival in the contemporary era.
A native of the city of Hangzhou, Zhimin (1927–) grew up in Shanghai. He 
became interested in Buddhism at a young age and, when he was a student at 
Datong University, studied under the renowned Buddhist scholar and lay 
17	
On the Tiexiangsi, see Bianchi 2001.
18	
The Jixiangsi, located at 2440 meters above sea level, is the monastery where Nenghai 
chose to spend his last years of life. In 1958 the Buddhist review Xiandai foxue 現代佛學 
reported positively on the activities of Nenghai’s community. See Bianchi 2017.
19	
The Shanghai jingang daochang was abruptly closed in the mid-1950s and has not yet 
been rehabilitated as a monastery. At present, it is a lay Buddhist association, where five 
to ten lay people gather every morning in order to carry on Nenghai’s tradition. For years 
these individuals have requested that the Shanghai municipality allow monks from other 
jingang daochang to move in permanently in order to revive the monastic community, 
but permission has not been granted yet (Zhao Lingen, personal communication, Decem-
ber 2013).
20	
Zhimin is the subject of a previous study of mine (Bianchi 2006). On this master, also see 
Jiang Jianchang n.d. Zhimin has held various public positions over the years, among 
which: President of the Sanmen County Buddhist Association, Permanent member of the 
Sanmen County Government, Deputy Director of the Taizhou Buddhist Association, and 
Secretary General of the Zhejiang Buddhist Association. In addition, since the 1990s 
Zhimin has been invited to transmit the dharma in Australia and Hong Kong, has main-
tained relations with Taiwanese Buddhist masters (namely: Richang 日常, abbot of Feng-
shansi 鳳山寺, and Haitao 海濤, founder of Taiwan Life TV; the latter visited the 
Duobaojiangsi during one of his trips to China). In 1994, the Taiwanese Buddhist founda-
tion Fotuo jijin hui 佛陀基金會 granted to Zhimin significant funding with which to 
finance the publication of sacred texts and other materials (e.g., the newsletter Duobao­
jiangsi tongxun 多寶講寺通訊).

<!-- Page 319 -->

306
Bianchi
Buddhist Fan Gunong 范古農 (1881–1951). In 1953, at the Shanghai jingang dao-
chang, Zhimin encountered Nenghai for the first time.21 This event marked a 
radical shift in his life: he was bestowed the “five great initiations” (wubu 
daguanding 五部大灌頂) of Vajrabhairava, followed the teachings and prac-
tices, and resolved to enter the monastic order. The following year Zhimin 
moved to Mount Wutai and took novice vows under Qingding and full ordina-
tion with Nenghai as the primary master of the ritual. He spent the next 
thirteen years on the mountain, eventually becoming one of the principle dis-
ciples and main heirs of Nenghai. In 1962, he was in charge of the courses on 
abhidharma at the Jixiangsi; he thus could inquire into the Abhidharma­
kośaśāstra (Jushe lun 倶舍論) by Vasubandhu, that was to become the in­spi­- 
rational work of his mission as an educator.22
After the long interruption of religious life during the Cultural Revolution,23 
Zhimin was officially rehabilitated in the early 1980s. He became a researcher 
at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences and subsequently taught at vari-
ous institutes of Buddhist Studies.24 Finally, in 1992 he assumed the office of 
abbot of the Duobaojiangsi, fulfilling his desire to found his own Institute of 
Buddhist Studies.
In Zhimin’s account, during the years he spent on Wutaishan Nenghai rec-
ognized his achievements and qualified him to transmit the dharma. 
Nevertheless, in the new era Zhimin felt the need to complete his training in 
tantric studies in order to obtain the formal title of tantric master; for this 
­reason, he established contacts with Daji 大吉, abbot of the Namo 南無 mon-
astery in Kangding, who met Nenghai when he was young and followed him to 
Lhasa in 1940; Daji’s previous incarnation had taught Tibetan language to 
21	
By 1951 Nenghai had already transmitted the “Vajrabhairava five great initiations” 
(Daweide wu bu daguanding 大威德五部大灌顶) to more than three hundred people 
in Shanghai; according to his biography, “the initiation ritual lasted ten days,... which were 
followed by three more days of teachings” (Dingzhi 1995, 39).
22	
Zhimin’s ideas on Buddhist education were inspired by the following sentence in the 
Abhidharmakośaśāstra: Fo zhengfa you er wei jiao zheng wei ti 佛正法有二謂教證為體 
(T 1558: 152b). Accordingly, Zhimin’s teaching strategies aim at combining doctrinal stud-
ies and religious practice (Zhimin n.d.1, Zhimin 1998a and Zhimin 1998b). Zhimin wrote 
essays and commentaries on the Abhidharmakośaśāstra; an example is Zhimin n.d.2.
23	
In 1966, the Jixiangsi was subjected to repeated attacks. Nenghai himself was badly tor-
tured and Zhimin was harassed and beaten until he lost mobility in his legs. Zhimin spent 
the following years in Shanghai with his father, himself a victim of the government cam-
paigns and labelled as a “reactionary academic authority.”
24	
Namely: Xiamen’s Nanputuo 南普陀, Xindu’s Baoguangsi 寶光寺 and Putian’s Guang-
huasi 廣化寺.

Nenghai in Kangding during the years 1926–1927. In 1995 Daji conferred to him 
the title of vajra-ācārya (jingang asheli 金剛阿闍黎) and tasked him with car-
rying on Nenghai’s mission in spreading Gelukpa teachings in China. In 
September 1997, Zhimin returned to Kangding and, within three weeks, Daji 
had transmitted to him more and new teachings and empowerments. In the 
following decade, Zhimin returned to Kangding yearly (at least when his physi-
cal condition allowed it) and introduced to Daji his most gifted disciples.25 
Among them is Zongzhou 宗宙, Zhimin’s designated heir and the only one of 
his disciples to have received the title of lama (lama wei 喇嘛位) that allows 
him to transmit tantric teachings.
Zhimin founded two monasteries which bear the same name: the above-
mentioned Duobaojiangsi in Sanmen county, inaugurated in 1992, and 
Shangyu’s Duobaojiangsi, where he moved in 2007 while retaining the role of 
abbot at both locations.26 At the beginning of the 1990s Zhimin was invited to 
assume the leadership of the first monastery by his own tonsure master 
Qingding, who was a native of Sanmen county; Zhimin accepted the position 
and created a “bodhimaṇḍa of joint study and practice” (jiaoxue yu xiuxing 
xiang jiehe de daochang 教學與修行相結合的道場), as was Nenghai’s aspira-
tion. Today the two monasteries are home to a community of approximately 
eighty monks and twenty nuns, the latter residing outside the Shangyu monas-
tic establishment.27 Both sites display a number of features that identify them

During my visits to the Namosi in the summer of 1999 and in February 2015, I met Chinese

26	
When asked about this, Zhimin explained that the Shangyu monastery is located in a 
quieter place, which is geomantically better positioned than the monastery in Sanmen. In 
addition, Shangyu is a big city, well connected with Hangzhou and Shanghai, thus making 
it easier for his disciples and devotees to visit him (Zhimin, personal communication,

27	
The first Duobaojiangsi is situated in Gaojian village (Sanmen county, Ningbo). It dates to 
the Eastern Jin dynasty, when it was founded as Longxiangyuan 龍翔院. In 1172 it was 
transferred to Longtou hill and assumed the present name; at that time, it became a 
branch of the Guoqingsi 國清寺 of Mount Tiantai 天台. During the 20th century the 
monastery suffered several damages and fell into disrepair; when it was restored in 1985, 
on the initiative of Qingding, only the main hall of the ancient complex had been pre-
served. In 1994 a consecration ritual was held by Qingding and Zhimin; on that occasion 
Zhao Puchu 趙樸初 (1907–2000), President of the Chinese Buddhist Association, wrote 
the characters for the monastery main sign. In 2001, a stūpa for Qingding relics was inau-
gurated on Longtou hill. As for the Shangyu Duobaojiangsi, it is a new monastic 
compound, whose construction was undertaken by Zhimin in 1999 and which in 2007 was 
officially registered as an “open monastery.” See Bianchi 2006, Jiang n.d., Zhimin 1999, 
other informative material and brochures available on the spot, and the monastery’s

<!-- Page 321 -->

308
Bianchi
as Sino-Tibetan Buddhist monasteries. Despite their rich architectural and 
iconographic elements derived from the Chinese tradition, these monasteries 
clearly distinguish themselves from other monasteries in China.28 For instance, 
reminiscent of Tibetan monasteries, most of the buildings have red walls with 
golden roofs topped with a dharma wheel. Moreover, halls display Tibetan 
liturgical objects and musical instruments, and are furnished with rows of 
benches on either side, because Tibetan Buddhist chanting requires a seated 
position. Finally, the sacred images by and large reference the Tibetan Buddhist 
pantheon and lineages, and include Yellow Mañjuśrī and Yamāntaka-
Vajrabhairava, the two principal meditation deities (yidam) in the Nenghai 
doctrinal tradition, as well as that of Tsongkhapa and his disciples, and those 
of Khangsar, Nenghai and Qingding.
In the monastic communities led by Zhimin, as in all other jingang dao-
chang, compliance with the vinaya requirements is a core principle. Daily life 
and the religious calendar are organized according to the rules and regulations 
enshrined in the ancient Buddhist behavioural codes, which were of para-
mount importance to Nenghai.29 For example, monks are required to 
participate in a bimonthly recitation of the Prātimokṣa and go on a three-
month summer retreat, as is prescribed by the vinaya canonical texts; in 
website: <http://www.duobaojiangsi.com>. This description also takes into account my 
personal experience within the monastery during the summers of 2000 and 2001, and the 
interviews I conducted on those occasions as well as on another visit in December 2013. 
28	
These features are common to all the monasteries associated with Nenghai’s jingang dao-
chang. On this issue, see Bianchi 2001, 57–69, 316–317. A similar mixture of Chinese and 
Tibetan architectural and iconographic elements is also shared by the monasteries 
belonging to the Tibetan Buddhist tradition founded in Chinese territory during the Qing 
dynasty. Particularly see Chayet 1985, Lessing 1942 and Mortari Vergara Caffarelli 1982.
29	
Not only did Nenghai write prolifically on this topic (e.g. Nenghai 1987), he committed 
himself and his disciples to strict observance of the rules; in the Jincisi he even founded a 
hall exclusively devoted to vinaya studies (Xuejietang 學戒堂). Nenghai connected this 
preoccupation with the importance held by monastic discipline in Tsongkhapa’s tradi-
tion. Interestingly enough, he preferred to refer to the texts of the Dharmaguptaka 
(T 1428), that is, the version followed in China, rather than to those of the Mūlasarvāstivādin, 
which are followed by Tibetan Buddhists. On the role of monastic discipline in Nenghai’s 
works and tradition, see Bianchi 2009, 310, 313–314, 319–322; Wen Jinyu 2003; also see 
Blofeld 1988, 39–40 (on strict vegetarianism and respect of vinaya regulations in Neng-
hai’s monasteries on Mount Wutai). On vinaya in Tsongkhapa’s works and personal life, 
see Thurman 1992, 12, and Wang-Toutain 2000, 723.

addition, it is forbidden for whoever enters the monastic walls to eat after 
noon, and younger monks are not allowed to converse alone with women.30
As for daily practice, at 3:30 a.m. the monks gather in the main hall for the 
morning chanting session (zaoke 早課), which lasts two to three hours.31 This 
ceremony focuses on the Shangshi gong 上師供 (Offering to the Lama),32 a 
fundamental guruyoga text in the Tibetan liturgy, which is recited in combina-
tion with other texts depending on the level achieved by individual monks. 
“Higher acolytes” (shangzuo 上座) devote themselves to the Yamāntaka-
Vajrabhairava texts:33 the extended version of the Daweide shisanzun yigui 大
威德十三尊儀軌 (Vajrabhairava Sādhana of Thirteen Deities)34 and the brief 
versions of the Wu da jingang yigui 五大金剛儀軌 (Sādhana of the Five Great 
Vajras).35 Those who have not been initiated into Highest Yogatantras (i.e. 
zhongzuo 中座, “intermediate acolytes,” and xiazuo 下座, “lower acolytes”), 
however, after the Shangshi gong engage in chanting of the Wuzi zhenyan 五字
真言 (Five Syllables Mantra),36 a lower tantric practice devoted to yellow 
Mañjuśrī, and the Yaoshi jing 藥師經 (Sūtra of Bhaiṣajyaguru).37 Morning 
hours are usually reserved for classes at the Institutes of Studies located in the 
two monasteries or, during the summer retreat, to public lectures to which lay 
practitioners and other devotees are admitted; on those occasions, favourite

modelled on monks’ debates in the great Gelukpa institutions. Afterward, the 
evening chanting session (wanke 晚課) takes place: lasting two to three hours, 
in the case of intermediate and lower acolytes it focuses on the recitation of 
the Wuzi zhenyan, while higher acolytes devote themselves to the Daweide 
yizun yigui 大威德一尊儀軌 (Sādhana of the Solitary Hero Vajrabhairava).40 As 
for other celebrations of the religious calendar, the eighth day of each lunar 
month is dedicated to tsog (huigong 會供), namely, a Tibetan tantric rite for 
presenting offerings.41 Finally, during the first week of the first month of the 
year Zhimin confers tantric initiations to monks, nuns and lay people alike.
The above overview of the tantric teachings practiced in the monastery has 
revealed a clear distinction between disciples who have access to highest 
tantric practices and those who do not. Lay people can only receive basic 
teachings42 and the transmission of lower Tantras (especially the Wuzi zhen-
yan), as is the case with monks and nuns who have just entered the monastic 
order. As explained by Zhimin, “With this practice, one can attain rebirth in a 
pure land, but to attain Buddhahood in this very life, one has to be initiated 
into the highest Tantras” (Zhimin, personal communication, December 2013). 
As a rule, in Zhimin’s monasteries Highest Yogatantra initiations are reserved 
for monastics and take place after three years of practice of the lower Tantras. 
At this point, the sādhanas of the “generation stage” of Yamāntaka-Vajrabhairava 
are imparted, whereas the “completion stage” is transmitted by Zhimin to a

select group of disciples.43 This gradual transmission of tantric teachings, 
which is inspired by the Tibetan lamrims (stages of the path) and is typical of 
the Gelukpa approach, clearly echoes Nenghai’s teaching strategies and is 
strictly applied by Zhimin.
Zhimin is the youngest among Nenghai’s direct disciples to be active after 
the Cultural Revolution, and the last one still alive. He stands out for his efforts 
to ensure the continuity of his master’s tradition, encouraging its growth and 
development. Other disciples have focused on the preservation of the purity of 
the doctrines and practices transmitted to them by Nenghai. Zhimin, by con-
trast, attempts to incorporate Nenghai’s tradition with new transmissions. 
Thus, in his monasteries Nenghai’s original tantric teachings are combined 
with select but significant new practices. While these practices belong to the 
same Gelukpa lineage as Nenghai’s, they are absent from the corpus of writings 
translated and transmitted by him. As Zhimin explained:
I believe that the duty of a disciple is to continue his master’s work. It 
took months for Nenghai to reach Tibetan areas, whereas we can go to 
Kangding on comfortable buses and reach Lhasa in a few hours by plane. 
We need to consider what our ‘venerable lama’ (lao shangshi 老上師) 
would do if he were in our place and act accordingly. His tradition is still 
alive, why should we keep it untouched and unchanged as if it were in a 
museum? (Zhimin, personal communication, July 2001).
	
Concluding Remarks
In a recent study, I considered the re-emergence of Nenghai’s monasteries as a 
sign of the increasing interest in Tibetan Buddhism shown by Han-Chinese in 
the contemporary era (Bianchi 2014). In these terms, the broader phenomenon 
of the ‘fever for Tibet’ not only comprises the newly founded centres of prac-
tice in Khams and Amdo or the Tibetan inspired Buddhist milieux located in 
Chinese cities, but also the revival of the Sino-Tibetan traditions of the first 
half of the 20th century. The former are headed by or refer to Tibetan masters 
and are thus likely to be perceived as ‘more Tibetan’, whereas the latter are 
43	
Highest Yogatantra practice comprises two stages: generation and completion. In both 
cases the practitioner is transformed into the meditation deity, but in the generation 
stage (associated with the “relative truth”) transformation is said to be only visualized, 
whereas during the completion stage (“absolute truth”) it is believed to be actually expe-
rienced. See Achard 1998, and Cozort 1986, 179–180 and passim.

<!-- Page 325 -->

312
Bianchi
preferred by their own Chinese devotees because they are felt to be more 
‘familiar’, easier to understand and accept.44
Nonetheless, it is clear that in Nenghai’s milieux the prevailing idea is not so 
much that of being affiliated with Tibetan Buddhism, but that of the co-pres-
ence of esoteric and exoteric teachings. For instance, echoing Nenghai, Zhimin 
claims:
Tantric teachings comprise exoteric Buddhism, whereas the latter does 
not include the former. Exoteric teachings are a part of tantric Buddhism, 
and thus tantric Buddhism cannot exist without exoteric Buddhism. On 
the other hand, the latter can also exist without the former. In other 
words: tantric Buddhism is ‘the second floor’ of the building, and exoteric 
Buddhism is the first floor. The first floor is necessary, only if there is the 
first floor the second floor can exist. But esoteric Buddhism is higher and 
attainment of Buddhahood is faster by it (Zhimin, personal communica-
tion, December 2013).
The exoteric/esoteric binary, which goes hand-in-hand with the idea of a meld-
ing of Chinese and Tibetan doctrinal aspects, clearly distinguishes Nenghai’s 
followers from other actors in the contemporary “Fever for Tibetan Buddhism.” 
At the same time, it reconnects them with Nenghai’s original idea of a “tantric 
revival” (mijiao fuxing 密教復興) to be carried out to create a more complete 
form of Buddhism in China. In such light, this Sino-Tibetan Buddhism can be 
considered as a tradition in its own right, where the Gelukpa component is a 
part of the whole and not its major characteristic. This helps to explain why 
little has been done to integrate Sino-Tibetan Buddhism and other Tibetan 
teachings. This reluctance to receive new transmissions is evident in the more 
“conservative” monasteries such as the Shijingsi and the Tiexiangsi, but it is 
found too in Zhimin’s communities, where only a handful of new doctrines 
and practices have been incorporated. As seen, the latter, moreover, were all 
taken from the same masters’ linage as Nenghai’s.
This impermeability of Nenghai’s tradition might call into question its 
very survival. Huang Yingjie 黃英傑 has noted that the subject of “initiation” 
(guanding 灌頂) is seldom discussed in Nenghai’s works and translations.45 
The few texts that take up the topic provide only a basic understanding of

­initiation, without specifically discussing the procedures of esoteric transmis-

master, as without being qualified to bestow initiation he was unable to trans-
mit the tantric teachings that Nenghai had conferred to him. That he requested 
the qualification from a master of the same lineage as Nenghai indicates his 
loyality to the master’s tradition; at the same time, it points to the idea that he 
was aware of the deficiency of the qualification to transmit the dharma that 
Nenghai had conferred to him.
Hence, unless Nenghai’s spiritual heirs follow in Zhimin’s steps, the master’s 
Sino-Tibetan Buddhism appears to be in mortal danger. Zhimin’s example is 
already followed by a number of second and third generation disciples of 
Nenghai in some Wutaishan monasteries belonging to the Sino-Tibetan tradi-
tion, a topic that I have explored in another study.47 This choice, however, is 
apt to be regarded as a betrayal of the master’s tradition by his more conserva-
tive and loyal followers.

321
Significance of the Ārya-tattvasaṃgraha-sādhanopāyikā
Chapter 12
On the Significance of the Ārya-tattvasaṃgraha-
sādhanopāyikā and Its Commentary
Jacob P. Dalton
In 1998, at the Eighth Seminar of the International Association of Tibetan 
Studies in Bloomington, Indiana, Kimiaki Tanaka brought to the atten-
tion of scholars a set of Tibetan sādhanas from Dunhuang based on the 
Sarvatathāgata-tattvasaṃgraha. Two years later, Tanaka published the 
results of his research, along with a complete transcription of the Ārya-
tattvasaṃgraha-sādhanopāyikā.1 With the present paper, I would like to build 
on Tanaka’s pioneering work by adding a few of my own preliminary observa-
tions regarding these same ritual materials. First, some remarks will be offered 
on the dates of the relevant manuscripts and of the text itself. This will be 
followed by a brief overview of the sādhana’s ritual structure and its possible 
relevance to the tantric traditions known to have circulated in eighth-century 
China and in today’s Japanese Shingon School.
I	
The Corpus of Manuscripts
The text standing at the center of the circle of manuscripts under discussion is 
titled the Ārya-tattvasaṃgraha-sādhanopāyikā. This title appears in the colo-
phon to the one complete copy of the work that we have. PT792 and ITJ551 
comprise this original manuscript in four densely packed poṭhi-style folios. 
Another copy (missing probably just its first folio) of more-or-less the same 
text appears in a poṭhi now found scattered across three manuscripts: ITJ417, 
1	 See Tanaka 2000. Unfortunately for me, the two relevant fifteen-page chapters are in Japanese. 
Tanaka was kind enough, however, to append to his book an English summary. It seems 
Tanaka’s central point was to deploy the early ninth-century imperial translation reforms that 
took place under the Tibetan emperor Khri lde srong btsan in order to date one of the 
Dunhuang STTS-based sādhanas to before these reforms and another to after them. All of this 
says little, of course, about the dates of the various manuscripts in which the texts were pre-
served, and these are what the present paper now turns to consider.
©	 koninklijke brill nv, leiden, 2017 | doi 10.1163/9789004340503_014

<!-- Page 335 -->

322
Dalton
PT300, and ITJ519.2 In fact, this original poṭhi contained two distinct texts, the 
first being the copy of our sādhanopāyikā, the second a closely related STTS-
based sādhana titled the Śrī-vajrahūṃkara-sādhanopāyikā that seems to 
reflect a slightly later period and adds some helpful details where ours does 
not. But for present purposes, I largely set this second text aside.
In addition to these two nearly complete copies of our sādhana, we have 
two manuscripts with just one folio each—PT265 and 271—that appear to rep-
resent two further copies of the same sādhana, and finally there is ITJ448, 
consisting of six densely packed folios that, when taken together with the addi-
tional folio at PT270, offer still another copy that is incomplete at its beginning 
and end. This last copy is of particular interest, for it is in the same hand, on the 
same sized paper, and in the same concertina-style format as an extensive 
commentary to our sādhana found in ITJ447. In addition to this twenty-six 
folio-side commentary, ITJ447 also includes twenty-three folios of appended 
notes relating to the same STTS-based ritual system.
These then comprise the corpus of manuscripts under discussion. Of course, 
there are other STTS-related texts from Dunhuang, but these form a tightly 
related group focused around what was originally a single text:
I.	 Ārya-sarvatathāgata-tattvasaṃgraha-sādhanopāyikā:
1) Pelliot tibétain 792 / IOL Tib J 551: Complete copy.
2) ITJ417 / PT300 / ITJ519: Almost complete (missing first folio).
3) PT265: Single folio from the middle of the sādhana.
4) PT271: Single folio from near the end.
5) ITJ448 / PT270: Another copy, with various appended notes—miss-
ing several folios from both beginning and end.
II.	Commentary to the Tattvasaṃgraha-sādhanopāyikā:
ITJ447: Same paper and handwriting as ITJ448 (missing first folio).
2	 ITJ519 has gone missing from the British Library, but a transcription is thankfully available in 
Tanaka’s article. Note too that in my entry on ITJ417 in Dalton and van Schaik 2006, I mistook 
the first folio (f. 38 using the British Library’s page numbers) of ITJ417/2 for the first folio of 
ITJ417/1. This means that ITJ417/1 is missing its first folio and not its second.

II	
Dating the Manuscripts
With some idea of the manuscripts involved, we may now turn to the question 
of dating them. We will examine the manuscripts one-by-one, beginning with 
our one complete copy of the sādhana: PT792/ITJ551 [figure 12.1]. This is also, 
incidentally, our only copy with a colophon, and it reads as follows:
This was written in payment for the monk Byang cub dbyangs. I pray that 
in this lifetime he be quickly purified of any illness, live a long time, and 
act for the benefit of sentient beings. And in future times, may he melt 
away and cleanse all his sins, then spontaneously accomplish the three 
bodies. May it be so for a spiritual mentor. This was edited [all] at once.”3
Whoever penned this, then, did so not for himself, but for a mentor, him­self a 
monk with an interest in studying or practicing the popular Tatt­va­saṃgraha- 
sādhana.
About the hand used in this manuscript, we can make a few observations. 
First, we see a careful hand, as indicated by several factors:
• tightly controlled vowel markers,
• letters of an even size,
• ba-s often (though not always) with all four sides still intact, that is, they
have not been reduced to triangles, or even circles, to save time, and we see
3	 PT792, 3r.3–4: ban de byang cub dbyangs kyi sku yon du bris te/ sku tshe ’di la snyun myur du 
byang ba dang tse ring zhing sems chan gyi don bya ba dang ma ’ongs pa’I dus du myi dge ba 
thaMs chad ni bzhu bsal nas sku gsum lhun gyis grub par smon te/ dge ba’I bshes nyen du shog 
shig // /lan cig zhus/.

<!-- Page 339 -->

326
Dalton
the same patience in the ga-s, which similarly maintain their full square 
top halves,
• lines of an even width throughout,
• descenders that remain quite vertical.
Overall, then, it is may be described as a relatively square style, with the cor-
ners of each letter sharp and the final descenders relatively short, so that the 
individual letters form a generally square shape.
All of this suggests that we have here a good example of what Sam van 
Schaik, in his groundbreaking 2013 article, “Dating Early Tibetan Manuscripts: 
A Paleographical Method,” has labeled the “square style” of the Tibetan impe-
rial period. As van Schaik observes, this is the same style typical of the 
manuscripts containing the Old Tibetan Annals and other historical or semi-
historical texts (though notably not the post-imperial-period manuscript 
containing the Tibetan Chronicle), as well as legal texts, dice divination texts, 
and texts on funerary practices—all, in other words, the kinds of works one 
might expect to be significant during the Tibetan imperial period, but not the 
professionally scribed Buddhist sūtras (van Schaik 2013, 121). Such texts often 
exhibit many, if not all, of the elements we have noted above in PT792/ITJ551— 
a careful hand, with relatively controlled vowel-markers, letters of even size, 
square ba-s, lines of an even width, and vertical descenders. Their letters also 
give the impression of a square, with sharp corners, short descenders, and gen-
erally square shapes.
We might also note the double-tsheg-s that appear with remarkable regular-
ity throughout PT792/ITJ551. Occasionally one may be reduced to a single 
tsheg, but even then, it is often the lower tsheg that is retained, i.e. one that 
appears below the headline. Elsewhere I have highlighted the fact that manu-
scripts with a large number of double tshegs are more likely to date to the ninth 
century than the tenth (Dalton, forthcoming).
Finally, we may add that throughout PT792/ITJ551, the contracted genitive 
markers (འི་) are attached to the immediately preceding syllable. This is signifi-
cant, for, as Brandon Dotson has observed,
Mid-eighth and early-ninth-century documents from both central Tibet 
and Dunhuang tend to attach the ’i and ’is forms of the genitive and 
ergative particles to the preceding syllable. Tenth-century Dunhuang 
manuscripts, on the other hand, usually insert a tsheg to mark ’i(s) as a 
separate syllable. For the period from the late Tibetan Empire to the early 
Guiyijun, that is, mid-ninth to late ninth century, the data tends to be 
mixed” (Dotson 2016, 147).

<!-- Page 340 -->

327
Significance of the Ārya-tattvasaṃgraha-sādhanopāyikā
As with the double tsheg, then, the attached genitive is another indicator, 
within the Dunhuang collections at least, that can suggest an earlier date. In 
short, if we are to attempt to date this PT792/ITJ551 on the basis of its handwrit-
ing, then all indications (the square style, the double tsheg-s, and the attached 
genitive particles) suggest a ninth-century date rather than a tenth-century 
one.
With this in mind, we turn to our next copy of the STTS sādhanopāyikā—the 
manuscript that is now divided between ITJ417, PT300, and ITJ519 (which I 
shall henceforth refer to as just ITJ417) [figure 12.2]. Now that we have estab-
lished some points of analysis, we can see quite quickly that we have in this 
manuscript another example of van Schaik’s early “square style.” When com-
pared with PT792, which we have just finished examining, we can see that 
ITJ417 exhibits all of the same characteristics—a careful hand, square letters, 
as well as the double tsheg-s and attached genitive particles. Here again, then, 
we seem to have a ninth-century manuscript. Our two most complete copies of 
the STTS sādhana both appear to have been penned in the ninth century.
Next, we have the two single-folio manuscripts: PT265 and PT271. PT265 
[figure 12.3] has a somewhat different, perhaps more relaxed, handwrit-
ing compared to PT792/ITJ551 and ITJ417. It is similar in many regards to the 
“square style,” but it may have been written more quickly; its ba-s are still gen-
erally four-sided, its lines are still of a relatively even width, and the descenders 
are still generally vertical, but the vowel-markers are somewhat less controlled, 
and the letters are not of such even size. And while the letters are still of a rela-
tively square shape, the descenders are longer, and the corners are considerably 
more rounded. In all of these ways, we might suggest the hand resembles van 
Schaik’s imperial-period “sūtra style,” the style used by the professional scribes 
of the imperial period. However, this “sūtra style,” being highly regularized, is 
not always reliable. Take ITJ98 [figure 12.4], for example: The manuscript con-
tains a copy of the Prajñāpāramitānāya-śatapañcāśatikā written in a generally 
similar style. Unlike the “sūtra style” manuscripts highlighted by van Schaik, 
which date to the imperial period, however, this manuscript likely dates to the 
tenth century; it is in a concertina format and, most significantly, bears the 
Stein site number Ch. 73.iii, which Takeuchi has identified as a bundle con-
sisting almost entirely of tenth-century manuscripts (Takeuchi 2012, 209–211). 
Given the existence of this and other tenth-century manuscripts in similar 
“sūtra style” hands, we should consider the possibility that the professional 
scribal training that one imagines may have defined the style might well have 
continued into the tenth century. If so, then van Schaik’s “sūtra style” would 
represent a less reliable tool for dating manuscripts than his “square style.” 
All this said, PT265 does exhibit many midline tsheg-s (though not double

<!-- Page 341 -->

328
Dalton
tsheg-s), and the genitive markers are all attached, both factors that suggest a 
ninth-century date for the manuscript, even if our judgement is somewhat less 
secure than it was for PT792/ITJ551 and ITJ417.
Turning to PT271 [figure 12.5], we find a somewhat more complex picture. 
On the recto, the hand is even less careful, the vowel-markers uncontrolled, 
and the tsheg-s drift between single and midline.4 Midway through the verso, 
however, the script changes into van Schaik’s square style. It is unclear whether 
the shift is the result of a different scribe taking over. The square style emerges 
quite suddenly on line three, and double tsheg-s begin to appear almost imme-
diately (with midline tsheg-s continuing too). From the point of the shift, too, 
there begins to be more evidence of an aging split-nib pen, with a faint parallel 
line appearing on the horizontal strokes of some vowels. On the other hand, 
there is some evidence of a similarly split-nib on the recto too, particularly on 
vertical strokes such as the shad markers. While the increased splitting on the 
second half of the verso could reflect a change of pen, and thus too of scribe, it 
might also be the result of a change in pen hold (causing the appearance of the 
split on horizontal rather than vertical strokes) and an increase in pressure on 
the nib while writing in the more careful square style. In any case, the writing 
does appear to be that of another ninth-century hand (and we may note that 
the genitive particles are attached throughout).
What remains is the final copy of the STTS sādhana, ITJ448/PT270, along 
with its sister commentary, ITJ447 [figures 12.6 & 12.7]. As noted above, both 
works are all written in the same hand, and it is a markedly different script 
from the manuscripts we have examined so far. The headless script is highly 
informal, giving a hurried impression, with densely packed folios in a concer-
tina format, holding nine or ten wobbly lines per page and little ornamentation. 
In many respects, the hand resembles van Schaik’s “headless official style,” in 
which all unnecessary strokes are eliminated and corners rounded out, and 
once again, this is a style seen primarily in ninth-century manuscripts (van 
Schaik 2013, 124). While double tsheg-s are not present, this is unsurprising 
given all the other shortcuts taken in haste by this hand. We can add, however, 
that the genitive particles are attached. In short, a paleographic analysis of 
ITJ448/PT270 and ITJ447 may also point to the ninth century.
It should be borne in mind that none of these paleographic analyses are 
watertight. The trends identified by van Schaik, Dotson, and myself are only 
that—initial observations about overall trends within certain portions of the 
Dunhuang collection. In all three cases, more research is required before

that of PT271 not to be identical.

<!-- Page 342 -->

329
Significance of the Ārya-tattvasaṃgraha-sādhanopāyikā
anything firm can be said. Be that as it may, it remains noteworthy that all of 
these Yoga-tantra materials point, in one way or another, to the ninth century. 
There may be some mistakes in these analyses, but taken together as a whole, 
the evidence cited here indicates something highly significant. As I have 
argued elsewhere, the vast majority of the Mahāyoga tantric manuscripts from 
Dunhuang date to the tenth century. But as soon as we turn to these crucial 
Yoga-tantra manuscripts, we find ourselves very much in an earlier time, in a 
realm of tantric practice that was sanctioned by the Tibetan empire, a Yoga-
tantra system whose canonical works were included in the ’Phang thang ma 
catalogue of officially sponsored translations.5 If any of the dates suggested 
here are reliable, then we may be seeing how the policies and the practices of 
the central Tibetan court were reflected in the tantric Buddhist manuscripts 
that circulated around ninth- and tenth-century Dunhuang.
III	
Dating the Text Itself
None of this tells us about the provenance of the original text of the 
Tattvasaṃgraha-sādhana itself. Given the apparent dates of the manu-
scripts, the text likely dates to no later than the early ninth century. Tanaka 
has argued that the existence of the sādhana implies that the STTS itself must 
already have been translated during the imperial period (i.e. during the late 
eighth or early ninth century), in order for it to serve as the sādhana’s canoni-
cal basis.6 The recent discovery of the ’Phang thang ma catalogue, as noted 
above, has confirmed Tanaka’s theory. At the same time, I would argue that 
the Tattvasaṃgraha-sādhana may not be a Tibetan composition written on 
the basis of an early Tibetan translation of the Tantra, but that it may itself be 
a translation of an Indic original. That a Sanskrit title is provided in the open-
ing lines of both PT792 and ITJ417 right away suggests this may be the case. 
5	 See Rta mdo 2003, p. 61, where the STTS, with its uttaratantra, is listed as an imperially sanc-
tioned translation, along with Śākyamitra’s influential Kośalālaṃkāra commentary, as well as 
one other commentary on the first section of the STTS.
6	 This despite the fact, as Tanaka notes, that the STTS does not appear in the Ldan dkar ma cata-
logue of early imperial translations. Heller (2007, 85–6) notes the possibility that the STTS 
might be seen in the Ldan dkar ma under the title, Rgyud kun las btus pa (listed in Lalou 1953, 
326, entry no. 319). While it remains difficult to say for sure, we may note that the Mkhas pa 
lde’u, p. 181, includes the same Rgyud kun las btus pa title in a list of Kriyā-tantras, attributing 
it to Nāgārjuna. If the Ldan dkar ma catalogue and Lde’u intended the same text, the latter’s 
classification of the title as Kriyā would make Heller’s identification of it with the STTS 
unlikely.

<!-- Page 343 -->

330
Dalton
While later Tibetans took to providing Sanskrit titles for their apocrypha, early 
Tibetans do not seem to have done so, and among the Dunhuang manuscripts, 
such titles often seem to indicate a true Indic origin (of some sort).
To conclude these observations on dating, what we seem to have here is an 
imperial-period Tibetan translation of an Indic STTS-based sādhana that itself 
may date from the second half of the eighth century. If there is any truth to the 
speculations that have been trotted out so far in this paper, then this sādhana 
is a valuable piece of evidence for understanding how early Yoga-tantra ritual 
practice evolved.
IV	
Contents: The Sādhanopāyikā’s Ritual Structure
So what, then, might we learn from this ancient text? Here I want to highlight 
two main points: First, the ritual structure of our sādhana, and second, the 
significance that this structure may have for our understanding of tantric 
Buddhism across East Asia, for as we shall see, its ritual forms may still be seen 
as a central element of contemporary Japanese Shingon practice.
To give some idea of how the sādhana’s procedures unfold, an outline sum-
marizing them is provided here:7
I. 	Uniting with the deity and offerings:
	
1. 	Four prostrations—one to each of the four Buddha-families, not 
counting the Buddha.
	
2.	 Purificatory incantation of the mantra, oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ 
sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho’ham.8
	
3. 	Uniting with the deity (called “the samādhi”):
	
	
a. 	Strike the vajrabandha mudrā and the vajrāveśa mudrā, with 
appropriate mantras.
	
	
b. 	Five stages of complete awakening (pañcābhisaṃbodhi): (i) emp-
tiness, (ii) moon disc, (iii) syllable, (iv) symbol, (v) deity.
	
	
c. 	Consecration (adhiṣṭhāna) of the gnosis deity (jñānasattva): By 
touching mudrā to one’s body.
	
	
d. 	Initiations (abhiṣeka): Installing on one’s head a five-family 
crown by means of mantras and mudrās.
7	 Note that the ritual building blocks for the prayers and procedures described here all may be 
found in the first chapter of the STTS, i.e. the only chapter that Amoghavajra translated in 
Taishō 865.
8	 PT300 inserts the construction of the ritual space after the recitation of this mantra.

<!-- Page 344 -->

331
Significance of the Ārya-tattvasaṃgraha-sādhanopāyikā
	
4. 	Offerings by means of the four secret goddesses, then the four outer 
goddesses.
II.	Accomplishing the activities:
	
5. 	Accomplishing the four mudrās:
	
	
mahāmudrā = body of the deity by means of the mantra jaḥ hūṃ 
vaṃ hoḥ!
	
	
dharmamudrā = speech by placing mantra’s syllables atop moon-
disc at one’s heart,
	
	
samayamudrā = mind by wielding the implement,
	
	
karmamudrā = activities by assuming the appropriate posture.
	
6.	 Mantra recitations.
	
7. 	Closing rites of dismissing the deities and final protections.
Setting aside the details of each step, one can see from this outline that, after 
the preliminary prostrations and purificatory rite, the sādhana is focused on 
two ritual sequences in both of which one imagines oneself as the deity. In the 
first stage, one performs the five stages of the pañcābhisaṃbodhi, then conse-
crates oneself with the gnosis deity and initiates oneself by installing a 
Buddha-crown on one’s head. The gnosis deity now present, one performs the 
offerings (thus too receiving them, as one is by now identical with the deity). 
This initial set of rites is then followed by a second sequence for identifying 
with the deity, namely the four mudrās by which one seals one’s union with 
body, speech, mind, and activities of the Buddha, and performs the final recita-
tions in order to accomplish the siddhis.9 Note too that no mention is made of 
generating the other Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who populate the rest of the 
Vajradhātu-maṇḍala. They are present in the form of the various ritual mo­
ments that make up the sādhana, but this must be left for a later discussion.
Further insight into the structure of the sādhana may be gained through 
recourse to the other STTS-based sādhana mentioned above, the *Śrī-vajra­
hūṃkara-sādhanopāyikā, a somewhat more elaborate manual focused on the 
Vajra Buddha-family that appears alongside our own Tatt­va­saṃgraha-sādhana 
in the manuscript ITJ417/PT300/ITJ519. The *Śrī-vajrahūṃkara-sādhanopāyikā 
opens with two four-line verses, both quoted from different points in the STTS 
itself and both, the implication is, describing the same ritual stages.
The first verse reads as follows:

Every day, one should first perform properly the self-consecrations 
(svādhiṣṭhāṇa) and so forth,
Then accomplish the rest, after which, one should perform as one 
pleases.10
In commenting on these lines, the late eighth-century Indian scholar Śākyamitra 
explains that, having first performed the svādhiṣṭhāna and so forth, one sec-
ondly completes the rest, after which, third, one does as one wishes. Regarding 
the last of these three ritual stages, he writes, “Having completed the mudrās 
[in the second stage], one performs whichever rites one wishes, be they a man-
dala rite, a recollection [of the Buddha] (rjes su dran pa), an accomplishment, 
or sundry minor rites.”11 Here, Śākyamitra’s first stage of the self-consecrations 
maps onto our own Part I above quite well. This is followed by completing “the 
rest,” which Śākyamitra glosses as “the mudrās,” that is, the four mudrās that 
structure Part II above. Then one “performs as one pleases,” which appears to 
correspond to the lines that close our Tattvasaṃgraha-sādhana: “Then, bind-
ing the karmamudrā, perform the recitations or meditations.”12 We may also 
note that the commentary in ITJ447 elsewhere explains that these recitations 
are to be performed variously, depending on the buddha-family with which 
one is associated.13 The tenth-century Ānandagarbha further elaborates on 
the above passage: “‘After which, one should perform as one pleases’ means 
that one cultivates the mahāmudrā and so forth and then, if one is tired, one 
rests and recites and cultivates some more without binding the mudrās. Then, 
when one is no longer tired or weary, one once again recites and cultivates 
while binding the mudrās.”14 Thus here again, the four mudrās structure the

V	
Conclusions: Significance of the Sādhana for the Study of Japanese 
Mikkyō.
I want to end by stepping outside of my area of expertise for a moment, to 
consider some possible parallels between the Tattvasaṃgraha-sādhanopāyikā 
and the ritual procedures specific to today’s Shingon School of Japanese 
Buddhism. It is well known that the Shingon School preserves elements of the 
STTS ritual traditions that are found in the writings of Amoghavajra and other 
early tantric masters working in eighth-century China. More specifically, as 
Robert Sharf has observed, the fundamental Shingon ritual sequence of the 
eighteen methods (jūhachi geiin), “appears to be a Japanese systematization of 
a ritual pattern found in [a] group of related Chinese manuals associated with 
Amoghavajra,” such as T.930, 1085, 1086, 1005a, and so on.17 It is based, in other 
words, on a period of STTS-based practice that is remarkably close to that of 
our own sādhana.
According to the Shingon tradition, the practitioner is supposed to begin 
with these “eighteen methods,” which effect the self-generation and the offer-
ings. He then performs the “invocation procedures” (nenju hō), which consist 
of (i) uniting with the “three mysteries” (sanmitsu) of the Buddha’s body, 
speech, and mind, and (ii) the “dispersed invocations” (go kuyō). Sharf explains 
that the “invocation procedures” constitute “the climax of virtually all Shingon 
invocation practices” (Sharf 2001, 183). Their union with the three mysteries is 
accomplished by means of three distinct rites: the “interpenetration of self 
[and deity]” (nyūga-ga’nyū), “formal invocation” (shōnenju), and the syllable-
wheel contemplation (jirinkan), corresponding to body, speech, and mind, 
respectively.18
Here I would like to suggest that the “eighteen methods” correspond to what 
I have called Stage I in the Tattvasaṃgraha-sādhana, while the “invocation 
procedures” correspond to Stage II with its four mudrās. The three Shingon 
rites that accomplish union with the three mysteries play a role that is almost 
identical to that of the four mudrās in our Tibetan Dunhuang sādhana. Like 
the three rites, the accomplishment of the mudrās is performed only after the 
self-generation and offerings have been completed, and like the three rites, 
they too effect a union with the body, speech, and mind of the Buddha, and in 
the same order. While the details of each rite differ, the larger ritual structure is 
identical. In Shingon practice, moreover, the three rites for unifying with the 
17

18	
For examples of each of these, see Sharf 2001, 160 and 183­–5.

<!-- Page 348 -->

Significance of the Ārya-tattvasaṃgraha-sādhanopāyikā
three mysteries are followed by the “dispersed invocations,” which again have a 
direct parallel in the Dunhuang sādhana in the performance of mantra recita-
tions and other meditations that are selected “as one pleases.”
In his 2003 article, Sharf highlights some confusion among the Shingon 
School’s commentators regarding, “how, if at all, the dispersed invocations fit 
into the overall narrative program of the Shidokegyō rituals.” As Sharf goes on 
to explain,
Commentators have explored, explicitly or implicitly, three possibilities. 
The first is that the practitioner disengages from the deity and reverts to 
his or her former self with the commencement of the dispersed invoca-
tions. The dispersed invocations then represent the activity of a 
bodhisattva; the practitioner, having “reentered the marketplace” (to bor-
row a popular Zen image), scatters invocations for the liberation of all 
sentient beings. The second possibility is that the dispersed invocations 
are themselves intended to reintegrate the practitioner into the world; 
they facilitate a gradual and controlled emergence from samādhi. The 
third possibility is that the entire sequence of dispersed invocations is 
performed while ensconced in the samādhi of the principal deity (Sharf 
2003, 80).
Given the apparent parallels between these dispersed invocations and the reci-
tations, the commentary to our Dunhuang sādhana might help to resolve this 
conundrum. In a closing discussion of what may result from the practitioner’s 
recitations, the commentary reads as follows:
One who accomplishes the siddhis of the tathāgata family and the vajra 
family will be reborn in Tuṣita heaven, the realm of Vairocana. One who 
accomplishes the ratna and padma families will be born in the world of 
Sukhāvatī, the realm of Amitāyus. The sign of nearing acomplishment for 
the tathāgata family is seeing all entities flying through space. The sign 
for accomplishing the siddhis of the ratna family is jewels appearing in 
the sky like stars. The sign for the vajra and karma families is black clouds 
and assorted weapons appearing in the sky. The sign for the padma fam-
ily is a wheel appearing in the sky. These will not be correctly perfected 
without cultivating the mantras.19

Through one’s recitations, then, one accomplishes the siddhis specific to the 
mantra recited. In other words, the third of the possible interpretations of the 
dispersed invocations that Sharf enumerates is in all likelihood the one fol-
lowed in the Indian and Tibetan traditions.
This is just one insight that can be gleaned from the Ārya-tattvasaṃgraha-
sādhanopāyikā. In other ways too, this ancient Tibetan manual from Dunhuang 
constitutes a bridge between, on the one hand, the early STTS-based ritual tra-
ditions of India and Tibet and, on the other, Amoghavajra’s eighth-century 
Chinese tantric writings. The apparent dates of the Dunhuang sādhana dis-
cussed in the first half of this paper place it in close temporal proximity to 
Amoghavajra and thus too to the textual traditions that stand at the very root 
of contemporary Shingon practice in Japan.

Chapter 13
Avalokiteśvara and the Dunhuang Dhāraṇī Spells of 
Salvation in Childbirth
Translated by Ilia Mozias and Meir Shahar 
Li Ling and Ma De Li and Ma
Birth, old age, sickness, and death have been primary concerns of the Buddhist 
faith since its inception. With the emergence of esoteric Buddhism, the power 
of its spells has been harnessed to aid at such pivotal moments in the life 
course. In this essay we discuss esoteric spells and scriptures that were meant 
to assist women in labor. Prior to modern medicine, childbirth posed real dan-
ger to mother and child alike. The medical risks involved were reflected in 
medieval ritual tracts, some of which have been discovered at the famed 
Dunhuang grottoes. We consider in particular The Dhāraṇī for Delivery from 
Childbirth Obstacles (Jiuchannan tuoluoni 救產難陀羅尼); The Writ of the 
Difficult [Ninth] Month (Nan yuewen 難月文); and The Sūtra of the Heart of the 
Buddha Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of Avalokiteśvara (Foding xin Guanshiyin jing 佛頂心觀
世音經). The latter scripture was used to expedite labor through the late-impe-
rial period. Accounts of childbirth rituals dating from as late as the sixteenth 
century still mention it.1
The charms and scriptures we investigate attempt to engage the divine pow-
ers of Avalokiteśvara. In this respect, they shed significant light on the growth 
of the Bodhisattva’s Chinese cult. Relied upon in the context of labor, the texts 
might elucidate Avalokiteśvara’s appeal to a female clientele. Moreover, the 
role of childbearing that was assigned to the Bodhisattva might have contrib-
uted to its eventual transformation from a male deity into a female one. 
(Another Tantric manifestation of Avalokiteśvara—as a horse-headed divin-
ity—is discussed by Meir Shahar in chapter 4.)

Avalokiteśvara and the Dunhuang Dhāraṇī Spells
The Printed Dhāraṇī for Delivery from Childbirth Obstacles and the 
manuscript of the Writ of the Difficult [Ninth] Month
The trove of medieval Dunhuang documents contains some thirty copies of a 
printed spell titled The Dhāraṇī of a thousand Turns of the Saintly Bodhisattva 
Avalokiteśvara Who Expiates all Crimes (Shengguan zizai pusa qianzuan miezui 
tuoluoni 聖觀自在菩薩千轉滅罪陀羅尼). Typically, one charm was printed on 
each page, but occasionally several copies of the same charm were printed on 
a single sheet of paper. Measuring 14 × 17 centimeters, the example reproduced 
in figure 13.1 depicts the Bodhisattva wearing a Buddha-adorned crown. The 
image is surrounded by a spell written in Sanskrit letters, as well as four lotus 
flowers, each bearing a sacred seed syllable (likewise written in Sanskrit). The 
only Chinese-language text (on the extreme left) reads:
This Dhāraṇī of a thousand Turns of the Saintly Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara 
Who Expiates all Crimes has the great power of expiating all crimes of a 
thousand turns, thereby obtaining the cleansed body of six purified fac-
ulties. The person wearing it will be absolved of all sins. This person will 
enjoy blessings, becoming a Buddha.2

The text specifies that in order to be effective, the charm has to be carried on 
the body. However, the purpose of this act is not provided. The answer is given 
by versions of the printed charm that include several rectangular boxes, each 
containing a Sanskrit spell and a brief Chinese explanation (see figure 13.2 
from the Pelliot collection). Accompanying the same text as in figure 13.1, the 
framed rectangular charms were apparently meant to be cut, rolled, and car-
ried on the body. The Chinese text on the top of each reads Dhāraṇī for Delivery 
from Childbirth Obstacles (Jiuchannan tuoluoni 救產難陀羅尼). Thus we know 
that these charms were meant to be worn by women in labor.3 (Some hand-
written charms addressed to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara were similarly 
relied upon to guarantee a safe delivery. See figures 13.3 and 13.4 of manuscript 
Or. 8210/S. 2498 from the Stein collection).
To be sure, concern with the dangers of childbirth did not originate with 
esoteric Buddhism. Rather it is apparent in such mainstream scriptures of the 
Mahāyāna as the Sūtra on the Past Vows of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva (Dizang 
pusa benyuan jing 地藏菩薩本願經). Translated by the Khotanese monk 
Śikṣānanda (Shichanantuo 實叉難陀, 652–710) the Sūtra propagates the virtue 
of assisting women at childbirth:

The fruits of karma are measureless and boundless, once again, Oh! 
Kṣitigarbha! If in their next lives the kings and the brahmans heed the 
elderly, the sick, and the women in labor—if in their mercy they extend 
to them medicine, food, and shelter, bringing them happiness—they will 
obtain merit beyond measure.4
The same emphasis upon the duty to assist women at childbirth is found in 
Nāgārjuna’s Treatise on the Five Sciences (Longshu wu ming lun 龍樹五明論), 
which instructs its readers to employ written charms for the purpose:
If this charm is written on a person’s back, the disease he suffers from will 
be cured. If it is carried by a pregnant woman, the demons heeding it will 
avoid her.5
The interest of the Buddhist community in the risks attendant to childbirth 
was reflected in ritual procedures. Prior to the beginning of labor, special cer-
emonies were held to guarantee the safety of mother and child. Discovered at 
the Dunhuang trove of medieval texts, The Writ of the Difficult [Ninth] Month 
(Nan yuewen 難月文) was recited as part of these prophylactic rites. Invoking 
the powers of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (alluded to as Guanyin 觀音 as 
well as the Mahāsattva of Great Compassion (大士弘悲)), it reads:
Toiling in labor, this woman is chaste and pure. Conducting herself 
according to the womanly etiquette she is most refined. Endowed with 
exceptional wisdom, she is fully prepared to be a paragon of motherhood. 
The karmic fruits of past eons, will guarantee her happiness in this life. 
A person who is confined in a female body will not avoid the dangers of 
pregnancy. Now that another ten days period has passed, and the new 
moon has come full circle, there is the danger of demons causing mis-
chief, ghouls bringing disaster. Hence you piously seek refuge in the three 
treasures of the Buddhist faith … A pledge is made that when the day 
approaches and the month has come full circle, a miraculous spirit will 
be born; mother and child will be safe, and there be no specter of danger.

343
Avalokiteśvara and the Dunhuang Dhāraṇī Spells
Through the Avalokiteśvara initiation (abhiṣeka), one will obtain the rec-
ipe of immortality …6
The Writ of the Difficult [Ninth] Month survives in a significant number of 
extant Dunhuang manuscript copies (e.g. P. 1441, S.1441.2, S.5561, S.5593, S. 5957, 
P.3765, Beitu 706, etc.) (See figure 13.5). Occasional differences notwithstand-
ing, the versions are quite similar. In addition to praying for the welfare of 
mother and child, the texts highlight the Confucian virtues of their family 
members. The following formula appears in all versions:
May the father retain his rank and salary, and the mother her exalted 
morality. May the brothers manifest unsurpassed filial piety, and the 
daughters exhibit paramount chastity.7
As all extant versions emphasize, The Writ of the Difficult [Ninth] Month was 
meant to be chanted. In this respect it supplements The Dhāraṇī for Delivery 
from Childbirth Obstacles, which was copied and carried on the body. The two 
methods—chanting and wearing—had a single goal: safeguarding the health 
of mother and child.
	
The Sūtra of the Heart of the Buddha Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of 
Avalokiteśvara
The Dunhuang trove of medieval manuscripts has yielded an apocryphal Sūtra 
in three chapters (juan 卷), which bear several titles, including: 1) The Sūtra of 
the Heart of the Buddha Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of Avalokiteśvara (Foding xin Guanshiyin 
jing 佛頂心觀世音經); 2) The Great Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Heart of the Buddha 
Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (Foding xin Guanshiyin pusa da 
tuoluoni jing 佛頂心觀世音菩薩大陀羅尼經); and 3) The Method of Safe and 
Speedy Delivery of the Heart of the Buddha Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of Avalokiteśvara 
(Foding xin Guanshiyin pusa liaobing cuichan fang quanzhong 佛頂心觀世音
菩薩療病催產方卷中).

344

Currently stored at the French National Library (Pelliot collection no. 3916), 
the apocryphal Sūtra was originally bound together with several other texts 
into one book, of which no fewer than 131 numbered pages survive. The book 
was fastened in the imported Indian Pothi style. Written on both sides, its 
pages were strung together by a thread that ran through a hole in the middle of 
each.
The following text is from the Sūtra’s second (middle) chapter, which bears 
the title of The Method of Safe and Speedy Delivery of the Heart of the Buddha 
Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of Avalokiteśvara. It appears on the fifty-fifth page of the bound 
Pothi volume:
… Suppose a woman is in labor, yet parturition does not occur. She is
subject to obstructing evil demons, which cause her to scream in pain, 
moan and wail. She has no one she can turn to. In such a situation, the 
Figure 13.5		
Dunhuang manuscript of the Writ of the Difficult [Ninth] Month. 
Pelliot Chinois 3765. National Library of France.

<!-- Page 358 -->

345
Avalokiteśvara and the Dunhuang Dhāraṇī Spells
dhāraṇī spell should be written in cinnabar ink [on a sheet of paper,] 
along with its accompanying secret character seal (mi zi yin 秘字印). The 
woman should drink the spell [which has been burnt, its ashes] secretly 
mixed with fragrant waters. Thereupon parturition will occur, and she 
will give birth to a wise boy or a beautiful girl, who will be loved by all.8
It is noteworthy that the apocryphal Chinese Sūtra draws upon a canonical 
Mahāyāna scripture. The reference to a wise boy and a beautiful daughter was 
inspired by a passage in the celebrated Sūtra of the Lotus of the Wonderful 
Dharma (Miaofa lianhua jing 妙法蓮花經). The Mahāyāna scripture is lacking 
the ritual procedure of writing, burning, and swallowing a charm. However, it 
does resemble the Chinese text in the central role that is assigned to 
Avalokiteśvara. As in The Sūtra of the Heart of the Buddha Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of 
Avalokiteśvara, the Sūtra of the Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma has the blessed 
offspring delivered by the Bodhisattva’s grace:
If a woman desires a son, she should pay homage and make offerings to 
the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. She will give birth to a virtuous and wise 
boy. If she desires a girl, she will give birth to a chaste and beautiful girl. 
Their roots of virtue having been planted in previous lives, they will be 
loved and respected by all.9
A possible key for the dating of the apocryphal Chinese scripture is provided 
by another text that was bound with it in the same Pothi style volume. Titled 
The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Heart of all Goddesses (Zhu xin mu tuoluoni jing 諸心
母陀羅尼經), the latter is presented as “Translated by Monk Facheng 法成 of 
the Xiuoduo 修多 Monastery in Ganzhou 甘州.” We know that monk Facheng 
(?–869) had been active at the Xiuduo Monastery between 842 and 846 (Ji 
Xianlin 1998, 351). Thus, we may assume that The Sūtra of the Heart of the 
Buddha Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of Avalokiteśvara was likely produced sometime after 
that date, perhaps around 850CE. It might further be noted that the Pothi bind-
ing style was not a feature of Dunhuang book-making prior to the ninth 
century. Therefore it is likely that our manuscript dates from around the sec-
ond half of the ninth century.
