346
Li And Ma
We have examined three child-bearing ritual texts that equally leverage the 
divine powers of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara: The Dhāraṇī for Delivery from 
Childbirth Obstacles; The Writ of the Difficult [Ninth] Month (Nan yuewen 難月
文); and The Sūtra of the Heart of the Buddha Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of Avalokiteśvara. 
These medieval texts attest the growth of the Bodhisattva’s Chinese cult no less 
than his attraction to a female clientele.
	
The Impact of the Sūtra of the Heart of the Buddha Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] 
of Avalokiteśvara
The apocryphal Sūtra of the Heart of the Buddha Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of Avalokiteśvara 
has never been included in printed editions of the Buddhist canon. Nonetheless 
it has exerted a significant impact upon Chinese religious practice. All through 
the Ming period (1368–1644) it was relied upon to assist women in labor. Below 
we survey some of the evidence for its abiding popularity.
As pointed out by Fang Guangchang, the Sūtra of the Heart of the Buddha 
Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of Avalokiteśvara was engraved in stone at the famed Fangshan 
房山 site some forty kilometers southwest of present-day Beijing. At least two 
copies of the child-bearing scripture were discovered at the site, where 
Buddhist scriptures had been inscribed since as early as the seventh century. 
Dating likely from the Liao (907–1125) or Jin (1115–1234) periods, the engraved 
texts closely correspond to the Dunhuang manuscript version, reproducing its 
three chapters alike (Fang Guangchang 2000)
Two printed copies of the Sūtra of the Heart of the Buddha Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of 
Avalokiteśvara are preserved at the Zhejiang Provincial Museum, one bearing 
the date of the Southern Song Qiandao 乾道 eighth year (1172). The two copies 
are especially interesting for bearing Daoist style talismanic characters that 
might correspond to the “secret character seal” that is mentioned in the ninth-
century Dunhuang text. The talismanic script is followed by the four characters: 
Nengjiu chan’nan 能救產難 (“capable of delivering from childbirth difficul-
ties”) (see figure 13.6). Hence, it is conceivable that the same ritual tradition—of 
writing Daoist style talismanic script in child-bearing Buddhist ceremonies—
informed the ninth century Dunhuang texts and the twelfth-century Jiang’nan 
scriptures. Spanning three centuries and thousands of miles, the Dunhuang 
and Zhejiang texts attest an ongoing ritual tradition that centered upon the 
Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
The popularity of the Sūtra of the Heart of the Buddha Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of 
Avalokiteśvara did not diminish in ensuing centuries. Printed and manuscript 
copies of the scripture that assisted women at childbirth survive from the Ming

period. For example, an illustrated printed copy dated 1440 is preserved at the 
Indianapolis Museum of Art. Like the preceding Song-period manuscript cop-
ies it includes Daoist style talismanic characters that are hailed as “The secret 
character seal that is capable of delivering from childbirth difficulties” (mi zi 
yin nengjiu chan’nan 密字印能救產難)).
The imperial family no less than ordinary folks relied upon Avalokiteśvara’s 
assistance at childbirth. Printed and manuscript copies of the Sūtra of the 
Heart of the Buddha Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of Avalokiteśvara were produced at the 
imperial palace. Dated 1597, one handsomely illustrated printed edition was 
dedicated by the Wanli Emperor (reigned 1573–1619) for his beloved consort Li 
(who bore him two sons). Another precious Imperial Palace copy originally 
belonged to the renowned Ming-period painter Dong Qichan 董其昌 (1555–
1636), who penned it with his own words of praise:
Those who aspire for offspring, recite this scripture. Relying on the divine 
spell’s merit, they are blessed with virtuous and wise boys.10
Titled The Dhāraṇī of the Five Seals of White Robbed Compassionate [Avalo­
kiteśvara] (Baiyi dabei wuyin tuoluoni 白衣大悲五印陀羅尼), Dong Qichang’s 
copy is currently treasured at the National Palace Museum in Taipei. It bears 
the seals of the Qianlong Emperor (reigned 1736–1795) and the Jiaqing Emperor 
(reigned 1796–1820). Providing a window onto the daily lives of the common 
folk, Ming-period fiction attests their reliance on the Avalokiteśvara charms at 
childbirth. The sixteenth-century Plum in the Golden Vase (Jin Ping Mei 金瓶梅) 
features a nun who lectures on the dangers of childbirth:
According to our Buddhist scriptures, the human realm is beset by yakṣa 
and rākṣasa demons. They like to devour people, depriving them of off-
spring. The robbery of fetuses in the womb is the work of pernicious 
demons.11
The nun goes on to recommend the printing of dhāraṇī scriptures to counter 
the vile creatures. We might assume that at least some of the charms she rec-
ommended harnessed the powers of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
The Ming period witnessed the widespread currency of The Water and Land 
rituals (whose prevalence in Yunnan esoteric Buddhism is discussed by Hou

349
Avalokiteśvara and the Dunhuang Dhāraṇī Spells
Chong in chapter 16). The rituals were intended primarily for those who had 
died without issue, leaving no descendants to perform ancestral worship on 
their behalf. It is for this reason that aborted fetuses and children who died at 
childbirth figured in these rites. As Chen Yunü has noted in her Ming-Period 
Buddhism and Society, the elaborate paintings that were used in the rituals 
often featured the unfortunate souls of the stillborn.12 This is the case with the 
Ming period wall paintings that have been preserved at the Baoning 寶寧 
Monastery (Shanxi Province) and the Pilu 毗盧 Monastery (Hebei Province). 
The expressive art works bear cartouches alluding to the “Orphaned souls, sub-
ject to severe cold and unbearable heat, of the aborted fetuses and the stillborn” 
(堕胎产亡严寒大暑孤魂众) (see figure 13.7). The paintings attest the concern 
of Ming-period society with the medical risks that were inherent in childbirth. 
The same risks informed the apocryphal Avalokiteśvara Sūtra, which was 
widely used by expectant women during the same period.

Postscript
Scholars have been puzzled by the riddle of Avalokiteśvara’s transformation 
from a largely male deity in India to a predominantly female one in China. The 
materials presented in this paper might point in the direction of a possible 
(albeit partial) answer to this thorny issue. We would like to suggest that the 
medieval charms and texts we have discussed might have prefigured the emer-
gence—during the Song Period (960–1279)—of the child-giving Guanyin 
(Songzi Guanyin 送子觀音; or Songzi Niangniang 送子娘娘), who became 
extremely popular in late-imperial art (see figure 13.8).13 The three texts we 
have discussed The Dhāraṇī for Delivery from Childbirth Obstacles (Jiuchannan 
tuoluoni 救產難陀羅尼); The Writ of the Difficult [Ninth] Month (Nan yuewen 難
月文); and The Sūtra of the Heart of the Buddha Crown [Uṣṇīṣa] of Avalokiteśvara 
(Foding xin Guanshiyin jing 佛頂心觀世音經) predate the earliest occurrence 
of the explicitly female child-giving Guanyin. Indeed they might have inspired 
its emergence. Thus, these texts are significant not only as regards the history 
of Chinese esoteric Buddhism, but also for shedding light on the emergence of 
a principal Chinese deity—the female Guanyin.
13	
On the child-giving Guanyin see Chün-Fang 2001, esp. 127–137.

Saṃpuṭa and Cakrasaṃvara Tantras in the Xixia Period
Chapter 14
Notes on the Translation and Transmission of the 
Saṃpuṭa and Cakrasaṃvara Tantras in the Xixia 
Period (1038–1227)*
Hou Haoran
In 1991, Chinese archaeologists unearthed more than thirty Tangut and Chinese 
documents from a square pagoda dating to the second year of the Da’an era 
(1075) of the Xixia period, located at the recesses of the Valley Baisigou (拜
寺溝) in the area of Mount Helan in the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. A 
major part of the finds consists of the cycle of the Tangut Saṃpuṭa, viz. The 
Root Text of the Saṃpuṭa (𘀄𘓄𗄊𗫡𗋈𘜼𗰜𗺓; F017-F019, three vols., 114 
folios) and several volumes of commentaries and other supplementary mate-
rials, that is, The Essential Text of the Saṃpuṭa (𘀄𘓄𗄊𗫡𗋈𘜼𗰜𗺓𗗙𗆔𘝞; 
F020, one vol., 19 folios), The Broad Meaning Text of the Saṃpuṭa (𘀄𘓄𗄊 
𗫡𗋈𘜼𗰜𗺓𗗙𗆈𗧘𘝞; F021, one vol., 29 folios), The Supplementary Text of 
the Saṃpuṭa (𘀄𘓄𗄊𗫡𗋈𘜼𗰜𗺓𗗙𘏒𗭪𘚻𘏒𗔡; F022-F024, three vols. 85 
folios), together with two Chinese explanatory texts on Cakrasaṃvara, i.e. The 
Ritual Text of the Cakrasaṃvara (Xiuchi weigui 修持儀軌 軌; F041, three piles, 
14 folios) and The Commentary on the Cakrasaṃvara (Jixiang shangle lun 
lüewen deng xukong bengxu 吉祥上樂輪略文等虛空本續; F042, fragments) 
etc.1 The excavation of these texts almost immediately inspired their decipher-
ment and translation. In the last two decades, Chinese scholars have made 
significant progress researching the recovery from the Baisigou Pagoda. Thus 
far, however, these Tangut tantric documents have escaped the notice of their 
Western counterparts. This paper aims to introduce this corpus of the Tangut 
Saṃpuṭa and Cakrasaṃvara, and conduct a preliminary survey on its transla-
tion and transmission in Xixia.

Previous Studies on the Tangut Saṃpuṭa
As Péter Szántó (2013) has already reviewed previous studies on the Tantra 
itself in Sanskrit and in Tibetan translation, there is no need to repeat the 
details here. The first pioneering study was undertaken by Elder (1978). Keiya 
Noguchi published a series of short studies on the Saṃpuṭa in Japanese.2 Based 
on the Sanskrit and Tibetan versions, Skorupski (1996) presents a brief intro-
duction to the structure and contents of the Saṃpuṭa, with its ten long chapters 
divided into sub-chapters. To date, while the Tangut version has not been fully 
edited, it has also not been completely neglected by scholarship.
Archaeological findings that the corpus of the Tangut Saṃpuṭa was printed 
by movable wooden type evoked in the 1990s heated discussion on Tangut 
typography (Niu Dasheng 2005; Shi Jinbo 1997, 2007, 505–52; Shi Jinbo and 
Yasen 2000). For the next decade, studies came to a standstill because scholars 
could not identify the Tibetan version of this text and assumed that it has been 
preserved only in Tangut translation (Nie Hongyin 2004, Sun Changsheng 
2004). The report of the Baisigou Pagoda published by the Ningxia Institute of 
Archaeology and Cultural Relics in 2005 made available photographic images 
of the complete version of the Tangut Saṃpuṭa (Ningxia 2005). In his 2006 
doctoral dissertation, Sun Changsheng presented an edition of the fourth vol-
ume of the Tangut Saṃpuṭa together with a Chinese translation of the second 
to fourth sub-chapters of the seventh chapter [henceforth chapter 7.2–4] (Sun 
Changsheng 2006). In light of Sun’s study, Shen Weirong has suggested that the 
Tangut title is a translation of the Tibetan dPal kun tu kha sbyor zhes bya ba’i 
rgyud, restored into Sanskrit as Śrī Saṃpuṭa Nāma Tantra. Shen Weirong argues 
moreover that, although this Tibetan translation is not extant, a variant ver-
sion is found in bKa’ ’gyur under the title (Śrī) Yang dag par sbyor ba zhes bya ba 
rgyud chen po (Toh. 381, Shen Weirong 2007).
These two pioneering works mark a turning point in the study of the Tangut 
Saṃpuṭa and establish a framework for further comparative philological and 
linguistic research. Subsequently, Sun Changsheng carried out studies on the 
chapter 10 and 8.3 of The Root Text of the Saṃpuṭa (Sun Changsheng 2007, 
2013).
In 2010, building on Sun Changsheng’s dissertation, another Chinese scholar, 
Sun Bojun, published a study on the mantras and dhāraṇīs in the fourth vol-
ume of The Root Text of the Saṃpuṭa. However, this study is conceptually 
confused and methodologically weak. The author makes an effort to recon-
struct the “original” Sanskrit version of the dhāraṇīs with help of the Tibetan 
2	 See Szántó (2013) for references to these eight studies published between 1984 and 1995.

357
Saṃpuṭa and Cakrasaṃvara Tantras in the Xixia Period
transliterations and the analogical dhāraṇīs in other Sanskrit texts, but ignores 
the existence of the Sanskrit manuscripts of the Saṃpuṭatantra (Sun Bojun 
2010).
In 2015, Sun Changsheng published two additional articles on The Root Text 
of the Saṃpuṭa. Based on the Chapter 5.1, the first of these (Sun Changsheng 
2015a) describes how Tanguts transliterated the place names of ancient India 
and analyses the cultural information embodied in the toponym. The second 
article (Sun Changsheng 2015b) illustrates a number of typographical mistakes 
that appear in the printings of The Root Text of the Saṃpuṭa. The year 2015 also 
saw, after more than a decade of research, the publication of Sun Changsheng’s 
monograph on the Tangut Saṃpuṭa (Sun Changsheng 2015c). The core of this 
work is a complete edition together with an annotated translation of the third 
to the fifth volumes of The Root Text of the Saṃpuṭa (Chapter 6.1–10.4). The cor-
responding Tibetan text is attached to each section. However as the author’s 
knowledge of Tibetan is limited, he does not make full use of the Tibetan text 
for understanding the Tangut syntax. In some cases, the translation seems 
rather a word-for-word transcription. The body of this work is supplemented 
by an adequate glossary of Buddhist terms, which is an essential resource for 
studying Tangut Buddhist terminology.
Scholars have made significant strides in the study of The Root Text of the 
Saṃpuṭa, and we now have a basic knowledge and preliminary translation of 
the text. We await further studies to resolve questions of Tangut syntax, pho-
nology, terminology and so on. As for the commentarial and supplementary 
materials of the Saṃpuṭa, viz. The Essential Text of the Saṃpuṭa, The Broad 
Meaning Text of the Saṃpuṭa, The Supplementary Text of the Saṃpuṭa, a project 
is being undertaken by Sun Changsheng at the Institute for Tangut Studies of 
Beifang Minzu University.3

The Translation and Transmission of the Tangut Saṃpuṭa.
Following the style of the Tangut Buddhist literature, each volume of The Root 
Text of the Saṃpuṭa begins with:
In the presence of Indian Paṇḍita Gayadhara,
Tibetan Rin-chen ’Gos Lo-tsā-ba Khug-pa Lhas-btsas translated it into 
Tibetan.
Deputy Director of the Bao’en Limin Monastery Piputifu translated it 
into Tangut.7
Thus, the original translation of the text from Sanskrit into Tibetan is credited 
to the Tibetan translator ’Gos Lo-tsā-ba Khug-pa lhas-btsas (ca. 11 cent., hereaf-
ter ’Gos Lo), who translated the work under the supervision of Indian Paṇḍita 
Gayadhara (d. 1103). The subsequent retranslation from Tibetan to Tangut was 
conducted by a monk named Piputifu.
6	 The dimension of the type area is 23.5 × 32 cm, framed in double-line rectangle column. This

lines whereby each page is folded in half inwards, and each half comprises ten vertical lines 
of twenty-two characters. As the majority of the text is in metrical rhythm of seven characters 
to a verse, there are two verses in a line, leaving three-character blank on-top, two-character 
blank in-between and three-character blank on-bottom; thus the layout of each side fells into 
upper and lower blocks. The text reads from top to bottom, right to left.

The Indian Paṇḍita Gayadhara
Gayadhara was a mysterious figure who is said to have made three trips to 
Tibet and worked in turn with ’Brog-mi Śākya ye-shes (992–1072?), ’Gos Lo and 
Gyi-jo Zla-ba’i ’od-zer.8 At first, Gayadhara worked with ’Brog-mi at Myu-gu-
lung where they completed a wealth of translations within three or five years, 
the most influential among which belong to the Hevajra cycle, often called 
The Three Tantras of Hevajra (Kye rdor gyi rgyud gsum), namely, the Hevajra, 
Saṃpuṭa and Vajrapañjara Tantras (Toh. 417–8, 381, 419). On his second trip, 
pretending to be Maitrīpā, he arrived at Pa-tshab in Myang-yul of gTsang 
where he collaborated with ’Gos Lo for two years in translating into Tibetan a 
number of Indian texts including The Three Tantras of Hevajra. Nowadays The 
Three Tantras of Hevajra are found in the Tohoku catalogue with Gayadhara 
and ’Brog-mi as their translators. Gayadhara’s translation of The Three Tantras 
of Hevajra together with ’Gos Lo seem not to have survived, though a num-
ber of translations collaborated by these two scholars are found in the Tohoku 
catalogue.9
While editing the Zhwa-lu manuscripts, Bu-ston Rin-chen-grub (1290–1364) 
revised ’Brog-mi’s translation of the Saṃpuṭatanra and selected it for inclusion 
in the Zhwa-lu bKa’ ’gyur. As is known, the Zhwa-lu redaction exercises an 
overwhelming influence on the canonicalization of Tibetan Buddhist litera-
ture, especially in the matter of the deletion of duplicates. Apparently ’Gos Lo’s 
translation of the Saṃpuṭatantra was excluded from the “standard” version of 
the canon.10 Alternatively, its authenticity was deemed suspect since Davidson 
points out that in the colophon of the Saṃpuṭatilaka (Toh. 382), a scripture 
8

The translations of ’Gos Lo and Gayadhara include two tantras and eleven esoteric works, 
such as tantric commentaries and instructions. In addition ’Gos is also known to have 
translated the Guhyasamājatantra with Gayadhara, but just like the rGyud gsum, it was 
not included in the bKa’ ’gyur and thus not come down to us. According to the Tohoku

’Gos Lo. Besides, Davidson (2005, 413) notes that Toh. 429 is mistakenly attributed to 
Gayadhara and ’Brog-mi due to an incorrect reading of the colophon, which gives the 
translators as Gayadhara and ’Gos Lo. Regarding the cooperation between Gayadhara and 
Khug-pa lha-btsas, see Bu-ston 1965–1971, vol. 24, 908 and ’Gos gZhon-nu-dpal 1974, 
318–321.

belonging to the cycle of the Saṃpuṭa, ’Brog-mi complained about plagiarists 
during his time, and Sa-skya Paṇḍita Kun-dga’ rgyal-mtshan (1182–1251) identi-

of the Saṃpuṭa with ’Gos Lo among its translators found its way into Xixia 
before the 1180s and survives to the present via its Tangut translation. A critical 
and comparative philological study of the Tangut Saṃpuṭa may assist our 
understanding of the life and career of ’Gos Lo, especially in light of the ques-
tions raised by Wedemeyer in a recent article.11
	
Piputifu the Translator into Tangut
The Deputy Director of the Bao’en Limin Monastery Piputifu translated 
the Saṃpuṭa into Tangut. “Bao’en Limin Monastery” probably refers to the 
destroyed monastic seat near the Pagoda. Tangut translators rendered Indian 
and Tibetan names into their language in three ways: transliteration, transla-
tion and transliteration combined with translation (Nie Hongyin 2002, 64–67). 
The name Piputifu falls within the third category: the first part 𘇜𘏞𘛛 [be po 
tjɨ] is a phonetic transliteration of the Sanskrit term Vibhūti, while the Tangut 
graph 𗼕 [ljo], which literally means “bless” or “fortune”, is presumably trans-
lated from the Sanskrit word bhadra.12 Thus the name “Piputifu” can be restored 
into Sanskrit as Vibhūtibhadra (Sun Changsheng 2004, 66–68). The translator 
Piputifu has not been identified yet, despite efforts made in that direction, but 
he seems to have been a person of Indian origin who has become an accom-
plished scholar of both Tibetan and Tangut languages. Piputifu rendered into 
Tangut not only The Root Text of the Saṃpuṭa, but also three explanatory scrip-
tures The Essential Text, The Broad Meaning Text and The Supplementary Text. 
The colophons of these three works are identical:
11	
Wedemeyer points out that while ’Gos Lo is described as one of the most productive 
translators of many important tantras as well as one of the most extraordinary lamas of 
his days, he is rarely mentioned in the standard Tibetological and Buddhological litera-
ture; much of the scant information on him comes from Tibetan Buddhist historical 
works, which portray ’Gos Lo as an advocate of the Guhyasamājatantra, a polemicist for 
the gSar-ma tradition as well as a disciple with controversial and fractious personality, 
standing in tension with his former teachers Zur-po-che and ’Brog-mi. Furthermore, 
Wedemeyer argues that ’Gos Lo has been long dwelt in the shadow of scholarly neglect, 
which resulted in a series of misunderstandings concerning his person and career. Exam-
ining two of his works, the sNgags-log sun-’byin and gSang-’dus stong-thun, Wedemeyer 
concludes that the image of ’Gos Lo as a puritan reformer of the gSar-ma movements can 
be traced to scholarly imagination and misinterpretation (Wedemeyer 2014, 240–260).
12	
Here Piputifu is transcribed from the Chinese name 毗菩提福, which is reconstructed by 
The Institute of Archaeology and Cultural Relics of Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region.

The Tibetan Compiler
Regarding his name E Fennu Jingang, 𘓲 [ŋwar] is a phonetic version of the 
Tibetan rNgog and 𗕣𗔊𗍥𘟙 is a literal translation of Zhe-sdang rdo-rje. 
The Tangut term 𘐀𘇂𗂧 sometimes serves as a shortened form of 𘇂𗂧. 
Transcribed in Chinese these two terms are 番中國 (Fanzhongguo) or 中國 
(Zhongguo), literally meaning “Central Land.” This name refers to dBus and 
gTsang in Central Tibet. The compiler is thus identified as rNgog Zhe-sdang 
rdo-rje (1090–1166), a son of rNgog Chos-kyi rdo-rje (1036–1102/1023–1090), 
one of the most prominent disciples of Mar-pa Chos-kyi blo-gros (1002/1012–
1079) (Sun Changsheng 2004, 68–70). This identification had long remained 
unconfirmed because scholars could not put a name to the Tibetan commen-
taries translated into Tangut in this collection. Following our conference in 
Jerusalem, Yael Bentor suggested that I look into the collected works of the 
rNgog bKa’-brgyud-pa tradition.
When I compared the Tangut documents to the works of rNgog Zhe-sdang 
rdo-rje, I was delighted to discover that the major part of The Broad Meaning 
Text of the Saṃpuṭa belongs to rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-rje’s commentary on the 
Saṃpuṭa Tantra, entitled dPal Sambu ṭa’i rnam bshad gzhung gsal ba’i sgron 
ma. Thus pages 4 to 10 of the Tangut text (F021–04–10; Ningxia 2005, 89–92) are 
a translation of rNgog’s explanations on chapter 6.3 of the Saṃpuṭa (Sambu ṭa’i 
rnam bshad 2011, 212–220). In the middle of the chapter the Tangut translation 
skips to chapter 7.3 that corresponds to the Tibetan text (Sambu ṭa’i rnam bshad 
2011, 232–233), and then to chapter 8.4 (F021–10–11). The next paragraph (F021–
11–12; Ningxia 2005, 92–93) that comments on chapter 6.2 corresponds to the 
(Sambu ṭa’i rnam bshad 2011, 211–212). The Tangut text next returns to chapter 
6.3, and then jumps to chapter 7.3 (F021–13; Ningxia 2005, 93). The remainder 
of The Broad Meaning Text (F021–13–29; Ningxia 2005, 93–101) is divided into 
eight paragraphs, each beginning with the Tangut phrase “Prostrating myself 
many times in front of the most wonderful teacher (𗩾𗤓𗨁𘘚𘃻𗗙𗍺𘐔),” 
on a separate line. This part, which contains numerous citations from the 
Sambu ṭa’i rnam-bshad seems to be interpreting certain difficult points of the

commentary. The apparent sequential disorder of the Tangut translation is 
still unexplained. Perhaps this and other related questions will be resolved by 
a comparative study of the Tibetan and Tangut versions of The Broad Meaning 
Text of the Saṃpuṭa currently being prepared by the author.
Still we can be confident that the corpus of the Saṃpuṭa from Baisigou 
Pagoda derives from rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-rje of the rNgog bKa’-brgyud-pa tra-
dition. Father and son rNgog Chos-kyi rdo-rje and rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-rje 
initiated this tradition, which for seven generations remained a distinct and 
identifiable transmission at the gZhung Valley.14 Both father and son were 
important and prolific exegetes, who introduced numerous tantric teachings 
to the mantrins of Tibet, of which the most distinguished was the pure teach-
ing of Hevajra from Mar-pa.15
With regard to the Saṃpuṭa, rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-rje first received the 
teachings from his father rNgog Chos-kyi rdo-rje, who seems to have not com-
posed any treatises on this subject. After his father’s death, rNgog Zhe-sdang 
rdo-rje further collected teachings on the Saṃpuṭa from his father’s former stu-
dent gNyan-ba tog-can, the uncle of Chag lo-tsa-ba Chos-rje dpal (1197–1263/4), 
viz. Chag Lo-tsā-ba dGra-bcom and from Rwa Lo-tsā-ba rDo-rje grags-pa 
(1016–1128?). Later he wrote an extensive commentary on the Saṃpuṭa namely 
the Sambu ṭa’i rnam-bshad. In the colophon, rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-rje relates 
that he worked on the commentary with Ācārya Asaṃkīrti, viz. Slob-dpon 
Thogs-med grags (1108–1144), the son of rNgog Zhes-sdang rdo-rje, who was 
responsible for emending and supplementing his writing (rNgog Zhe-sdang 
rdo-rje 2011, vol. 5, 253).16

puṭatantra, the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgītitantra, the Mañjuśrīguhyapannatantra and the

The Transmitter of These Scriptures Mi-la Mi-bskyod rdo-rje
His titles rGyud-bzhi thabs-mkhas and Guoshi indicate that he was skilled in 
the Four Classes of Tantras and held the position of State Preceptor (Guoshi) at 
the Tangut court. The first part of his name 𗢧𘃜 [mer rjar] phonetically cor-
responds to Mi-la, a Tibetan clan name, and the latter part 𗅋𗚛𗍥𘟙 is a 
translation of Mi-bskyod rdo-rje, an initiating name of the Guhyasamājatantra. 
As Guoshi Mi-la Mi-bskyod rdo-rje transmitted and taught all three commen-
tarial documents penned by rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-rje to Piputifu, he seems to 
have been largely responsible for introducing the Saṃpuṭa teachings of the 
rNgog tradition into the Tangut land.
Thus, the first step in understanding how the cycle of the Saṃpuṭa arrived 
at Xixia from Tibet is to identify this Guoshi Mi-la Mi-bskyod rdo-rje. Unfor­
tunately, the early historical sources of the rNgog bKa’-brgyud-pa lineage bears 
no record of him. However in a list of the disciples of rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-
rje in the gDams-ngag bka’-rgya-can lnga-yi bla-ma brgyud-pa’i rnam-thar, the 
name Cog-ro Chos-rgyal, an abbreviated form of Cog-ro Chos-kyi rgyal-mtshan, 
attracted my attention.17 He will be the subject of the next section.
	
Cog-ro Chos-rgyal
Born in mDo-smad in 1108, Cog-ro Chos-kyi rgyal-mtshan (1108–1176), was a 
follower of rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-rje, but is better known as an outstanding 
disciple of Mar-pa Do-pa Chos-kyi dbang-phyug (1042–1136), from whom he 
received the teachings of Cakrasaṃvara in their entirety, including the hidden 
precepts.18 His life-story is told in the Deb-ther sngon-po and the Khrid-brgya’i 
(rNgog slob rgyud dang bcas pa’i gsung ’bum, Vol. I, 1–34, Pe cin: Krong go’i bod rig dpe 
sgron khang, 2013), he authored volumes 9 and 10. 
17	
The disciples of rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-rje are: slob ma rtsag dharma rāja/ ’gar bkra shis rin 
chen/ mtshe’u dar re/ mtshur dum bu kha pa/ rma bya pa chen po/ mal yer pa ba/ tre bo 
mgon po/ ngor rje kun dga’ ’od/ gshen pa rdo rje seng ge/ ram rdo rje grags/ myam med 
shākya ye shes/ cog ro chos rgyal/ mal nag pa/ lha phyug mkhar pa/ rngog tsha chos sku/ 
dran ston mtha’ bral/ rgya nam mkha’ dbang phyug/ lho nag pa gnyal pa rngog/ rgyal tsha 
rin chen mgon po sogs mtha’ yas pa byung//. See ’Phrin-las rgya-mtsho 2009, 347.
18	
There is even a rumor that the violent deaths of Mar-pa Do-pa and his son around 1136 
were connected to the master having given the secret instruction of the “Four Stages” (rim 
bzhi) to Cog-ro Chos-rgyal. This is considered quite dangerous. See the bibliography in the 
following note.

Saṃpuṭa and Cakrasaṃvara Tantras in the Xixia Period
brgyud-pa’i lo-rgyus.19 Having received teachings on the Hevajra cycle from 
rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-rje, Cog-ro Chos-kyi rgyal-mtshan wrote an exegesis, to 
date unrecovered, on the Hevajra, entitled Rin-chen ljong-shing zhes bya ba’i 
yig-cha. Still we have reason to believe that Cog-ro Chos-rgyal might have been 
familiar with rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-rje’s teachings on the Saṃpuṭa. In other 
words, it is possible that Cog-ro Chos-kyi rgyal-mtshan and Guoshi rGyud-
bzhi thabs-mkhas Mi-la Mi-bskyod rdo-rje followed the same lineage of the 
Saṃpuṭa.
It ought to be borne in in mind that the Saṃpuṭa has never been taught 
as an independent teaching but rather as an explanatory Tantra in the 
cycles of the Hevajra and Cakrasaṃvara (Elder 1978, 13–15; Szántó, 2013, 
350). In his Sambu ṭa’i rnam bshad, rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-rje in following 
Durjayacandra,20 regards the Saṃpuṭa as one of the six explanatory tantras of 
the Cakrasaṃvara.21 However, we find also that rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-rje takes 
the Saṃpuṭa as a nidāna of all Tantras and as a commentary shared by many 
Tantras, in particular the Cakrasaṃvara and Hevajra.22 As mentioned above, 
two documents recovered from the ruins of the Baisigou Pagoda, are related to 
the Cakrasaṃvara.23 Hence the corpus of the Saṃpuṭa unearthed in this loca-
tion was most probably associated with the transmission of the Cakrasaṃvara.
Returning to the biography of Cog-ro Chos-rgyal, according to the Deb-ther 
sngon-po, after the death of Mar-pa do-pa, he studied the Vajravārāhī cycle 
under the chief disciple of Ha-mu dkar-po, called dPyal-lo Kun-dga’ rdo-rje, 
and for six years engaged in meditation in the vicinity of gNam-mtsho. Later 
Cog-ro Chos-rgyal established the Me-dge lha-’tsho Monastery where he wrote

The Deb-ther sngon-po tells us that after the death of Cog-ro Chos-rgyal, his 
system of explanation was maintained by dGe-bshes Gushrī ’Brom-pa.25 Shen 
Weirong (2011) has suggested that Gushrī ’Brom-pa held the post of State 
Preceptor at the Tangut court.26 Although many details about the life and 
works of Cog-ro Chos-kyi rgyal-mtshan remain unclear, it is certain that his 
teaching on the Cakrasaṃvara spread to Xixia, as his widely admired commen-
tary has recently been recovered in its Chinese translation of the Tangut era. 
This commentary entitled Xinyi jixiang yinxuewang jilun wubixiuximu yiqie-
zhongzuishengshangleji benxu xianshiji (新譯吉祥飲血王集輪無比修習母一
切中最勝上樂集本續顯釋記, No. A00969, hereafter Xianshiji) is kept in the 
China National Library. It was first recovered and studied by Shen Weirong and 
was later included in the doctoral dissertation of Wei Wen at Remin University 
(Shen Weirong 2011, Wei Wen 2013a). The above-mentioned research has the 
document as a Ming Dynasty manuscript that was based on a printed version 
produced during the Tangut period. The title indicates that the scripture is a 
“new translation” of the Tibetan text dPal khrag ’thung gi rgyal po ’khor lo sdom 
par brjod pa rnal ’byor ma bla na med pa rgyud thams cad kyi bla ma bde mchog 
bsdus pa’i rtsa rgyud kyi don gsal ba, a commentary on the Cakrasaṃvara. To 
date, the Tibetan version has not been identified. The Chinese translation is 
not complete but preserves only the third volume of the original set in four 
volumes, commenting on the fourth to ninth chapters of the Cakrasaṃvara.

The Emperor ascertained it thoroughly.27
Shen has identified the compiler Śākya Bhikṣu Zhuang-lang Fachuang as Cog-ro 
Chos-kyi rgyal-mtshan, without providing further detail. Wei adds that Cog-ro, 
alternatively written as Cog-gru, refers to a renowned Tibetan clan from the 
Hexi Corridor (河西), to which belonged the famous Tibetan translator Cog-
gru Klu’i rgyal-mtshan of the Early Spread of Buddhism. Wei argues further 
that, the velar nasal shedding which often occurred in the Tang and Wudai 
Northwest Dialect caused zhuang to be pronounced like cog, but he does not 
reconstruct the phonetic of zhuang. A study on the phonetic notations found 
in the Tangut-Chinese bilingual dictionary Fanhan heshi zhangzhongzhu (番
漢合時掌中珠) shows that the initial consonants of the Chinese zhi-zhuang-
zhang group (知莊章) marked by syncretism and pronounced as [tʂ] by the 
Tangut period (Zhang 2000, 74–76). In view of these two arguments, I recon-
struct the phonetic of zhuang as [tʂua], corresponding to the pronunciation 
of cog in Amdo Tibetan. Regarding lang (𠺘), Wei cites Sun Bojun, who found 
evidence from the dhāraṇīs of the Tangut period that the graph is used to 
transliterate the Sanskrit syllable ro (Wei Wen 2013b, 308; Sun Bojun 2010, 79). 
Hence it is fully confirmed that Zhuang-lang is a phonetic transliteration of the 
Tibetan clan name Cog-ro, and Fachuang is literally a translation of Chos-kyi 
rgyal-mtshan.28
We shall now consider the title Śākya Bhikṣu of Cog-ro Chos-kyi rgyal-
mtshan. In Tangut Buddhist literature, Tibetan monks are normally granted 
the title 𘐀𘇂𗂧 or 𘇂𗂧(Central Land), while the religious title Śākya Bhikṣu 
is customarily given to monks of Chinese and Tangut origins. Hence the title 
Śākya Bhikṣu given to Cog-ro Chos-rgyal indicates an ambiguous ethnic identi-
fication that recalls the case of Rtsa-mi Lo-tsā-ba Sangs-rgyas Grags-pa (ca. 11th 
century). Born in the mDo-smad area, rTsa-mi is called in Tibetan sources 
either Bod-gyi Lo-tsā-ba (Tibetan translator) or Mi-nyag Lo-tsā-ba (Tangut 
translator) (Sperling 1994, 801–824). This identificatory admixture correlates

Let us turn to Śramaṇa Huizhao, who transmitted Cog-ro’s commentary

Wei,30 I put forward the following proposal for his status. This Expounder of 
Sūtra, Vinaya and Abhidharma Jizhen Guoshi Śramaṇa Huizhao appears to 
be a prominent monk of Chinese or Tangut origin, since at times the family 
name Li (李) is attached to his name. A Buddhist expert and linguist adept 
in Tangut and Tibetan languages, Jizhen Guoshi Śramaṇa Huizhao made a 
career in religious education, translation and saṅgha administration. During 
his lifetime, he was active in two areas: the capital Xingqing and the bor-
der region Edzina. In Xingqing, he served as State Preceptor. After retiring, 
Jizhen Guoshi Śramaṇa Huizhao returned to Wuminxiansheng Monastery 
(五明顯生寺) near Khara-Khoto, where he propagated religious teachings and

According to Songshi Xiaguozhuan (宋史夏國傳), from the year 1126 to 1136, the Tangut 
Emperor Chongzong Li Qianshun (崇宗李乾順, r. 1086–1139) waged several wars against

Dunnell argues that the Tangut graphs for 𗮔 and 𗭺 are interchangeable. Thus the two 
names 𘟛𗮔 and 𘟛𗭺, which transliterate into Chinese as 慧照 (huizhao) and 慧明 
(huiming), are identical, referring to the same person. To this point, Wei supplements that 
慧照 / 明 (huizhao/ming) is also written as 惠照 / 明 (huizhao/ming), as the Chinese 
characters 慧 and 惠 are phonetically and semantically similar to each other. In this way, 
Dunnell and Wei have recovered a considerable number of documents associated with 
our Guoshi Huizhao/ming (Cat. 391, Tang 97, inv. 810; Cat. 393, Tang. 101; Cat 404, Tang. 119, 
inv. 2621; Cat. 422, Tang. 168, inv. 5923; Cat. 711, Tang. 241, inv. 2543; Cat. 810, Tang. 150). 
Fractional information on Huizhao can be summarized as follows: the name Huizhao 
occurs twice with the surname Li (Cat. 381; Cat. 711). It indicates that he was most proba-
bly of Tangut or Chinese origin; Huizhao is designated as: “Deputy Director of the Saṅgha, 
Superintendent of the Three Studies Academy Śramaṇa Huiming/zhao” (Cat. 393, Tang 
101) and “Wumingxiansheng Monastery Expounder of Sūtra, Vinaya and Abhidharma 
Tibetan-Tangut Bilingual Bhikṣu Li Huiming/zhao” (Cat. 391, Tang 97, inv. 810). In the lat-
ter document, Huiming/zhao seems to be outranked the Wutaishan State Preceptor 
Knowledgeable in Three Vehicles Yang Zhichuang, as his name is listed at the first place as 
a translator. Besides, Wei has identified additional seven Tangut translations by Huizhao/
ming on the subject of the Cakrasaṃvara and Six Yogas of Nāropa, including 
𗤁𗹙𘝵𘓷𘄴𗑾 (Cat. 602–605, Tang. 371), 𗧠𗵋𘍞𗋅𗟻𗡶𘄳𗑾 (Cat. 593, 594, Tang. 325) 
and so forth. See Dunnell 2009, 58–64 and Wei Wen 2013b, 305–307.

translated Buddhist texts. Scholars have discovered a considerable number of

The translator Huiyun of Huangjian Yanshou Monastery has not yet been 
identified, yet his title supplies us with a vital evidence for dating this docu-
ment: “Huangjian” (皇建) is the reign title of Xiangzong Li Anquan (r. 1210–1211). 
Thus this line on the title page cited above should be interpreted as,
During the Huangjian era (1210/11), the Śramaṇa Huiyun from the Yanshou 
Monastery translated this work under an Imperial Edict.31
The last line of the colophon “The Emperor ascertained it thoroughly” implies 
that the Emperor Li Anquan assumed the duty of verifying the accuracy of the 
translation.
	
Sumatikīrti’s Journey to the Tangut Kingdom
Among the many recovered translations by Guoshi Huizhao, one document, 
which is entitled 𗠁𗫻𗟻𗡶𗹙𘅫 (Cat. 391, Tang. 91, inv. 810), deserves special 
attention. This text is a consecration text for stūpas and religious paintings, 
that according to Nishida Tatsuo, was translated into Tangut from the Tibetan 
31	
Wei suggests that the Xianshiji may have been produced between 1216 and 1227. He points 
out that in the phrase “Huangjian Yanshou Monastery”, Huangjian does not indicate the 
date of the translation, but that the monastery was built in the Huangjian era (1210–1211). 
Wei further argues that in the document (Cat. 393, Tang. 101) dated to 1216, Huizhao is not 
associated with the title Guoshi, see n. 29. Accordingly, he suggests that the document of 
the Xianshiji, in which the title Guoshi is attributed to Huizhao, must have been trans-
lated after the year 1216. Wei may have come to this conclusion based on the assumption 
that Guoshi was a life-tenure. Our limited knowledge of the Tangut Saṅgha Official Sys-
tem makes it difficult to refute Wei’s argument. However, I take Huangjian as the reign 
title of the Emperor Xiangzong, which simply indicates that the document was translated 
in the year 1210/11. Further evidence for my position is that in a pretext of a block printing 
the Huayan Sūtra (Avataṃsaka, TK. 88), which records an explicit manufacture date of 
1083, there appears a Śramaṇa Shouqiong (守瓊), who is said to have come from the Great 
Yanshou Monastery (大延壽寺) and to have been responsible for the printing and distri-
bution of the copies. If this Great Yanshou Monastery is indeed the same monastery 
where Huiming resided, the Yanshou Monastery would surely have been built up by the 
year 1083. See Wei Wen 2013, 307–308, Shi Jinbo 1988, 238.

work Rab-tu gnas-pa’i chos-ga (pratiṣṭhā-vidhi, Toh. 3139) (Nishida 1975, 34). Its

The Great Indian Paṇḍita of Five Classes of Knowledge (pañcavidyā) 
Sumatikīrti composed it,
sPyan-snga Lo-tsā-ba Prajñākīrti translated it into Tibetan,

In his bDe-mchog chos-’byung,33 Bu-ston relates that the Indian master 
Sumatikīrti came twice to Tibet and worked with several eminent Tibetan 
masters, such as rNgog Blo-ldan shes-rabs (1059–1109), Mar-pa Do-pa Chos-
kyi dbang-phyug, Klog-skya gZhon-nu ’bar, Lo-tsā-ba Prajñākīrti (Grags-’byor 
shes-rab) and others. Independently or with the assistance of his Tibetan 
colleagues, Sumatikīrti translated a large number of Indian texts and revised 
previous translations of both Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna scriptures. He was 
especially instrumental in the translation and propagation of Cakrasaṃvara 
teachings in Tibet. Bu-ston offers an interesting record of the later years of 
Sumatikīrti. In his bDe-mchog chos-’byung, he tells that, Sumatikīrti made his 
way into Tangut and served as initiating lama to the king. Later he built a 
monastery called Bhadanta Vihāra close to the boundary between Tangut and 
China. Sumatikīrti never returned to Tibet or Nepal but passed away in the 
Tangut land. The passage in question translates as follows:
Later Sumatikīrti said: “I am going to Mt. Wutaishan of China to search 
for certain substances for accomplishments.” Not heeding anyone who 
tried to dissuade him, he arrived to Tibet, after which he reached the 
Tangut-Xia kingdom. As a great merit arose, the Tanguts asked him to 
stay. He settled down there, serving as initiating lama to the king. After­
ward he wandered everywhere through the kingdom …

temple called Bhadanta Vihāra in the direction of China, where he 
ripened and liberated innumerable living-beings through Cakrasaṃvara

Saṃpuṭa and Cakrasaṃvara Tantras in the Xixia Period
and spread the Buddhist teachings widely. The Cakrasaṃvara cycle flour-

Kramer, in his study of rNgog Blo-ldan shes-rab, points out that rNgog collabo-
rated with the Indian master Sumatikīrti mainly during rNgog’s final years, ca. 
1092–1109 (Kramer 2007, 42–44). Accordingly, I assume that Sumatikīrti left 
Central Tibet after the death of rNgog Blo-ldan shes-rab, on a pilgrimage to Mt. 
Wutaishan, travelling via the mDo-khams region to the Tangut domain, where 
he served as the initiating lama of the Tangut king. In this case the Tangut King 
during that time must have been Chongzong Li Qianshun.
	
Conclusion
The unearthing of the corpus of the Tangut Saṃpuṭa and Cakrasaṃvara 
as well as other related tantric documents provide us with new insights on 
the Tibetan influence on Tangut Buddhist culture. Relying on both historical 
records and unearthed documents, this paper attempts to gather the fragmen-
tary evidence into a more complete picture of the spread and development of 
Tibetan tantric Buddhism in Xixia. In light of above findings, we can recon-
struct the transmission line of the Cakrasaṃvara from Tibet to Xixia through: 
Sumatikīrti, Mar-pa Do-pa, Cog-ro Chos-kyi rgyal-mtshan, Gushrī ’Brom-pa, 
… Jizhen Guoshi Huizhao, and Śramaṇa Huiyun. Similarly the lineage of the 
Saṃpuṭa cycle would be: rNgog Zhe-sdang rdo-rje, Cog-ro Chos-kyi rgyal-
mtshan, … rGyud-bzhi thabs-mkhas Guoshi Mi-bskyod rdo-rje, and Piputifu. 
These two lines cross at the point of Cog-ro Chos-kyi rgyal-mtshan, who was 
spiritually related to both Mar-pa Do-pa Chos-kyi dbang-phyug and to rNgog 
Zhe-sdang rdo-rje. The reconstruction presented here is by no means defini-
tive, but rather aims to advance the research of these Tangut tantric materials.

<!-- Page 385 -->

372
Hou
To date, the decipherment of Tangut Buddhist literature has relied almost 
entirely on Chinese sources, especially on Mahāyāna texts, while most transla-
tions of Tibetan tantric works during the Xixia period remain unidentified.35 
Scholars have not yet fully mined Tibetan sources, having underestimated their 
worth for Tangut grammar and linguistic studies. Our current understanding 
of the relations between Tibetan and Tangut Buddhism is thus tenuous, based 
mainly on scanty information extracted from fragmentary records found in 
Tibetan sources. While the field has advanced and findings have accumu-
lated, the patron-priest (yon-mchod) relation between the Tibetan lamas and 
the Tangut court has retained center stage.36 A grasp of the Tibetan impact 
on Tangut Buddhism, however, demands more than the investigation of a 
single issue in Tibetan historiographical writings. Rather, such understanding 
requires a framework for the comparative study of Tibetan and Tangut lan-
guages. As well, it calls for further philological investigation into the abundant 
Tibetan tantric works in both Tangut and Chinese languages held in the Khara-
Khoto and other collections.

Mongol Rulers, Yugur Subjects, and Tibetan Buddhism
Chapter 15
Mongol Rulers, Yugur Subjects, and Tibetan 
Buddhism
Translated by Ilia Mozias and Meir Shahar
Yang Fuxue and Zhang Haijuan Yang and Zhang
Tibetan Buddhism has played a pivotal part in Asian history. The formation of 
a distinct ethnic group with an equally distinct culture, the Yugurs (Chinese: 
Yugu zu 裕固族) is an excellent example of such influence. Officially recog-
nized as one of China’s fifty-six national minorities, the Yugurs reside in 
present-day Gansu Province. Their origins can be traced back to the Yuan 
period (1279–1368), when the local Uighur population (Chinese: Weiwuer zu 維
吾爾族) was ruled by a Mongol clan, (hereafter: the Bin 豳 Clan, after the title 
that was bestowed upon its chieftains by Kublai Khan (1215–1294)). The leaders 
of the Bin Clan were ardent supporters of Tantric Buddhism. Under their influ-
ence the Mongols and Uighurs converted to the Tibetan faith, a move that 
served to unite them. Their common religion enabled the Mongol rulers and 
their Uighur subjects to forge a very particular identity, to wit, the Yugur 
nationality.
The dual ethnic origins of the Yugurs—Uighur and Mongol—are linguisti-
cally attested. To this day, the Yugurs are split down the language divide: one 
group speaks a variant of the Uighur (Turkic) language whereas the other con-
verses in a Mongolian dialect. At the same time, their shared Tantric beliefs 
distinguish both subgroups from the Uighur Muslim population in Western 
Xinjiang Province while their Uighur heritage differentiates them from the 
Mongols to the north. Tibetan Buddhism has cemented a unique cultural iden-
tity, merging its originally distinct Mongol and Uighur elements. The Yugur 
case is a compelling example of the weight religion can carry in the creation of 
national identity.
This paper examines the processes by which Tibetan Buddhism became the 
Yugurs’ national religion. While scholars have examined the characteristics of 
the Yugur religion, its origins in the Mongol era have been largely overlooked.1 
The paper draws upon written documents and stele inscriptions from Chinese 
1	 On the Yugurs and their religion see, among others, He Weiguang 1999, 27; Zhong Jinwen 1991; 
He Weiguang and Zhong Fuzu 1998; He Weiguang and Zhong Fuzu 2000; Tang Jingfu 1996; Gu 
Xiefeng 2010; Abuduweli 2011.
©	 koninklijke brill nv, leiden, 2017 | doi 10.1163/9789004340503_017

<!-- Page 391 -->

378
 yang And Zhang
Central Asia, charting the roles of Mongol rulers, Uighur subjects, and Tibetan 
monks in crafting the Yugur identity. The period covered ranges from the thir-
teenth through the seventeenth century: From the patronage that the Mongol 
Yuan-Dynasty rulers extended to Tibetan Buddhism, through the subsequent 
Ming Dynasty (1368–1644) and into the first decades of the Qing Dynasty 
(1644–1911).
	
The Mongol Patronage of Tibetan Buddhism in Chinese Central 
Asia
Relations between the Uighurs and Tibetan Buddhism date back to the time of 
the Mongol empire. These relations became especially close after Tibetan 
Buddhism became the state religion of the Yuan dynasty (1279–1368), which 
was established by Kublai Khan (r. 1264–1294). During the first decades of 
Mongol rule, in the area of the Gansu Hexi corridor Uighur monks acted as 
intermediaries between the Mongol conquerors and Tibetan Buddhism. The 
“History of Sakya lineage” records that when Sakya Pandita (1182–1251) dis-
cussed Buddhist Dharma with Godan Khan (1206 –1251), an Uighur monk 
served as their interpreter. When, in Liangzhou, Sakya Pandita expounded 
Buddhist sūtras, “persons of great wisdom and merit from the Jin, Tibet, Uighur, 
Xixia and other countries came to listen to Buddhist Dharma” (Cai Rang 2004, 
50). Thirteenth-century Mongol rulers came into contact with Uighurs, who 
were well-versed in Tibetan Buddhism.
The thirteenth-century Uighurs whose descendants were to become the 
present-day Yugurs resided for the most part in the Gansu corridor. This popu-
lation was referred to in the literature of the Song-Period (960–1127) as the 
“Yellow-Headed Uighurs” (Huangtou Huihe 黄头回纥), a name which appears 
also in Central Asian sources.2 In the last decades of the thirteenth century, 
the Yellow-Headed Uighurs came under the control of a Mongol clan headed 
by Chagati Khan’s (1183–1242) fourth-generation descendants Chūbaī (Chinese: 
Chubai 出伯) and Qabān (Chinese: Haban 哈班). The two brothers took a stra-
tegic decision to align themselves with Kublai Khan to the east, rather than 
with the Chagatai Khanate to the west. The decision has had far-reaching con-
2	 Consult the entry on Khotan (Yutian 于闐) in Chapter 490 of the Songshi 宋史; and also sec-
tion four of the chapter on the barbarians (Fanyi si 蕃夷四) in the Song huiyao jigao 宋會要
輯稿. The Yelow-Headed Uighurs (Sárigh Uighurs) are mentioned in the writings of the 
Chagatai historian Mirza Muhammad Haidar (?–1551); see Elias and Ross 1972, 406.

<!-- Page 392 -->

379
Mongol Rulers, Yugur Subjects, and Tibetan Buddhism
sequences for the religious history of the Gansu corridor. Unlike the Uighurs of 
Xinjiang Province who—along with their Chagatai rulers—converted to Islam, 
the Yellow-Headed Uighurs of the Gansu corridor followed Emperor Kublai 
Khan in embracing Tibetan Buddhism.
Kublai Khan’s Yuan Dynasty bestowed upon the loyal Chūbaī, Qabān, and 
their descendants a series of royal titles including “Prince of Xi’ning” (Xininng 
Wang 西寧王) and “Prince of Bin” (Binwang 豳王). I will hereafter refer to the 
tribe of the two brothers as the Bin Clan. Adopting Tibetan Buddhism, and 
merging with its Uighur subjects, the Mongol rulers of the Bin Clan were to 
become part of the present-day Yugur nationality.
In the early years of the Yuan dynasty, the Mongol rulers, in order to consoli-
date their political power, promoted Buddhism in general and Tibetan 
Buddhism in particular. In 1246 a representative of the Mongol court, prince 
Godan met Sakya Pandita, the fourth of the Five Venerable Supreme Masters of 
the Sakya School. This event marked the incorporation of Tibet into the Mongol 
sphere of influence, no less than the adoption of Tantric Buddhism by the 
Mongol conquerors (Fan Baoliang and Shui Tianchang 1997, 84). The founder 
of the Yuan dynasty, Kublai Khan, appointed the fifth Supreme Master of the 
Sakya School, Drogön Chögyal Phagpa (1235–1280), as State Preceptor, making 
him supreme leader of all Buddhist communities in the empire. The emperor 
himself, as well as many members of the imperial family, converted to 
Buddhism. The members of his imperial court followed Kublai’s example, 
Tibetan Buddhism practically becoming the state religion.
Whereas the Mongol conquerors of the Chinese empire embraced Tibetan 
Buddhism, the Central Asian Uighurs were for the most part adherents of the 
(older) Chinese-style Buddhism. The religion of the Uighurs of the Gansu 
(Hexi) corridor—the future Yugurs—was a mix of Tibetan and the Chinese 
traditions. The balance shifted towards Tibetan Buddhism under the impact of 
the Mongol rulers. Beginning in the last decades of the thirteenth century the 
eastern Uighurs of the Gansu corridor gradually adopted Tibetan Tantric 
Buddhism.
The standard Chinese histories provide no information about the religious 
leanings of the Bin Clan. However their Tibetan Buddhist affiliation might be 
gleaned from manuscripts and stele inscriptions that were discovered in 
Dunhuang and other Chinese Central-Asian locations. Let us firstly consider 
two Dunhuang steles that were erected by the Prince of Xining Suleiman 速來
蠻, a member of the Bin clan: 1) The “Stele of the Six-syllable mantra from the 
Mogao cave” (莫高窟六字真言碣 Mogao liuzi zhenyan jie) (dated 1348); and 
2) “Record of the Restoration of the Huangqi monastery” (重修皇慶寺記, 
Chongxiu Hunagwing si ji), (dated 1351). In addition to the Mongol Prince of the

<!-- Page 393 -->

380
 yang And Zhang
Bin Clan Suleiman, several other donors are mentioned in the inscriptions 
including Yang’asha (養阿沙, Yaghan Shāh), Sudansha (速丹沙, Sultān Sh(āh)), 
and Asuday (阿速歹, Āsutāī) (Li Yongning 1982). It is noteworthy that the 
names of several donors—including Suleiman and Yaghān Shāh—betray an 
Islamic influence that predated the Bin Clan’s adoption of Tibetan Buddhism. 
In any event, the inscriptions themselves attest the donors’ Buddhist affilia-
tion. They record the establishment of a Buddhist monastery, transcribing the 
powerful six syllables mantra of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (Zhang 
Haijuan and Yang Fuxue 2011, 92–93).
The Buddhist leanings of the Bin Clan are similarly attested by a fourteenth-
century Uighur translation of the Tibetan Śrī-Cakrasaṃvara. Discovered at the 
Dunhuang Grottoes by Aurel Stein, the text bears Chinese and Uighur colo-
phons, respectively reading:
1.	
[This text] was translated by the venerable Ācārya from Hami (Kumul), 
following the instructions of Master Istonpa …  On the 4th day of the 6th 
month of the Tiger Year (being the 10th year of the Yuan-Dynasty 
Zhizheng reign period) [1350], I the humble Sarïγ Tutung from city of Üč 
Lükčüng, copied it under orders of Prince Asuday. Amen! Amen!3
2.	
vzir-lïγ baxšï-nïng adaq-lïγ qooš linxu-a-sïnga oγul yükünürmn (“I, 
Asuday, compassionately ordered the monk to devotedly copy this 
scripture”).
Prince Asuday of the Mongol Bin Clan is not mentioned in the standard Yuan 
History (Yuanshi 元史). His name is recorded, however, in the above-men-
tioned Dunhuang steles, which were erected by his father, the Prince of Xining, 
Suleiman. The text produced under Asuday’s patronage was a translation from 
the Tibetan of a Buddhist scripture. The colophon attests that it was copied in 
1350 in Shazhou (Dunhuang) by the Uighur Buddhist Master Sarïγ Tutung from 
Üč Lükčüng (modern Lukeqin in Shanshan county in Southwest Xinjiang), 
who followed the orders of Prince Asuday. It illustrates the Bin Prince’s devo-
tion to Tibetan Buddhism, no less than his patronage of Uighur Buddhist 
monks.
3	 哈密尊者阿阇黎(Ārya Ācārya)遵佟巴(Istonpa)大師之令翻譯 …… 至正十年(1350)虎年
六月初四日我三魯克沁(Üč Lükčüng)城之後學薩里都(Sarïs Tutung)奉阿速歹(Asuday)
王子之令寫。善哉！善哉！ The text is numbered: Or. 8212–109 (old number Ch. xix. 003); 
see Zieme and Kara 1970, 160–162; Yang Fuxue 1998, 123–124.

<!-- Page 394 -->

381
Mongol Rulers, Yugur Subjects, and Tibetan Buddhism
A Mongolian document discovered in 1989 in the northern edges of the 
Dunhuang Mogao caves similarly attests the patronage that was extended by 
the Mongol rulers to the Buddhist faith:
Because the teacher of the state, the master of ordination, lama Dorĵi-
Kirešis-Bal-Sangbo-lama (rDo-rje bka’-shis dpal-bzan-po) with his 
disciples are going to pass through Bars-Köl, Biš-Baliq and other areas in 
the region of Qara-Qočo, performing Buddhist pious acts and praying for 
blessing for all sentient beings, nobody is allowed to obstruct their 
journey. It is forbidden to impound their money, carriages, camels or 
horses.4
The person giving the order was Kedmen Baghatur, who likely served as gover-
nor of the Turpan Region. Contemporaneous with the Bin Clan control of the 
Gansu corridor, his order evinces the support that was given during the four-
teenth century by diverse Mongol commanders to the Buddhist faith (Zhang 
Haijuan and Yang Fuxue 2011, 90).
In addition, the Princes of the Bin Clan supported the construction of 
Buddhist monasteries and cave temples. For example, the patronage that was 
extended by the Bin Prince Nomdaš for the restoration of the Wenshu 
(Mañjuśrī) Monastery is recorded in a bilingual Chinese-Uighur inscription, 
which was discovered at Jiuquan (Geng Shimin and Zhang Baoxi 1986). Another 
Buddhist establishment, the Huangqi Monastery, was restored by the Xining 
Prince Suleiman, as recorded in the above-mentioned stele inscription. Prince 
Suleiman likewise sponsored the erection of the Six-Syllables Mantra Stele, 
transcribing the powerful Tantric spell in six different scripts: Tibetan, Sanskrit, 
Uighur, ‘Phags-pa, Tangut and Chinese. It might further be noted that the 
Dunhuang Mogao Cave number 464 was restored by Uighur believers under 
the patronage of the Bin Princes (Yang Fuxue 2012a). Finally, Uighur poems 
discovered at the Dunhuang Mogao Caves praise the Bin Prince Suleiman for 
his support of the Buddhist faith, attesting the close relation between the 
Mongol ruler and his Uighur subjects (Yakup 2011).
During their control of the Gansu corridor, the Mongol Princes of the Bin 
Clan propagated Buddhism, resisting the Islamic encroachment from the West. 
It is noteworthy that they lend their support not only to the region‘s traditional 
Chinese-style Buddhism, but also to Tibetan Buddhism. Under Mongol patron-
age the Uighurs of the Gansu corridor established two centers of Tibetan 
Tantric Buddhism: In Dunhuang and in Jiuquan. The latter center has yielded 
4	 Document number B163:42; see Matsui, 2008, 160.

<!-- Page 395 -->

382
 yang And Zhang
an important document attesting that Buddhism was practiced by some 
Uighurs as late as the seventeenth century. It is an Uighur translation of the 
Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra, titled Altun önglüg yaruq yaltrïqlï qopta kötrül-miš 
nom iligi atlïγ nom bitig, and dated to the 26th year of the Kangxi reign (1687). 
Discovered in Jiuquan, the text was copied in Dunhuang by several Uighur 
Buddhist clerics including Bilgä Talui Šabï, Ratna Vijra Šabï, and Čaxsapat 
Manggal Toyin (Suvarṇaprabhāsa 1992, 343–344; Kaya 1994, 207).
Today, the Uighur language is written in Arabic letters. The 1687 Uighur 
translation of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra, however, is written in the earlier 
Uighur script, which was invented in the eighth century. The Uighur Buddhist 
Sūtras survive in this anceint Uighur script (which is called in Chinese Hugu 
wen 回鶻文). Scholars have deemed the 1687 Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra the latest 
extant specimen of the ancient Uighur script, until the recent discovery of 
roughly contemporaneous inscriptions from the Thousand-Buddhas Caves 
(Wanfo Dong 萬佛洞) in Jiuquan. Bearing dates ranging from 1551 to 1713 the 
Thousand-Buddha inscriptions are written in the same ancient Uighur script. 
Furthermore, they mention a monk named Bilgä Talui, who is likely the very 
same Bilgä Talui Šabï who contributed to the 1687 translation of the 
Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra (Israpil and Zhang Baoxi 2012). The emergence of the 
Buddhist Yugur nationality should be considered in the context of the diffu-
sion—in the ancient Uighur script—of Buddhist scriptures. The 1687 
Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra, like the Uighur inscriptions from the Thousand-
Buddhas Caves, attests that Uighur clerics propagated Buddhist sūtras, written 
in the ancient Uighur script, all throught the early eighteenth century.
	
Monk Blue-Ox
Dating from the Wanli reign period (1573–1619), The History of the Su-Garrison 
Chinese and Barbarians (Suzhen huayi zhi 肅鎮華夷志) mentioned a “Monk 
Blue-Ox” (Qingniu heshang 青牛和尚),who had been active during the pre-
ceding Jiajing period (1522–1566). The brief account of the mysterious monk is 
intriguing for its suggestion of Uighur involvement in Tibetan Buddhism:
There was once a “Monk Blue Ox.” His name was Gege-Bashi. He was a 
foreign cleric hailing from Tibet. He pulled a blue ox, recited the Buddhist 
scriptures, and begged alms for a living. Arriving at Shazhou (Dunhuang) 
he took refuge with the Yuan Prince of Erjiao [Anding], Dawo. He mar-
ried the Prince’s daughter.5
5	 時有青牛和尚，曰哥哥把失者乃巫師臧之番僧，牽青牛一隻，念經乞化為生逰至
沙州地界，投元之達臥耳交王部下，娶達女為妻. See Li Yingkui 2006, 275–276.

<!-- Page 396 -->

383
Mongol Rulers, Yugur Subjects, and Tibetan Buddhism
The Chinese text identifies the foreign monk as belonging to the Tibetan per-
suasion, an affiliation that is corroborated by the fact of the cleric’s marriage. 
At the same time the monk’s name is unmistakably Uighur: Bashi is the likely 
Chinese transliteration of the Turkish/Uighur word baqši (“Buddhist master”), 
and Gege probably transliterates the Turkish/Uighur word kök (“blue”) 
(Clauson 1972, 321, 708). (Blue is a favorite Uighur color, often making its 
appearance in personal names).6 The local magnate with whom the Uighur 
practitioner of Tibetan Buddhism sought refuge was a descendant of the 
Mongolian Prince of Bin, whose title was changed during the Ming Period to 
Prince of Anding 安定 (or, as the text has it, Prince Erjiao).7
	
Conclusion
During the Yuan Dynasty, the Mongol Princes of the Bin tribe maintained close 
relations with the Yellow-Headed Uighurs of the Gansu Corridor. Embracing 
the local Uighur culture, the rulers eventually comingled with their subjects, 
giving birth to a new ethnic group: The Yugurs. Tibetan Buddhism cemented 
the cultural identity of the novel nationality. Their Tantric faith distinguishes 
the Yugurs from the Xinjiang Uighurs, who are followers of Islam. At the same 
time, their Uighur heritage differentiates the Yugurs from the Mongols of Inner 
Mongolia. The Yugurs feature a unique culture that combines Mongol and 
Uighur elements within the expansive rubric of Tibetan Buddhist practice.8

The Chinese Origins of Dali Esoteric Buddhism
Chapter 16
The Chinese Origins of Dali Esoteric Buddhism
Translated by Ilia Mozias and Meir Shahar 
Hou Chong
Situated between China, Tibet, and India the Dali 大理 region of Yunnan 
Province is home to a living tradition of esoteric Buddhism. The origins of this 
esoteric tradition—which is known as the “Religion of the Ācāryas” (Azhali 
jiao 阿吒力教, or Asheli jiao 阿阇梨教)—have long puzzled scholars. Each of 
the civilizations surrounding it has been proposed as the source of Dali eso-
teric Buddhism. Some have argued that Yunnan inherited its esoteric tradition 
from medieval China; others have sought similarities between it and the adja-
cent Tibetan tradition; others still have claimed that the Tantric movement 
had been transmitted to Yunnan directly from its native India. Adding to the 
confusion, some scholars have highlighted the singularity of the “Religion of 
the Ācāryas,” considering it a distinct system in its own right. This supposedly 
autonomous tradition is sometimes referred to as Dianmi 滇密 (Yunnan 
Esoteric Buddhism).
In this essay I examine the origins of Yunnan esoteric Buddhism from the 
perspective of written documents and art works that can be traced back—
directly or indirectly—to the Dali-Kingdom Period (937–1253). I demonstrate 
the indebtedness of these documents to earlier Chinese sources. The Dali 
scriptures are textually related to Chinese antecedents (some of which have 
been discovered at the famed Dunhuang grottoes in Chinese Central Asia). 
Hence, I suggest that the foundations of Dali esoteric Buddhism were laid in 
medieval China. The Dali religion is an offshoot of the esoteric tradition that 
crystallized in medieval China.
The essay is divided into three parts: The first examines three Dali manu-
scripts that outline the esoteric “ritual of feeding the hungry ghosts” (shishiyi 
施食儀); the second analyzes the scriptural sources of the famed Kunming 
dhāraṇī-pillar (jingchuang 經幢); and the third returns to the above-men-
tioned manuscripts in the larger context of the Water and Land Rites to which 
they were intimately related. The three sections alike evince the indebtedness 
of the Dali materials to earlier Chinese antecedents. Evidently, the Dali 
Kingdom inherited its esoteric tradition from medieval China.
The essay builds upon earlier research projects of mine that have sought to 
demonstrate the Chinese origins of Yunnan esoteric Buddhism. In previous

studies I have inspected other texts and art works dating from the Nanzhao 南
詔 (738–902) and Dali Kingdom (937–1253) periods, all of which similarly draw 
upon Chinese sources (Hou Chong 1995, 2001, 2006, 2012a, 2012b).
	
Feeding the Hungry Ghosts
In 1956, Fei Xiaotong 費孝通 and his colleagues conducted field work at the 
small village of Beitangtian 北湯天 in the outskirts of Dali. The village was 
home to the Dong 董 clan, whose members had served—during the Dali-
Kingdom period—as “national preceptors.” The clan’s ancestral temple yielded 
several manuscripts, which shed invaluable light on the evolution of Dali eso-
teric Buddhism. Three of these concern the ritual of feeding the hungry ghosts 
(Hou Chong 2006, 2012c):1
a	
The Esoteric Ritual of Food Distribution [ for the Hungry Ghosts]
Dating from the Dali-Kingdom period (937–1253), this single-scroll (juan 卷) 
handwritten manuscript is fastened by “whirlwind binding” (xuanfeng Zhuang 
旋風裝). Severely damaged, its opening and ending are missing. It is currently 
stored at the Yunnan Provincial Library. It has not been included in any printed 
edition of Buddhist canon.
The text consists entirely of the invocation writs (qiqing wen 啟請文) that 
are used in esoteric ritual. It carries several titles and colophons including: 
“Written by the State Preceptor, the Ācārya [Teacher] Wang Dezhang” (Guoshi 
azuoli Wang Dezhang shu 國師阿左梨王德彰書); “The National Preceptor 
Abhiṣeka [Initiation] Ācārya [Teacher] Wang Qiande” (Guoshi guanding azuoli 
Wang Qiande 國師灌頂大阿左梨王乾德); and “The Food-Distribution [Rituals] 
for Averting Calamities and Attaining Purity” (Xizai chujing sanshi 息災觸淨散
食). Hence modern scholars have titled it The Esoteric Ritual of Food Distribution 
[ for the Hungry Ghosts] (Mijiao sanshi yi 密教散食儀).
b	
Rituals for the Dharma Assembly of Unobstructed Lamps and Food
The contents of this early-Ming handwritten manuscript date to the Dali-
Kingdom period. A copy is preserved in the library of the Yunnan Academy of 
Social Sciences. The manuscript bears no title and its opening is missing. 
Originally in scroll form, it was cut and bound as a book at some unknown 
1	 On later-period Dali manuscripts that concern the feeding of hungry ghosts see Hou Chong 
2008a, 119–126.

<!-- Page 404 -->

391
The Chinese Origins of Dali Esoteric Buddhism
date. It is not found in any edition of the Buddhist canon, but a modern printed 
edition is available (Fang Guangchang 2011, 25–38).
Contemporary scholars dubbed the text Rituals for the Dharma Assembly of 
Unobstructed Lamps and Food (Wuzhe dengshi fahuiyi 無遮燈食法會儀) on the 
basis of similar expressions in the body of the text. That the rituals in question 
figured in eleventh- and twelfth-century Yunnan is attested by references to 
Dali-Kingdom institutions, monasteries, and monks.
Puzzlingly, the manuscript is dated, “The thirty-fifth year of Emperor 
Hongwu”. This emperor reigned for no more than thirty-one years (1368–1398). 
The alleged thirty-fifth year of his reign was in fact the fourth year (1402) of the 
reign of his successor, the Jianwen Emperor (reigned 1399–1402). The latter’s 
throne was usurped by the Yongle Emperor (reigned 1403–1424) who sought to 
obliterate his predecessor’s memory, eliminating his reign years—hence the 
confused dating, attesting that the current manuscript was copied during the 
Yongle reign (between 1403 and 1424) from an earlier one (dated 1402).
It might be mentioned that the text’s calligraphic style—and orthographic 
errors—might help us decipher contemporary Dali manuscripts such as The 
Compass of State Protection (Huguo Sinan chao 護國司南抄).
c	
Rituals for the Bodhimaṇḍa of Unobstructed Widespread Offerings
Fastened in butterfly-style binding (hudie zhuang 蝴蝶裝), a copy of this hand 
written manuscript is preserved at the Yunnan provincial library. Missing its 
title page, I have chosen to name it the Rituals for the Bodhimaṇḍa of Unob­
structed Widespread Offerings (Guangshi wuzhe daochang yi 廣施無遮道場儀). 
The text appears in no printed edition of the Buddhist canon.
It has previously been thought that the text is identical to the Rituals for the 
Bodhimaṇḍa of the Great Black God [Mahākāla] (Dahei tianshen daochang yi 大
黑天神道場儀) (on which see the following chapter by Megan Bryson). 
However, a careful comparison of the two Dali Kingdom manuscripts reveals 
significant differences. Indeed, Rituals for the Bodhimaṇḍa of Unobstructed 
Widespread Offerings might be considered extremely important not only as a 
source on Dali esoteric Buddhism but also as an example of the Sinicization of 
Buddhism at large.
The rituals of feeding the hungry ghosts that are outlined in the above three 
manuscripts are by no means unique to Dali. On the contrary, identical ritual 
procedures have been outlined in earlier Chinese sources. Particularly signifi-
cant in this respect is the ninth- or tenth-century Supreme Scripture of the Vajra 
(Jingang jun jing 金剛峻經, P. 3913), which has been discovered at the Dunhuang 
grottoes. The Supreme Scripture does not merely predate the Dali texts; it is 
also much longer, elaborating upon the same rituals in much greater detail.

<!-- Page 405 -->

392
Hou
Hence, the direction of influence must have been from the Chinese scripture 
to the Yunnan manuscripts rather than vice-versa (Hou Chong 2008b).
The Supreme Scripture of the Vajra recalls other Dunhuang manuscripts that 
portray the feeding of hungry ghosts. These texts—P.3861, P.3861, BD05298, 
S.3427, S.1147, S.1160, S.4454, S.5232, and P.3162—share with the Dali scriptures 
language, rituals and divinities. Thus, for example they equally celebrate the 
Five Tathāgatas (Prabhūtaratna-tathāgata 多寶如來, Abhayaṃkara-tathāgata 
離怖畏如來, Vipulakāya-tathāgata 廣博身如來, Surūpakāya-tathāgata 妙色身
如來, Āmṛta-rāja-tathāgata 甘露王如來); they quote the same mantras; and 
they provide identical guidelines for the construction of the maṇḍala and the 
distribution of food (Hou Chong 2010, Shi Jingpeng 2013). Particularly instruc-
tive is the appearance in the Dali texts of the Chinese concept of the “precepts 
that are grounded in the purity of the mind” (xindi jie 心地戒). This concept 
evolved in Chan circles—indeed the Supreme Scripture of the Vajra details a 
genealogy of teachers that is based upon Chan sources. This same genealogy is 
reproduced in a Dali manuscript—The Ritual Chapter of the Progressive 
Attainment of the Perfect Realization of Nine Contemplation (Ci chengjiu jiuguan 
jiguo yigui pin 次成就九觀極果儀軌品) (Guo Huiqing 2008, 115). The occur-
rence of a Chan genealogy in a Dali esoteric text attests its Chinese origins. The 
synthesis of esoteric rites and Chan hagiography originated in China. There 
can be no doubt as to the Chinese origins of the Dali esoteric rites. (On the rela-
tion of Chinese Chan to esoteric Buddhism see Robert Sharf’s chapter 4 and 
Lin Pei-ying’s chapter 5).
	
The Kunming Dhāraṇī-pillar
Among the most striking monuments of Dali-Kingdom art is a sculpted pillar 
inscribed with the Uṣṇīṣa vijaya dhāraṇī (Foding zunsheng 佛頂尊勝) (The 
Spell of the Glory of the Buddha’s Crown). Arranged in eight different layers, 
nearly three hundred images of Buddhist divinities are carved on the pillar, 
which rises over six meters. It was originally part of the Kunming Kṣitigarbha 
monastery (Dizang si 地藏寺), which was destroyed in the nineteenth century. 
Currently, the pillar is stored at the Kunming Municipal Museum, which is 
located on the same spot as the defunct temple (see figures 16.1 and 16.2).2
The practice of inscribing the Uṣṇīṣa vijaya dhāraṇī on pillars was intro-
duced to Yunnan from China. Recent scholarship has revealed the enormous 
significance of such stone monuments in medieval Chinese religious practice. 
2	 On the pillar’s modern vicissitudes, see Chen Guyi n.d.

<!-- Page 407 -->

394
Hou
By merely passing underneath the pillar’s shadow, or being blessed by a gush of 
wind carrying microscopic particles of it, a person would be cleansed of evil 
karma. Saving the souls of the living and the dead alike, dhāraṇī monuments 
were erected throughout Tang-period China (Liu Shufen 2008; Paul Copp 2014, 
141–196). The presence of the Uṣṇīṣa vijaya pillar in Dali religious representa-
tions speaks to the Chinese roots of the latter. In the following brief comments 
I will go one step further, arguing that additional texts that are inscribed on the 
same pillar likewise communicate the indebtedness of the “Religion of the 
Ācāryas” to Chinese Buddhism (exoteric and esoteric alike). In this respect my 
analysis differs from that of Angela Howard, who has sought in the Kunming 
pillar influences ranging from Burma and India to Tibet (Howard 1997).
In addition to the Uṣṇīṣa vijaya spell (inscribed in Sanskrit letters), the pillar 
is engraved with four Chinese-language texts:
a.
 The Record of [how] the Buddhist Follower and Prime Minister of the Dali
Kingdom, Yuan Douguang, Respectfully Erected the Uṣṇīṣa vijaya Precious
Pillar (Dali guo Fodizi yishi buxie Yuan Douguang jingzao Foding Zun­
sheng baochuang ji 大理國佛弟子議事布燮袁豆光敬造佛頂尊勝寶
幢記). This inscription details the political circumstances under which
the pillar was erected around 1200 CE, naming the relevant civil and

military officials. Of the several inscriptions that are carved on the pillar, 
it is the only one transcribed in local gazetteers and collections of stele 
inscriptions such as the Newly Compiled Yunnan Gazetteer (Xinzuan 
Yunnan tongzhi 新纂雲南通志) and the Selected Inscriptions on Metal 
and Stone (Jinshi cuibian 金石萃編). The inscription has been translated 
by Angela Howard (Howard 1997, 69–71).
b.
 The Heart Sūtra, or in its full title: The Sūtra of the Heart of the Perfection
of Transcendent Wisdom (Bore boluomiduo xinjing 般若波羅蜜多心經
(Prajñā­pāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra)), in Xuanzang’s 玄奘 (602–664) famed
translation (see figure 16.3). The occurrence of this—the most popular
of all Chinese scriptures—on the Yunnan sacred relic is ample evidence
of its derivation from a Chinese model.
c.
The Four Great Vows of the Bodhisattva (Si hong shiyuan 四弘誓願).
Found in a vast number of Chinese-language Mahāyāna scriptures, this
text—like the preceding one—attests the Chinese impact on Dali
Buddhism.
d.
The Vow of the Venerable Vairocana (Dari zun fayuan 大日尊發願). This
has been the least studied of the four Chinese documents. I provide

below a transcription of this esoteric text (see appendix), of which the 
only other printed edition is riddled with errors.3
The Vow of the Venerable Vairocana draws upon Chinese scriptures dedicated 
to the principal esoteric deity. Its significance lies not only in its attestation of 
the monument’s Chinese orientation, but also in that it has informed its ico-
nography. In my view, the Vow of the Venerable Vairocana provides the key for 
the identification of the pillar’s nearly three hundred carved images. In the 
brief comments that follow I will use this largely neglected document to iden-
tify some of the pillar’s sculpted images, correcting what I consider to be errors 
in previous scholarship:
On the first (lowest) level of the pillar are eight writhing dragons, depicting 
the Vow of Venerable Vairocana reference to the “Eight Elevated Dragon Kings” 
(Longwang bashangshou 龍王八上首); on its second level are the four Heavenly 
Kings (Lokapālas) following the inscription’s allusion to the “Esoteric Devas at 
the Four Gates” (Simen yao mi tian 四門要密天). They should be identified as: 
Dhṛtarāṣṭra 持國天王 in the east, Virūḍhaka 增長天王 in the south, Virūpākṣa 
廣目天王 in the west, Vaiśravaṇa 毘沙門天王 in the north.
Correctly identified by Angela Howard, on the pillar’s third level are four 
Buddhas. Proceeding clockwise, they are (in the east) Akṣobhya Buddha 阿閦
佛; (in the south) Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha 寶生佛; (in the west) Amitābha 
Buddha 阿彌陀佛; and (in the north) Amoghasiddhi Buddha 不空成就佛 
(Howard, 1997, 40).
The fourth level features four Bodhisattvas which, judging by the Vow of 
Venerable Vairocana, ought to be identified (proceeding clockwise from east to 
north) as Vajragarbha (Jin’gang zang 金剛藏); Ākāśagarbha (Xukong zang 
虛空藏); Avalokiteśvara (Guanzizai 觀自在); and Gaganagañja (虛空庫) (who 
is also known as Viśvakarma 毗首羯磨 or Vajrakarma 金剛業). According to 
the eighth-century Amoghavajra, the fourth one became known as “Store of 
Emptiness” (Gaganagañja) due to his miraculous ability to fill the empty space 
with treasures, transforming it into a veritable treasury (See T. 871, 18:292a).
The failure of previous research to identify the four Bodhisattvas seems to 
have stemmed from the short shrift scholars have given to the Vow of the 
Venerable Vairocana. In this work, the Bodhisattvas are identified with the four 
types of pure cognition: “Great mirror cognition” (Dayuanjing zhi 大圓鏡智); 
“Equality in nature cognition (Pingdengxing zhi 平等性智); “Wondrous observ-
