397
The Chinese Origins of Dali Esoteric Buddhism
ing cognition” (Miaoguancha zhi 妙觀察智); and Unrestrained activity 
cognition (Chengsuozuo zhi 成所作智) (see appendix).
The third and fourth levels, as well as the fourth and fifth levels, are sepa-
rated by octagonal cornices, which are each ornamented with images of 
floating Buddhas. The total number of sixteen bands—eight in each octagonal 
cornice—correspond to the “Sixteen Blessed Eons” (Yishiliu xianjie 一十六賢
劫; Sanskrit: Bhadra-Kalpa) that are mentioned in the pillar’s Vow of the 
Venerable Vairocana.
The pillar is crowned by a wish-granting jewel (Sanskrit: cintā-maṇi) under 
which are eight female divinities, which should be identified with the “Greatly 
compassionate eight female deities” (Dabeiba fomu 大悲八佛母) that are 
mentioned in the Vow of the Venerable Vairocana. Their images are similar to 
those of Uṣṇīṣa vijaya-related female divinities that have been found elsewhere 
in Yunnan (Wang Ningsheng 1980. 153; Sun Taichu 1983, 82).
Erected at the height of the Dali Kingdom period, the Kunming dhāraṇī pil-
lar demonstrates the impact of both exoteric and esoteric Chinese Buddhism. 
The former include the The Four Great Vows of the Bodhisattva and the 
immensely popular Heart Sūtra. The latter feature the Uṣṇīṣa vijaya dhāraṇī 
and The Vow of the Venerable Vairocana, which draws upon Tang-Period scrip-
tures that are dedicated to the august esoteric god.
	
Water and Land Rites
The rites of the “Water and Land Dharma Assembly” (Shuilu fahui 水陸法會) 
are considered a distinctive feature of the Chinese religious tradition. 
Appeasing the hungry ghosts of water and land, the elaborate rites work to 
ensure the welfare of the living. The water and land rites, which tradition 
ascribes to Emperor Liang Wudi 梁武帝 (464–549), evolved during the medi-
eval period to include esoteric elements (Hou Chong 2014). Dunhuang 
manuscripts attest the centrality of esoteric divinities and ritual tools—man-
tra, mudrā, and maṇḍala—in the performance of the magnificent rites.4 
4	 Consider the following Dunhuang manuscripts: 1) Dongdu fayuan wen 東都發願文 (P. 2189); 
2) Tanfa yize 壇法儀則 (available in a significant number of copies including P. 3913, S. 2144, 
Beidun 02074 and more); 3) Jingangjie da Piluzhena fo she zhuishang dacheng mimi 金剛界
大毘盧遮那佛攝最上大乘秘蜜 (S. 2272 back); 4) Jingang nianba jie, sanshi fa 金剛廿八
戒、散食法 (available in a significant number of copies including P. 3861, S. 2685, Beidun 
06504 back, and more); 5) Jietan sanshi huixiang fayuan wen 結壇散食迴向發願文 (S. 2144 
back, S. 3875, S. 5232, and Beidun 05298); 6) Sanshi wen 散食文 (available in a significant 
number of copies including S. 3914, S. 4306, P. 3149 and more); 7) Wuzhe dahui shuwen 無遮

<!-- Page 411 -->

398
Hou
During the Song and Ming periods, the water and land rites gained increasing 
popularity, influencing the visual arts. The pantheon of esoteric divinities that 
were summoned to pacify the hungry ghosts became the subject of elaborate 
paintings.
My recent research indicates that the Chinese Water and Land rites were 
practiced in the Dali Kingdom. Preliminary results of my investigation having 
been published elsewhere (Hou Chong 2010, Hou Chong 2012d, Hou Chong 
2013, Hou Chong forthcoming), I will merely mention some of the texts that are 
the focus of my current research: 1) The Rituals for the Dharma Assembly of 
Unobstructed Lamps and Food (Wuzhe dengshi fahuiyi 無遮燈食法會儀) (text b 
of the three mentioned above); 2) Rituals for the Bodhimaṇḍa of Unobstructed 
Widespread Offerings (Guangshi wuzhe daochang yi 廣施無遮道場儀) (text c of 
the three mentioned above); and 3) Rituals for the Bodhimaṇḍa of the Great 
Black God [Mahākāla] (Dahei tianshen daochang yi 大黑天神道場儀) (on 
which see the following chapter by Megan Bryson). These Dali texts share a 
nomenclature, pantheon of esoteric divinities, and ritual procedures with the 
Water and Land manuals from Dunhuang. They are reminiscent especially of 
the Maṇḍala Ritual Methods (Tanfa yize 壇法儀則) (which is available in a sig-
nificant number of Dunhuang manuscripts such as P. 3913).
The Water and Land Rites continued to figure in Yunnan all through the 
Ming period (1368–1644), which brought a new influx of esoteric Buddhist 
texts from China. The Dong Clan’s ancestral temple has yielded a Ming-period 
manuscript titled The Rituals of the Bodhimaṇḍa of the Great Dharma Un­
obstructed and Widespread Feast (Chongguang fashi wuzhe dazhai daochang yi 
重廣法施無遮大齋道場儀) (sometimes referred to as the Rituals of the Water 
and land Feast (Shuilu zhai yi 水陸齋儀). Outlining the ritual procedures that 
crystalized in Song-period China, the text is attributed to monk Zujue (祖覺, 
1087–1150). The Chinese Water and Land Rites have served as a model for 
Yunnan religious practice.

Chapter 17
Chapter 17
Between China and Tibet: Mahākāla Worship and 
Esoteric Buddhism in the Dali Kingdom
Megan Bryson
Mahākāla, the “Great Black One,” was a tutelary deity for the rulers of the Dali 
大理 kingdom (937–1253), which governed a large swath of territory between 
Song China and Tibet. Of the six ritual texts found only in Dali, one is a sādhana 
text that describes his seven forms as well as his consort; modern scholars have 
called this untitled manuscript Dahei tianshen daochang yi 大黑天神道場儀 
(Rituals for the Bodhimaṇḍa of the Great Black God). In addition, two food-dis-
tribution ritual texts—the Wuzhe dengshi fahui yi 無遮燈食法會儀 (Rituals for 
the Dharma Assembly of Unobstructed Lamps and Food) and Guangshi wuzhe 
daochang yi 廣施無遮道場儀 (Rituals for the Bodhimaṇḍa of Unobstructed 
Widespread Offerings)—include Mahākāla and his consort in their list of dei-
ties invited to the ritual area. Images of Mahākāla appear in the 1170s painting 
Fanxiang juan 梵像卷 (Roll of Buddhist Images), the Buddhist carving site 
Shibao shan 石寶山, and several other places in Dali territory. These sources 
suggest that Mahākāla was one of the most important figures in the pantheon 
of the Dali kingdom.
Mahākāla played a similarly prominent role in Tibetan Buddhism, but does 
not appear to have had a sizeable cult in the Song dynasty (960–1279). Given 
Dali’s proximity to Tibet, it would thus seem likely that Dali-kingdom Buddhists 
adopted their Mahākāla worship from their neighbors to the northwest, espe-
cially considering the Tibetan source of the Tangut Mahākāla cult seen in 
materials from the Western Xia kingdom (1038–1227). However, sources from 
the Dali kingdom show that their Mahākāla worship relied primarily on 
Chinese texts and Indian iconography; there is no evidence that Dali Buddhists 
looked to Tibet for materials related to the deity. In this, the Dali-kingdom 
Mahākāla cult more closely resembles the worship of Mahākāla in Japan, 
which also used Chinese materials as a foundation.
Japan’s geographical position explains why its Mahākāla tradition would 
come from China rather than Tibet, but why would Buddhists in the Dali king-
dom, located near both Song China and Tibet, look to the region with a less 
developed system of Mahākāla worship? Moreover, why would they borrow 
this deity’s iconography from a different area, so that it conforms to neither 
©	 koninklijke brill nv, leiden, 2017 | doi 10.1163/9789004340503_019

<!-- Page 416 -->

403
Between China and Tibet
Tibetan nor Chinese Mahākāla images? This paper argues that ruling elites in 
the Dali kingdom adopted their Mahākāla cult from China due to historical 
contact between the two regions, but represented their Mahākāla as Indian to 
align themselves with Buddhism’s source. Furthermore, Mahākāla’s relative 
obscurity in Song Buddhism allowed him to offer his protective powers espe-
cially to the Dali kingdom.
The combination of Chinese texts, Indian images, and local innovations in 
the Dali kingdom’s Mahākāla cult represents its esoteric Buddhist tradition in 
general. Recent work by Hou Chong and Henrik Sørensen (including the for-
mer’s contribution to this volume) has shown that most esoteric Buddhist 
texts from the Dali kingdom either came from Tang-Song China or relied heav-
ily on Chinese texts. The art historians Lee Yü-min and Moritaka Matsumoto 
have argued that Dali-kingdom Buddhist sculpture and painting also followed 
Tang-Song stylistic models (Lee Yü-min 1991; Matsumoto Moritaka 1976). 
However, these Buddhist images often used Indian iconographies that did not 
appear in China. The rulers of the Dali kingdom, like Buddhists everywhere, 
combined texts, images, and rituals from multiple sources with local practices 
to create a distinct regional tradition of esoteric Buddhism. In fact, I suggest 
that rather than ascribing a distinctive hybridity to Buddhism in so-called bor-
der regimes such as the Dali kingdom or Western Xia kingdom, this hybridity 
should be taken as a characteristic of Buddhism in political centers, as well. 
Rather than treating border regions like centers, we might be better served by 
treating centers like border regions, with expectations of fragmentation and 
variety instead of wholeness and homogeneity.
The regional esoteric Buddhist tradition that Dali rulers created was rooted 
in their political interests. Mahākāla’s Dali-kingdom cult shows how important 
such political interests were in the Buddhist networks of the tenth through 
thirteenth centuries. Both the Dali kingdom and the Tangut Xia kingdom bor-
dered Song China and Tibetan territory, and rulers of both regimes used 
esoteric Buddhism to establish distinctive politico-religious identities. Ruth 
Dunnell has compared Tangut Buddhism to Japanese Buddhism in this respect 
(Dunnell 1996, 12). While this comparison works for understanding the process 
by which regional Buddhist traditions develop, Dali Buddhism is closer to that 
of Japan in its stronger Chinese orientation.
Two reasons justify focusing on the political dimensions of esoteric Buddhism 
in the Dali kingdom. As Ronald Davidson has argued, esoteric Buddhism (and 
Hinduism) arose in seventh-century India after the Gupta Empire collapsed 
and several feudal kingdoms arose in its place. Esoteric Buddhists appealed 
to regional rulers by presenting their teachings as a ruling technology, and by 
using royal metaphors that identified kings with powerful enlightened beings

<!-- Page 417 -->

404
Bryson
(Davidson 2002, 121). Of course, Buddhism included governing ideologies long 
before the rise of esoteric Buddhism: the figure of the cakravartin, or “wheel-
turning king,” was a Buddhist monarch whose political authority rested on his 
religious devotion.1 What esoteric Buddhism offered was a new ritual reper-
toire that promised to further strengthen the king’s politico-religious power.
Secondly, of the limited surviving sources for Dali-kingdom esoteric 
Buddhism, most come from the court. Visual and textual materials related to 
Mahākāla are again representative in this respect: the god’s sculptures appear 
at sites whose carvings were sponsored by high officials, and his image is 
included in the court-sponsored Fanxiang juan; the three ritual texts that men-
tion Mahākāla come from Fazang si 法藏寺, the family temple of the Dong 董 
clan who served as “national preceptors” under the Dali kingdom. It is possible 
that Mahākāla worship extended throughout Dali-kingdom society, but no 
sources from the Dali kingdom attest to this.
	
Esoteric Buddhism
Mahākāla, who arose as a wrathful manifestation of the god Śiva, is often con-
sidered an “esoteric” or “tantric” deity. (On the relation between Śiva and the 
Tantric Avalokiteśvara see Shahar’s essay (chapter 6)). His fearsome expres-
sion, violent implements, and accessories of serpents and skulls could identify 
him as an esoteric dharma guardian, and there are tantras that instruct practi-
tioners to use his mantras, mudrās, and maṇḍalas to obtain various benefits 
(Stablein 1976). However, just because Mahākāla appears, or even originated, 
in an esoteric context does not mean that every text or image related to him is 
esoteric. For example, of the three ritual texts from the Dali kingdom that men-
tion Mahākāla, the Dahei tianshen daochang yi and Guangshi wuzhe daochang 
yi have significant esoteric content, but the Wuzhe dengshi fahui yi does not 
invoke the system of ritual techniques that characterizes esoteric Buddhism. 
Similarly, even wrathful images of Mahākāla could be sponsored or propitiated 
for general protection or blessings without entailing esoteric worship.
Determining whether Mahākāla worship in the Dali kingdom was “esoteric” 
requires clarifying this category, a notoriously difficult task. I use “esoteric” 
rather than “tantric” in this case because Dali-kingdom sources display more 
similarities with the esoteric traditions of Tang through Song China (see Lü 
Jianfu’s contribution to this volume for a discussion of this terminology). 
1	 The use of “his” is intentional, as women’s “five obstacles” prevented them from performing 
the cakravartin’s role.

<!-- Page 418 -->

405
Between China and Tibet
Charles Orzech and Henrik Sørensen have argued convincingly that the term 
“esoteric” is more appropriate to the Chinese context than “tantric” (see the 
latter’s contribution to this volume): with one possible exception, no Chinese 
texts were classified as tantras; the Chinese term mijiao 密教, “secret teach-
ings,” corresponds more closely to “esoteric”; and most Chinese texts omit the 
transgressive elements that characterize the tantra genre.2 “Esoteric” does 
not map perfectly onto the terms people used in Tang through Song China, but 
sources from this period suggest that people did conceive of a distinct tradi-
tion or lineage (though not in the sectarian model of later Japanese Shingon or 
Tibetan Buddhism), whether called “Great Yoga” or mijiao.3 I follow Sørensen 
in treating esoteric as a larger category of which tantric is a subset, so that all 
tantric Buddhism is esoteric, but not vice versa (Sørensen 1994, iii).
Delimiting the boundaries of esoteric Buddhism presents additional chal-
lenges because the terms “esoteric,” “tantric,” and “yoga” have been used in 
different ways in different contexts, and because many features of esoteric 
Buddhism (such as dhāraṇī, mantras, and wrathful deities) appear in exoteric 
materials, too. Ronald Davidson has proposed viewing esoteric Buddhism as a 
polythetic category that provides “an interrelated web of parameters that serve 
in aggregate to define specific kinds of category,” so that the category does 
not depend on a single variable (Davidson 2002, 119). In the case of esoteric 
Buddhism, this would mean that the presence or absence of mantras would 
not in itself define a text as esoteric; rather, this classification would depend on 
the other elements and their interrelationships.
I treat esoteric Buddhism as a system in which practitioners invoke enlight-
ened beings with ritual techniques—including mantras, mudrās, sādhana, 
abhiṣeka, homa offerings, and so on—that entail the identification of the prac-
titioner with those beings. In accordance with the royal model, the practitioner 
thereby gains mastery over a particular area that can be as large as the universe 
itself. Esoteric ritual often requires initiation from an ācārya, or preceptor, and 
often involves transgressive themes related to violence, sexuality, and con-
sumption for the purpose of transcending dualistic conceptions. Wrathful 
deities such as Mahākāla play important roles as expedient manifestations of 
Buddhas such as Mahāvairocana. Their violent appearances can signify 
destruction of spiritual obstacles, military power that supports a kingdom, and 
the eradication of worldly dangers such as floods or famine.
2	 See Orzech 2011. Yang uses the term “tantric” in his recent study of the god Ucchuṣma’s Chinese 
cult because Ucchuṣma worship is more closely connected to transgression. See Yang Zhaohua 
2013.
3	 For studies of Chinese categories, see Orzech, 2006, Sharf 2002 and McBride 2004.

<!-- Page 419 -->

406
Bryson
As Richard Payne has noted, any understanding of esoteric Buddhism 
should be rooted in a particular historical context (Payne 2006, 22). To locate 
Mahākāla worship in the Dali kingdom against the larger backdrop of esoteric 
Buddhism in the tenth to thirteenth centuries, this paper will first examine 
texts and images of Mahākāla in Tang through Song China, including their 
transmission to Japan, and then turn to Mahākāla worship in Tibet and the 
Tangut Xia dynasty. The terminus ad quem for this study is the Mongol con-
quest of the late thirteenth century because this marked the end of the Dali 
kingdom and the Mongols introduced the Tibetan Mahākāla to Chinese areas, 
thereby changing the landscape of the god’s cult.
	
Mahākāla in China and Japan
Mahākāla was known in China prior to the Mongol conquest, but even consid-
ering the loss of many Buddhist texts from the Tang dynasty, his cult does not 
seem to have achieved the prominence of comparable dharma guardians such 
as Vaiśravaṇa or Hārītī. Yijing 義淨 (635–713) wrote in his Nanhai jiguinei 
fazhuan 南海寄歸內法傳 (Record of the Buddhist Dharma Sent Home from the 
Southern Seas) that Mahākāla was “still unknown north of the Huai [River], 
but was enshrined in several places in Jiangnan.”4 However, I have found no 
evidence of any Mahākāla images or temples in southeast China from the Tang 
through Song. Considering that Yijing describes Mahākāla as a god of the 
kitchen and granary worshiped alongside Hārītī, it is possible that he was 
enshrined in this capacity in Chinese temples but never appeared in written 
records due to his minor status.5
When Mahākāla appears in Chinese texts—both translations and indige-
nous creations—in the Taishō canon, he is usually a minor guardian deity 
listed alongside similar figures such as Rudra, Maheśvara, and Vaiśravaṇa. 
Almost all of these texts can be considered “esoteric” in the sense that they use 
mantras, mudrās, and maṇḍalas for particular deities to empower the practi-
tioner. For example, the Tang translation of Suiqiu ji de dazizai tuoluoni 
shenzhou identifies several deities who will protect those who uphold the titu-

<!-- Page 420 -->

407
Between China and Tibet
lar dhāraṇī: Vajraguhya, the four devarājas (including Vaiśravaṇa), Indra, 
Brahma, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, Kumāra, Vināyaka, Mahākāla, and Nandīśvara.6
Mahākāla plays a more important role in Yixing’s 一行 Dapilüzhena chengfo 
jingshu, which identifies him as the wrathful form that the supreme Buddha 
Mahāvairocana takes to subdue the flesh-eating ḍākinīs.7 This text belongs to 
the esoteric Buddhist tradition introduced by the three masters of the Tang: 
Yixing studied under Śubhākarasiṃha (Shanwuwei 善無畏; 637–735), who 
translated the Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra (Chn. Dapilüzhena chengfo 
jing; T. 848) into Chinese, and Yixing’s commentary is reportedly based on his 
master’s teachings (Lü Jianfu 1995, 208). Mahākāla’s role as a manifestation of 
Mahāvairocana contributed to his popularity in Japanese Buddhism, where 
the Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra became a central Shingon text.
Another text by a Tang esoteric master features Mahākāla in a less positive 
role. Amoghavajra’s (Bukong 不空; 705–774) re-translation of the Renwang 
huguo boreboluomiduo jing 仁王護國般若波羅蜜多經 (Prajñāpāramitā Scrip­
ture for Humane Kings to Protect Their Countries; hereafter Renwang jing) 
recounts the tale of King Kalmāṣapāda, who heeds the advice of his non-Bud-
dhist spiritual advisor to collect 1000 heads and offer them to “the Great Black 
God, Mahākāla of the Graveyard” (Zhongjian Mohejialuo Dahei tianshen 塚間
摩訶迦羅大黑天神).8 Liang Bi’s 良賁 (717–777) commentary on this text iden-
tifies Mahākāla as a god of war and as an incarnation of Maheśvara, another 
form of Śiva.9 In both texts Mahākāla retains his earlier non-Buddhist identity 
and comes across as an ambivalent figure.
Chinese translations and commentaries from the Tang through Song show 
that Mahākāla belonged to the pantheon of esoteric Buddhism, but that he 
was not a central figure. The same image emerges in visual arts from the same 
place and time. I have found no images of Mahākāla from the Chinese interior 
(that is, the eastern and central parts of Tang and Song territory) prior to the 
Mongol conquest, including sites such as Dazu and Bazhong in Sichuan that 
include the similar dharma guardians Hārītī and Vaiśravaṇa. Mahākāla does 
appear at Dunhuang, but even there he is a secondary figure in images related

God stretches an elephant hide and horizontally holds a spear, one end of 
which pierces a human head, and one end of which pierces a ram.”11 Huilin 慧
琳 (737–820), a disciple of Amoghavajra, described the eight-armed Mahākāla’s 
appearance in the Yiqie jing yinyi 一切經音義 ‭: his front pair of hands hold a 
trident horizontally across his body; the second right hand holds a black ram; 
the second left hand holds a hungry ghost by its hair; the third right hand holds 
a sword; the third left hand holds a khaṭvāṅga; and the rear pair of hands 
stretches a white elephant skin over his head.12 Huilin included the gloss of 
“Mahākāla” in his section on the second fascicle of the Renwang jing‬, suggest-
ing continuity between the textual and visual traditions related to the deity.
Mahākāla’s Chinese iconography does not appear in Dali, Tibet, or the 
Tangut Xia kingdom, but it does appear in Japanese sources, which relied on 
Chinese materials. There is only one text in the Taishō canon devoted to 
Mahākāla, the Daikoku tenjin hō 大黑天神法 (Methods of the Great Black God), 
and Iyanaga Nobumi has identified it as a tenth- to eleventh-century Japanese 
work compiled mainly from Chinese texts (Iyanaga 2002). Iconographic manu-
als from the Kamakura period (1185–1333) also cite Chinese translations and 
commentaries in their sections on Mahākāla.13 Among the Chinese texts the

Between China and Tibet
Daikoku tenjin hō quotes is the Yiqie jing yinyi, meaning that it gives the same 
iconography for Mahākāla as found in Dunhuang paintings (T.1287p355c12–16). 
However, the Daikoku tenjin hō and Kamakura-era iconographic manuals also 
describe Mahākāla’s iconography from Yijing’s Nanhai jiguinei fazhuan: “He 
sits on a small platform while holding a bag of money. One foot hangs down to 
the ground. He is rubbed with oil daily so that he is black in appearance.”14
Much of the content of the Daikoku tenjin hō could be considered esoteric: 
it describes Mahākāla’s rituals as top-secret and forbids practitioners from 
revealing them, even for a great deal of money (T.1287p355c8–11). In Japan, the 
image of a ferocious Mahākāla raising an elephant hide over his head and 
holding weapons appeared in Shingon illustrations of the Garbhadhātu-
maṇḍala, placing it within an esoteric framework (Iyanaga 2002, 300–301). Yet 
Mahākāla was also worshiped in Japan as a god of wealth and as god of the 
kitchen. He became one of the “Seven Gods of Good Fortune” (Shichifukujin 七
福神), whose cults did not entail esoteric ritual practice. Japanese Buddhists 
later developed their own forms of Mahākāla, as seen in the set of six forms of 
the god that appeared in the Edo period (Chaudhuri 2003, 70).
Mahākāla became known in Tang China through the works of Indian eso-
teric masters and their disciples, but he seems to have remained a secondary 
figure in Tang-Song Buddhism. Though Japanese Mahākāla worship depended 
on Chinese texts, it turned into a much more prominent cult in both its eso-
teric and exoteric manifestations. Some Chinese esoteric materials presented 
Mahākāla as a violent figure who wielded weapons, impaled people and ani-
mals, and received bloody offerings. However, though some texts tie him to the 
goddess Hārītī, there are no references to sexual practices in his texts or images, 
and his worshipers are not instructed to consume impure substances. The 
Chinese and Japanese Mahākāla thus contrasts with the Mahākāla worshiped 
in Tibet and adopted by the Tanguts.
	
Mahākāla in Tibet and the Western Xia
The worship of Mahākāla in Tibet began after the century-long age of fragmen-
tation that followed the Tibetan empire’s collapse in the ninth century 
(Davidson 2005; Dalton 2011). The famous translator Rin-chen bzang-po (958–
1055) is credited with introducing the god’s texts and image to Tibet by the 
eleventh century. According to legend, Rin-chen bzang-po had a vision of 
14	
T.1287p356b16–21; Nanhai jiguinei fazhuan, T. 2125p209b22–23; Kakuzen shō, 265; Asaba 
shō, 235.

<!-- Page 423 -->

410
Bryson
Mahākāla on a pilgrimage to Bodh Gayā in which he saw the god “trampling 
upon a dwarf and holding a knife and a skull, one above the other, level with 
his heart and a gaṇṭi [gaṇḍī] held central in his hands” (Snellgrove and 
Skorupski 1980, 99). Mahākāla then promised to accompany Rin-chen bzang-
po back to Tibet to protect the Buddhist doctrine. This form of Mahākāla was 
known as Gur-gyi mgon-po (Skt. Pañjara-nātha), a term that has been trans-
lated variously as “Lord of the Tent,” “Lord of the Pavilion,” and “Lord of Death.”15 
In accordance with Rin-chen bzang-po’s description, Gur-gyi mgon-po stands 
with bent legs upon a corpse; his two arms hold a knife and skull bowl, with a 
gaṇḍī (long wooden gong used to summon monks) balanced horizontally 
across them.16 He has a fierce expression and wears a tiger skin, serpents, and 
garlands of severed heads. Gur-gyi mgon-po is a compact figure with a large 
belly, which contrasts with the relatively lean, muscular Mahākāla of Dunhuang 
and Bezeklik.
The “Lord of the Pavilion” became popular as a central protector of the 
Sakya school of Tibetan Buddhism, but this was not the only form of Mahākāla 
known in early Tibet. An eleventh-century mural of Mahākāla from the assem-
bly hall at Alchi depicts the god standing on a corpse with his left leg extended 
and right leg bent. His overall appearance is the same as the Gur-gyi mgon-po 
form, but he only has two arms: the right holds a vajra chopper and the left 
holds a skull bowl (Pal, 1982, D25). Among the secondary deities in the painting 
is the goddess Palden Lhamo (dpal-ldan lha-mo), a wrathful Tibetan transfor-
mation of Śrī Devī who rides a mule (Rhie 2004, 49–50). An eleventh- or 
twelfth-century stone statue of Mahākāla depicts the deity seated on a corpse 
in the posture of royal ease with his right foot hanging down. He has four arms: 
the top right hand holds a sword; the top left hand holds a ‭khaṭvāṅga‬ staff; and 
the lower right hand holds a vajra chopper right over the skull bowl in his lower 
left hand (Rhie and Thurman, 1991, 186–87)
These images are closer than the Gur-gyi mgon-po images to Indian 
Mahākāla iconography from the Pāla Empire (eighth to twelfth centuries). 
A Pāla-period stone statue from Bihar depicts a standing four-armed Mahākāla 
that holds a sword in his upper right hand, a ‭khaṭvāṅga‬ in his upper left hand,

a knife in his lower right hand, and a lotus bowl in his lower left hand.17 The 
twelfth-century Sādhanamālā describes the two-armed Mahākāla as hold-
ing a knife and skull bowl; the four-armed Mahākāla adds to this a sword and 
‭khaṭvāṅga‬ (Bhattacharyya 1968, 345–46). It instructs worshipers of the two-
armed Mahākāla to:
Conceive [yourself] as Śrī Mahākāla Bhaṭṭāraka who is two-armed and 
one-faced and has blue colour. He is three-eyed, has fiery radiance, and 
carries the Kartṛī [i.e., knife] and the Kapāla [i.e., skull bowl] in his right 
and left hands respectively. He bears five skulls on his brown hair which 
rises up on his head, and is decorated with a chain of severed heads. He 
looks terrible with bare fangs, and is decked in ornaments of serpents 
and a sacred thread made out of a snake. He is short and from his mouth 
trickles forth blood (Bhattacharyya 1968, 345).
Tibetan images of Mahākāla share a general iconographic source with Chinese 
images of the deity that manifests in certain features: some Tibetan images 
of the six-armed Mahākāla dating to as early as the thirteenth century hold 
an elephant hide over their heads; Gur-gyi mgon-po’s horizontal gaṇḍī echoes 
the horizontal spears held by Mahākāla at Dunhuang; and Mahākāla’s attire 
and implements draw from a common repertoire. However, Tibetan Mahākāla 
images appeared later than their Chinese counterparts and reflect a different 
trajectory. Textual sources from Tibet display similar divergence from Chinese 
materials in their more transgressive content. William Stablein dates the 
earliest extant version of the Mahākālatantra to the mid-twelfth century, con-
temporaneous with the Dali kingdom. This text describes Mahākāla in sexual 
union with his consorts, gives instructions for killing, and directs practitioners 
to consume, among other things, human flesh and bodily fluids (Stablein 1976, 
34, 196, 212, 231, 239).18 Mahākāla appears in several different forms that differ 
in their number of heads and limbs, but share a wrathful demeanor (Stablein 
1976, 218–27).
Mahākāla’s prominence in Tibetan Buddhism rose with the Sakya school’s 
ascendance in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and it was the Sakya mas-
ter ’Phags-pa (1235–1280; Basiba 八思巴) who initiated Qubilai Khan into the 
rites of Hevajra-Mahākāla (Franke 1978, 59). Mahākāla became a key tutelary

deity for the Mongols, who spread his cult to eastern China. However, Tanguts 
had embraced Mahākāla long before Mongol rulers did, and in fact may have 
sparked the Mongols’ interest in Mahākāla (Sperling 1994, 801). The Tangut 
example offers an instructive point of comparison because the Tanguts, like 
the Dali rulers, were located between China and Tibet.
While the vast majority of texts from the Dali kingdom were written in 
Sinitic script (and the rest were Sanskrit dhāraṇīs that also circulated in China), 
Tangut Buddhist texts were written in Chinese, Tangut, and Tibetan. The 
Tangut language reflects the Xia kingdom’s geographic position between Song 
China and Tibet: they developed their script based on Sinitic characters, but 
their spoken language bore more similarities to Tibetan (Dunnell 1996, chapter 
two). Similarly, Tangut Buddhism drew on both Chinese and Tibetan sources: 
the Chinese translation of the Jinguangming zuishengwang jing 金光明最勝王
經 (Skt. Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra) was popular, and Liangzhou’s Huguo si 護國
寺 suggests familiarity with the Renwang jing; Tangut monks, such as the 
twelfth- and thirteenth-century figures Fashizi 法獅子 (Tib. Chos-kyi seng-ge) 
and Fahui 法慧 (Tib. Chos-kyi shes-rab), translated tantric Tibetan texts from 
the Sakya and Kagyu lineages (Dunnell 2009, 54, 57).19 Unlike the Buddhism 
of the Dali kingdom, Tangut Buddhism seems to have drawn significantly from 
the two major bordering regions.
Judging from the number of extant texts and images devoted to him, 
Mahākāla was one of the most important deities to the rulers of the Western 
Xia. Elliot Sperling suggests that it was the twelfth-century translator Rtsa-mi 
Lo-tsā-ba Sangs-rgyas Grags-pa who popularized Tangut Mahākāla worship. 
Rtsa-mi—whom Sperling identifies as Tangut rather than Tibetan—trans-
lated, edited, or revised at least four texts in the Tibetan canon directly related 
to Mahākāla, and a recently published Kagyu collection links him to several 
more (Sperling 1994, 802–803).20 Aside from these Tibetan works, several texts 
from Khara-Khoto written in Sinitic script are devoted to Mahākāla, including 
two from the Western Xia period, the Dahei genben mingzhou 大黑根本命呪 
(Root Mantra of Mahākāla) and Dahei zan 大黑讚 (Praise of Mahākāla) (Shen

Weirong 2010, 422–23).21 These texts exemplify the hybridity of Western Xia 
Buddhism in that they were written in Sinitic script but in their content more 
closely resembled Tibetan sources.
Similarities between Tibetan sources and the Western Xia Dahei genben 
mingzhou and Dahei zan appear in Mahākāla’s mantra and the offerings made 
to him. Mahākāla’s “root mantra” in the Dahei genbenming zhou is identical to 
the one still used by the Sakya school, which shows a clear connection between 
the Western Xia text and Tibetan Mahākāla worship.22 This connection is also 
evident in the texts’ emphasis on bloody offerings. The Dahei genben ming-
zhou outlines a food distribution ritual in which the practitioner offers “the 
five grains, highland barley, pork, fish, beef, onions, garlic, and various bloody 
foods” to Mahākāla.23 Elsewhere in the ritual the practitioner recites a man-
tra to transform offerings of blood and flesh into ambrosia (Shi Jinbo et al. 
1998, 332). Both texts describe Mahākāla and his retinue as devourers of blood 
and flesh: in the Dahei genben mingzhou the six mothers and flesh-eaters of 
the ten directions who surround Mahākāla “each open their mouth and drink 
blood”; the Dahei zan identifies its main deity as “Mahākāla the blood-drinking 
king” (Shi Jinbo et al. 1998, 335). Though Mahākāla also appears as a wrath-
ful deity in Chinese Buddhist texts, and receives offerings of human heads in 
Amoghavajra’s version of the Renwang jing, these texts do not instruct wor-
shipers to make offerings of flesh and blood. Instead, the bloody offerings in 
the Dahei genben mingzhou and Dahei zan resemble the offerings prescribed 
in the Mahākālatantra.
Mahākāla’s Tangut iconography also bears more similarities to Tibetan 
images of the deity than to images from Dunhuang and descriptions in the 
Taishō canon. The Dahei genben mingzhou and Dahei zan describe him as short 
and squat, with three eyes, red and yellow hair, adornments of venomous 
snakes, a garland of human heads, and a tiger-skin loincloth. The two texts dif-
fer in some respects: in the Dahei genben mingzhou the two-armed Mahākāla 
has a raven’s beak and holds a sword in his right hand and a skull bowl in his 
left, while in the Dahei zan a four-armed Mahākāla holds a sword and fruits of 
the five desires in his two right hands, and a skull bowl and trident in his two

Images of Mahākāla from twelfth- to fourteenth-century Khara-Khoto 
resemble the descriptions in the Dahei genben mingzhou and Dahei zan. For 
example, a thangka that has been identified as Acala might actually depict 
Mahākāla: it shows a wrathful blue-black, four-armed, three-eyed deity wear-

Mahākāla maṇḍala includes multiple images of ravens as well as Palden 
Lhamo, which connects it to Tibetan iconography. Tangut images of Mahākāla 
display neither the elephant hide nor the horizontal staff that appear in 
Dunhuang paintings and descriptions of Mahākāla in Taishō texts.
Though several points of continuity link Mahākāla worship in China and 
Japan with his worship in Tibetan and Tangut Buddhism, these two traditions 
differ considerably. Tibetan and Tangut forms of Mahākāla iconography and 
ritual draw more on developments from the Pāla Empire, while the main 
sources for Chinese and Japanese Mahākāla cults appear to have entered China 
in the Tang dynasty. Though Mahākāla appears in esoteric Chinese and 
Japanese materials that link him to ḍākinīs and non-Buddhist human sacrifice, 
these texts do not prescribe offerings of human flesh or blood, or sexual prac-
tices. Mahākāla’s iconography as it appears in Tang sources and Dunhuang

However, these two iconographic forms differ in significant ways, as well. The 
examples of Japan and the Western Xia illustrate the different ways in which 
Mahākāla worship has developed based on Tang-Song sources in contrast to 
Tibetan sources. The Tangut case further shows how one region between China 
and Tibet developed its Mahākāla cult, which provides an instructive contrast 
to the Dali kingdom.
	
Between China and Tibet: Mahākāla in the Dali Kingdom
The Dali kingdom ruled an area that encompassed modern-day Yunnan prov-
ince, as well as parts of Burma, Laos, Vietnam, Sichuan, and Guizhou. It was 
founded in 937 after an interregnum of three short-lived regimes following the 
collapse of the Nanzhao kingdom (南詔, 649–903). Though extant texts from 
the Nanzhao and Dali kingdoms are limited, almost all of them are written in 
Sinitic script, and the handful of Sanskrit works—mainly dhāraṇī—circulated 
in Tang-Song China, as well. Unlike the Tangut rulers, Nanzhao and Dali kings 
did not develop their own script. The rulers of these kingdoms also actively 
sought out Chinese learning: in 829 the Nanzhao army raided Chengdu for 
skilled workers and kidnapped the Tang official Zheng Hui 鄭回 to advise the 
Nanzhao ruler; Dali court representatives, in trading with their Song counter-
parts, sought to acquire Buddhist texts as well as classical literature, rhyme 
dictionaries, and materia medica.27 Conversely, there is no evidence that 
Nanzhao and Dali rulers sought out texts from Tibet, India, or Southeast Asia. 
However, Dali rulers did not look to China for all of their Buddhist materials. 
Material and visual culture from the Dali kingdom suggests that Buddhism 
there, as elsewhere, combined texts and objects from different sources with 
local culture to create a distinctive regional tradition. Mahākāla embodies this 
process in his Indian image and Chinese texts.
Dali-kingdom rulers looked to their Nanzhao predecessors for governmen-
tal structure, official titles, and religious traditions. Extant sources for the 
Nanzhao and Dali kingdoms are asymmetrical: there are few records from the 
Nanzhao, but several Tang records about Nanzhao; conversely, Song emperors’ 
desire to avoid quagmires in the southwest mean there are few Song writings 
about Dali, but more materials from the Dali kingdom have survived. The vast

<!-- Page 429 -->

416
Bryson
majority of these materials are Buddhist texts and art, which makes Buddhism 
the best way of understanding the Dali kingdom.
By the ninth century Nanzhao rulers had embraced Buddhism, and in 899 
the last Nanzhao king Shunhuazhen 舜化貞 (r. 897–902) commissioned an 
account of how Buddhism entered the region. The resulting Nanzhao tuzhuan 
南詔圖傳 (Illustrated History of Nanzhao) credits Acuoye Guanyin 阿嵯耶觀
音 (Ajaya, “Invincible,” Avalokiteśvara) with introducing Buddhism to Yunnan 
and helping found the Nanzhao kingdom in the form of an Indian monk (Li 
Lin-ts’an 1967, 147–48). The story takes pains to refute the rumor that the Tang 
monk-pilgrim Xuanzang 玄奘 (600–664) was responsible for this, and instead 
emphasizes the Indian origins of Nanzhao Buddhism. The Nanzhao tuzhuan 
also indicates that Nanzhao rulers adopted esoteric Buddhism specifically. 
Both its images and text suggest that the Nanzhao ruler Longshun 隆舜 (r. 877–
897) performed an abhiṣeka rite with Acuoye Guanyin.28 The text additionally 
celebrates Acuoye Guanyin for “opening the marvelous gate of the esoteric.”29 
In addition, Nanzhao rulers probably favored Amoghavajra’s version of the 
Renwang jing, which championed an esoteric model of Buddhist kingship. This 
is shown by a 908 subcommentary on the Renwang jing called Huguo sinan 
chao 護國司南抄 (Compass for Protecting the Nation Subcommentary) that has 
only been found in the Dali region.30 Nanzhao Buddhism thus already com-
bined Chinese texts with Indian images: Acuoye Guanyin’s iconography recalls 
India or Southeast Asia, and he appears in the form of an Indian monk, while 
the Huguo sinan chao was based on a Tang text and its commentary.31
Nanzhao court Buddhism reflects its geopolitical position. Chinese dynas-
ties maintained official outposts in Yunnan since the Han dynasty (206 
BCE–220 CE), and the earliest dated Buddhist materials from the Dali region

latter of which would have been used to sprinkle water on the abhiṣeka initiate. The text 
claims that Longshun was “sprinkled by the basin” (lin pen 淋盆) in 897, which probably 
also refers to the abhiṣeka rite. See Li Lin-ts’an 1967, 137 and 150.

Between China and Tibet
were images on the 698 funeral stele of a Tang official. Nanzhao rulers had 
their longest and closest diplomatic relationship with the Tang court, though 
they strategically cultivated ties with Tibet and gained suzerainty over the Pyu 
kingdom in what is now Burma. It is not surprising that Nanzhao records use 
Sinitic script and show familiarity with Chinese texts, including classical works 
such as the Yi jing, Shi jing, and Shi ji.32 However, Nanzhao rulers would always 
be “barbarians” (man 蠻) in the eyes of Tang representatives. Buddhism—spe-
cifically its esoteric forms—offered an alternative model of kingship that 
allowed Nanzhao rulers to claim a privileged position by virtue of their prox-
imity to India.
Dali rulers presented themselves as heirs to the Buddhism of Acuoye 
Guanyin: the Fanxiang juan reproduced several scenes from the Nanzhao 
tuzhuan, and multiple Dali-kingdom statues of Acuoye Guanyin survived. 
However, Acuoye Guanyin does not appear in any of the texts that have only 
been found in Dali. Mahākāla is unique in appearing both in Dali Buddhist art 
and texts, and his worship in the Dali kingdom offers a point of comparison to 
his cults in other regions. As noted above, his images display Indian iconogra-
phy, but his texts show continuity with Tang and Song Buddhism.
The two food distribution ritual texts from Fazang si—Wuzhe dengshi fahui 
yi and Guangshi wuzhe daochang yi—list Mahākāla and his consort among 
the deities invited to the ritual area to partake of the offerings. His consort 
goes by the names Fude Longnü 福德龍女, “Dragon Maiden of Good Fortune,” 
and Baijie Shengfei 白姐聖妃, “Holy Consort White Sister,” names that do not 
appear outside of the Dali region.33 The texts include Mahākāla and his con-
sort in a group of similar deities from India that were converted to protect 
the buddhadharma, such as Vināyaka and Hārītī. Other deities in these texts 
clearly come from Chinese tradition, such as Hebo (Earl of the River), the gods 
of the Five Marchmounts and Four Rivers, and gods of the soil and granary. 
In the Guangshi wuzhe daochang yi Mahākāla also appears in more esteemed 
company at the beginning of the extant manuscript: “With a sincere heart we 
gaze up and invite to the esoteric assembly those who pervade the dharma 
realm: dharma nature Vairo[cana] Buddha, dharma king Śākya[muni] Buddha,

418
Bryson
Śakra Devānām-Indra, the god Mahākāla, and the class of the two provisional

The genre of the Wuzhe dengshi fahui yi and Guangshi wuzhe daochang yi 
also points to China, specifically the regional tradition of shuilu 水陸 (water 
and land) food distribution ritual that developed in Song-dynasty Sichuan. 
Both texts use the term shuilu, and both give instructions for making offerings 
of food to all sentient beings. It is likely that shuilu rituals entered the Dali 
kingdom from Sichuan, and the Dali court created its own version(s) (Stevenson 
2001, 44). Mahākāla and his consort seem to have distinguished Dali food dis-
tribution offerings from their Chinese counterparts, where I have not found 
Mahākāla among the invited gods. Conversely, the Western Xia text Dahei gen-
ben mingzhou includes rites of food distribution, but does not use the term 
shuilu and its food offerings consist of flesh and blood. The absence of such 
transgressive elements in the two Dali food distribution texts indicates that 
they belonged to different ritual systems, though the Dali texts were related to 
esoteric practices.
Charles Orzech has shown that esoteric food distribution rituals arose dur-
ing the Tang as competition for the Buddhist and Daoist rites for the dead 
(Orzech 1994, 52). Orzech theorizes that shuilu rituals emerged in the Song 
because the Huichang persecution of 845 cut off the esoteric lineage and fur-
ther development of its shishi rituals. Shuilu rituals incorporated elements of 
the esoteric shishi, such as mantras and dhāraṇīs, but did not adopt the eso-
teric system in which the shishi rituals were based (Zhou Shujia 1982, 398). 
While the Wuzhe dengshi fahui yi does not belong to an esoteric system, the 
Guangshi wuzhe fahui yi frequently uses the term “esoteric,” mi 密 or mimi 秘
密, to refer to its teachings; focuses on Vairocana as the main object of venera-
tion, or benzun 本尊; and begins by inviting the gods of the three divisions of 
the garbhadhātu.35
One section, titled “Pinnacle of the Esoteric Lineage” (mizong jiujing 密宗究
竟), describes the “octagonal wheel altar” (bajiao zhi luntan 八角之輪壇), also 
called a “yoga altar,” with the benzun in the center surrounded by the esoteric

教外別傳) etc.

419
Between China and Tibet
maṇḍala (mimi zhongwei 秘密中圍).36 Each section ends with the instruction 
to empower (Chn. jiachi 加持; Skt. adhiṣṭhāna) the offerings with a mantra, 
though the mantras themselves are not given.37 However, the rituals pre-
scribed in the Guangshi wuzhe daochang yi differ from esoteric food distribution 
rituals that appear in the Yuan dynasty, such as those in the Yujia jiyao yankou 
shishi yi 瑜伽集要焰口施食儀, which suggests that the Guangshi wuzhe dao-
chang yi developed separately.38
Though these texts only mention Mahākāla in passing, his inclusion is sig-
nificant because of his absence in similar texts from China and the contrast 
between Dali-kingdom food distribution ritual and that of the Western Xia. 
The Dahei tianshen daochang yi, which is structured around seven manifesta-
tions of Mahākāla, gives an even clearer image of textual sources for Mahākāla 
worship in the Dali kingdom.
The partial manuscript of the Dahei tianshen daochang yi appears next to 
that of the Guangshi wuzhe daochang yi on the reverse of the Yuanjue jing shu. 
Their contiguous placement led the scholars who first examined the manu-
script to see them as a single text, but Hou Chong has shown that the two 
sections do not match up, and there are red dots on the Dahei tianshen dao-
chang yi, but not the Guangshi wuzhe daochang yi. He concludes that the 
Yuanjue jing shu was copied on the back of these two separate manuscripts 
(Hou Chong 2006, 27).
I have published a more in-depth study and translation of the Dahei tian-
shen daochang yi elsewhere, so here I will focus on the parts of the text that 
relate to its esoteric content (Bryson 2012, 3–69). The Dahei tianshen daochang 
yi is similar to the Guangshi wuzhe daochang yi in that it could have been used 
in an esoteric setting. Its sections for different deities—Mahākāla’s seven 
forms and his consort—resemble sādhana manuals that describe deities in 
detail so that practitioners can visualize and identify with them. In the Dahei 
tianshen daochang yi these sections end with instructions for the practitioner 
to perform empowerment with the deity’s mantra (though the mantras are not

the Yuan texts, such as the names of the thirty-five buddhas, identification with Guanyin, 
and recitation of the mantras of the seven tathāgatas.

Bryson
given). The text ends by identifying the twenty-eight gods of Mahākāla’s 
maṇḍala.
The Dahei tianshen daochang yi describes Mahākāla’s seven forms as expe-
dient manifestations of ultimate reality:
Outwardly he manifests seven forms of gods, like a mustard seed contain-
ing Mt. Sumeru; inwardly he realizes the single truth of Vairo[cana], like 
suchness encompassing the whole world. His appearance is wrathful as 
he sweeps away heterodox gods and demons; his heart is compassionate 
as he points the way to the Lotus Realm.39
Each of his forms has its own function, such as controlling lifespans, vanquish-
ing bandits, and commuting prison sentences. I have found no other examples 
of Mahākāla appearing in a group of seven gods, or having seven forms, and a 
Yuan temple record from western Yunnan suggests that this was a regional 
development. Yang Sen’s 楊森 1326 Qixian shan Bao’en fancha ji 棲賢山報恩梵
剎記 (Record of Bao’en Buddhist Monastery on Mount Qixian) mentions “seven 
transformations of the god Mahākāla” (Mohejialuo qizhuan tianshen 摩訶迦羅
七轉天神) painted on the temple walls.40
The specific forms range from familiar figures to names that only appear in 
Dali: Dahei tianshen (i.e. Mahākāla-deva), Anle Jialuo 安樂迦羅 (Kāla of Peace 
and Joy), Riyue Jialuo 日月迦羅 (Kāla of the Sun and Moon), Jinbo Jialuo 金鉢
迦羅 (Kāla of the Golden Bowl), Zhongjian tianshen 塚間天神 (God of the 
Graveyard), Dishi Jialuo 帝釋迦羅 (Indra Kāla), and Baozang Jialuo 寶藏迦羅 
(Kāla of the Treasure Store). Dahei tianshen and Indra are self-explanatory, 
while Baozang is another name for the Indian wealth god Jambhala, whose 
functions overlapped with those of Mahākāla (Iyanaga, 367–68).
Of the remaining forms, the God of the Graveyard appears to come from 
Amoghavajra’s Renwang jing, which was known in the Dali region by the early 
tenth century, and two partial manuscripts of which survived at Fazang si. The 
God of the Graveyard’s inclusion in the Dahei tianshen daochang yi further 
supports the theory that Dali-kingdom Buddhism drew heavily on Tang eso-
teric texts.
Two other forms, Kāla of Peace and Joy and Kāla of the Golden Bowl, do not 
appear in the Taishō, but do appear elsewhere in Dali-kingdom Buddhist

materials. Frames 121 and 122 of the Fanxiang juan are labeled Kāla God of the 
Golden Bowl (Jinbo jialuo shen 金鉢迦羅神) and Yakṣa God of Great Peace 
(Da’an yaocha shen 大安藥叉神), respectively, and match the gods’ descrip-
tions in the Dahei tianshen daochang yi. The Yakṣa of Great Peace and Joy (as 
Da anle yaocha 大安樂藥叉) also appears in another text that has only been 
found in Dali, the Zhu fo pusa jingang deng qiqing yigui 諸佛菩薩金剛等啟請
儀軌 (Ritual Procedures for the Invitation of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajra Beings, 
etc.). The section devoted to the Yakṣa of Great Peace and Joy takes up sixteen 
pages of the manuscript reproduction, while most deities have fewer than ten 
pages each.41 This attests to the development of a distinctive tradition of Dali 
kingdom Buddhism, and Mahākāla’s importance within it.
In addition to Mahākāla’s seven forms, the Dahei tianshen daochang yi 
devotes a section to Mahākāla’s consort, here called Baijie Shengfei. As with 
the Kāla of Peace and Joy and Kāla of the Golden Bowl, the textual description 
of Baijie Shengfei perfectly matches frame 123 of the Fanxiang juan, which is 
labeled Dasheng Fude Longnü 大聖福德龍女, “Great Holy Dragon Maiden of 
Good Fortune.” This ties together the different names for Mahākāla’s consort in 
the food distribution texts and reinforces the link between the Dahei tianshen 
daochang yi and Fanxiang juan.
Though I refer to Baijie Shengfei or Fude Longnü as Mahākāla’s consort (as 
the Dahei tianshen daochang yi identifies her), neither the Dahei tianshen dao-
chang yi nor Fanxiang juan suggest any sexual contact between them. While 
Mahākāla and his various forms appear as ferocious, barely clothed, serpent-
wearing hulks in the Fanxiang juan, Fude Longnü wears long Chinese robes 
and looks like an elegant lady, except for the serpent coils beneath her feet and 
hood of three serpents rising over her head. No hint of ferocity or sexuality 
emanates from her demure countenance.
The Dahei tianshen daochang yi similarly does not instruct practitioners to 
make offerings of blood or flesh to Mahākāla, though its lack of ritual specific-
ity makes it difficult to determine how Dali-kingdom Buddhists would have 
used it. Overall, the Dahei tianshen daochang yi has more in common with 
Tang esoteric Buddhist texts than with Tibetan tantras dedicated to Mahākāla. 
Its language also points more to China: the Dahei tianshen daochang yi and 
Guangshi wuzhe daochang yi are written in elegant Chinese, including matched

The genres of the three Dali-kingdom texts that mention, or are dedicated 
to, Mahākāla, support the theory that Dali-kingdom Buddhists looked primar-
ily to China for their esoteric Buddhist texts. There is clearly a connection 
between these texts and Dali-kingdom Buddhist art, as shown in the correla-
tions between the Fanxiang juan and Dahei tianshen daochang yi. However, 
the seven images of Mahākāla from the Nanzhao or Dali kingdoms do not 
resemble the god’s descriptions in the Taishō, paintings at Dunhuang, or depic-
tions in Japan. Yet neither do they resemble Tibetan or Tangut images of the 
deity.
The Mahākāla in frame 124 of the Fanxiang juan represents Dali-kingdom 
Mahākāla iconography. Though the name Mahākāla means “Great Black One,” 
he is depicted in white form, possibly a nod to the legend in which he (as a 
manifestation of Vairocana) smears ashes on himself in defeating the ḍākinīs.43 
Mahākāla appears in a wrathful form, wearing a ferocious expression and 
adorned with serpents and skulls. He has four arms: the upper left holds a 
waisted drum; the upper right, a trident; the lower left, a lasso; and the lower 
right, a skull bowl. This Mahākāla image closely resembles other images of the 
god from the Nanzhao-Dali period, which have four or six arms and hold the 
same implements.44
The Fanxiang juan includes Mahākāla alongside a set of deities that makes 
sense in connection with the Dahei tianshen daochang yi, but the stone carv-
ings of Mahākāla always appear alongside Vaiśravaṇa. In cave 6 at Shibao shan, 
the two gods flank a set of eight vidyārājas (“brilliant kings”; Chn. mingwang 明
王), with the Buddha Vairocana in the center.45 This Mahākāla has four arms, 
only one of which is complete (it holds a skull bowl). The Mahākāla in cave 16

the other Mahākāla images. See Lee Yü-min 1995, 43, figs. 1, 2, 4; and 44, fig. 5.

423
Between China and Tibet
has six arms, which hold (in order of right to left, and top to bottom) a trident 
piercing a human head and a waisted drum; a sword and a skull bowl; and a 
lasso and rosary. Santai shan, near Kunming, depicts a four-armed Mahākāla 
with a trident and waisted drum in his upper pair of hands, and a rosary and 
skull bowl in his lower pair. In each of these examples, Vaiśravaṇa appears in 
martial form: he wears a suit of armor, and holds a trident in one hand and a 
miniature pagoda (or nothing at all) in the other. The final carving example 
from Guiyuan si 歸源寺 in the Dali plain depicts Mahākāla on one side of a 
stone slab, and Vaiśravaṇa on the other (the paint is recent). Mahākāla has six 
arms that hold (in order of right to left, and top to bottom) a sword and waisted 
drum; trident and skull bowl; and rosary and human head.
Though the artistic style of the Fanxiang juan and stone carvings draws pri-
marily on Tang through Song models, the iconography is a different matter. Lee 
Yü-min argues that Dali-kingdom Mahākāla images were based on the god’s 
iconography in Gupta India (fourth-sixth centuries CE) because textual sources 
from the fifth through seventh centuries describe Mahākāla with a fierce 
expression, wearing garlands of skulls and a necklace of serpents, and holding 
a trident (Lee Yü-min 1995, 28, 35). I believe that Pāla-period Mahākāla images 
bear more resemblance to Dali-kingdom images: they have four arms that hold 
a sword, vajra-chopper (kartṛī), skull staff (khaṭvāṅga), and skull bowl, and 
wear similar attire (Lee Yü-min 1995, 29). This conforms to the description of 
the four-armed Mahākāla in the Sādhanamālā (Bhattacharyya 1968, 346). The 
Sādhanamālā’s description of the six-armed Mahākāla, however, resembles 
the Dali-kingdom images even more closely: he holds a vajra-chopper, rosary, 
and double-headed drum (ḍamaru) in his right hands, and a skull bowl, tri-
dent, and lasso in his left hands (Bhattacharyya 1968, 346).
Dali-kingdom images of Mahākāla differ from distinctively Tibetan iconog-
raphies, such as the “Lord of the Pavilion” form, as well as the form in which he 
holds up an elephant hide, the form in which he sits holding a money bag, and 
the form in which he holds a fruit. Iconographic sources suggest that Mahākāla’s 
Dali-kingdom iconography came directly from India or was at least modeled 
conceptually on Indian iconography. Of course, iconography is not bound to 
its geographical origin, and these Mahākāla images could have entered Dali 
through other routes. However, the differences between Dali-kingdom images 
of Mahākāla and Tang-Song Mahākāla iconography suggest that Mahākāla was 
at least not represented as “Chinese.” This contrasts with the textual sources of 
the Dahei tianshen daochang yi and two food-distribution texts from Fazang si.
Vairocana matches the image of Vairocana in frame 84 of the Fanxiang juan. See Luo Zhao 
2003, 365.

424
Bryson
	
Conclusions
Despite Mahākāla’s relative obscurity in Tang-Song Buddhism, Dali-kingdom 
Buddhists seem to have adopted at least their main textual sources for his wor-
ship from China. Their choice of Chinese materials rather than Tibetan stems 
from the longer presence of Chinese officials and settlers in central Yunnan, 
and the closer interactions between Tang and Nanzhao. While some Buddhists 
in the Dali kingdom were proficient in Sanskrit, there are no records of Tibetan 
documents in the area from this period.
Dali-kingdom Buddhists adopted from their Nanzhao predecessors a tradi-
tion of esoteric Buddhism that was intimately connected to royal power. 
Mahākāla’s inclusion in the royally sponsored Fanxiang juan, the presence of 
his ritual texts at the family temple of the Dali kingdom’s national preceptors, 
and his multiple images at carving sites sponsored by Dali-kingdom elites 
shows that his worship fit into the esoteric Buddhism of the Dali court. He was 
a powerful guardian who could offer special protection to the Dali kingdom.
The Indian appearance of Dali-kingdom Mahākāla statues could be a coin-
cidence: Indian monks or other travelers may have brought Indian Mahākāla 
statues to Dali, where people saw them as the god’s true form. However, it 
seems likely that artists, monks, or ritual masters in the Dali kingdom would 
have encountered alternative iconographies in texts or images. I believe that 
Mahākāla’s Indian image plays the same role in Dali-kingdom Buddhism that 
Acuoye Guanyin’s Indian image played for Nanzhao and Dali rulers. That is, 
regardless of how the iconography entered Dali, the deities looked Indian, and 
thereby conferred authenticity upon Dali Buddhism. For rulers of the Dali 
kingdom, who were primarily focused on Song China among their various 
neighbors, Mahākāla could offer his special protection precisely because he 
was not popular in the Song: his loyalties were not divided.
Mahākāla’s worship in the Dali kingdom demonstrates how historical and 
political factors shaped esoteric Buddhist networks; geography alone did not 
determine how texts and images traveled from region to region. The Western 
Xia and Dali kingdoms both occupied areas between the Song dynasty and 
Tibet, but their respective Mahākāla cults show how their rulers drew selec-
tively from different Buddhist traditions. In this, they are the norm rather 
than the exception. The hybridity assumed for so-called border kingdoms like 
Dali also applies to their “central” counterparts. Paying attention to esoteric 
Buddhism in border kingdoms not only treats places like Dali as central, it 
also decentralizes Tibet and China and allows their hybrid, fragmented, and 
regional traditions to emerge.
